modules.title: What investing and trading mean
modules.subtitle: Start with goals, time horizons, and uncertainty
modules.objective: Distinguish saving, investing, and trading; calculate a simple return and explain why a profit is uncertain.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Think of money as having a job to do. Some money may be needed for an upcoming expense; other money may be available for a goal years away. Saving, investing, and trading describe different ways of using that money. Before comparing returns, understand the purpose and the uncertainty involved. The example below starts with a simple change in value so you can learn how to describe a result clearly.

## The idea

Saving sets money aside for future use. Investing commits capital to an asset with an uncertain future payoff. Trading buys and sells assets in an attempt to benefit from price changes. Their boundaries overlap: an investor still trades when entering or leaving a position. The useful distinction is the purpose, holding period, and evidence behind the decision.

A long-term investor might study a business's ability to generate cash over years. A short-term trader might study an order imbalance over minutes. Neither time horizon guarantees success. Start by asking: **What am I buying, why might it pay me, when might I need the money, and how could I lose it?**

## A worked example

Maya spends $200 on a fictional investment and later receives $220 when she sells it. Ignoring costs and distributions, the gain is $20 and the return is $20 / $200 = 10%. If the sale brings $170 instead, the return is −15%. A hoped-for 10% return is an expectation, not money already earned.

$$R = \frac{\text{ending value} - \text{starting value}}{\text{starting value}}$$

Always state the time period. A 10% return over one month and a 10% return over five years are different outcomes. Compare investments over matching periods and account for costs before deciding which performed better.

### Follow the calculation

Start with the amount Maya put in: $200. That is the starting value and the number we use as the comparison point. If she sells for $220, subtract the starting value to find the gain: $220 − $200 = $20. The gain tells us how many dollars she made, but it does not yet tell us how large the gain was relative to the investment.

To find the return, divide the $20 gain by the $200 she invested. The answer is 0.10. Multiplying by 100 converts that decimal into 10%. In words, Maya gained 10 cents for every dollar she invested during this period.

Now follow the loss case in the same order. Selling for $170 gives a change of $170 − $200 = −$30. Dividing −$30 by $200 gives −0.15, or −15%. The negative sign tells us that she lost money. Notice that we still divide by the original $200, because we are measuring the result relative to the money she committed.

These examples deliberately leave out fees and dividends so you can learn the basic calculation first. Later lessons add those cash movements. For now, practise explaining both the dollar result and the percentage result, and always state the period over which they occurred.

## Build a decision before a position

Write a goal, a time horizon, a reason for the investment, and a condition that would invalidate that reason. Money needed soon has less time to recover from a fall. A promise of high returns with no risk is a reason to investigate the claim, not a substitute for evidence.

For this course, use hypothetical money. No brokerage account or coding experience is needed. Reading, arithmetic, and explaining your choices are enough. The optional Python example lets you change the numbers; its separate synthetic trading rule is not a recommended strategy.

## Connect to later courses

Graham & Dodd develops the distinction between price and estimated value. Statistical foundations teaches how to express uncertainty instead of treating a successful outcome as proof of skill.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Research on real brokerage accounts puts numbers on the difference between investing and trading. Barber and Odean followed 66,465 U.S. households at a large discount broker from 1991 to 1996. The households that traded most earned 11.4% a year while the market returned 17.9%. The average household turned over about 75% of its portfolio each year, and the authors suggest that overconfidence can explain both the heavy trading and the poor results. Every round trip pays a spread and often a commission, so an active decision has to earn those costs back before it earns anything.

Very short horizons make the arithmetic harder still. Chague, De-Losso and Giovannetti observed everyone who began day trading Brazilian equity futures between 2013 and 2015 and kept going for at least 300 days. Of those persistent traders, 97% lost money and only 0.4% earned more per day than a bank teller's starting pay; the authors found no evidence that traders improved with practice. Attention shapes short-term activity too. In a high-frequency study of Robinhood users, Ardia, Aymard and Cenesizoglu found that users favoured stocks with extreme negative moves and often bought within an hour, which looks more like a reaction to salient prices than a researched plan.

These samples come from particular markets, periods and account types, so they do not prove that every active decision is a mistake. They do explain why this course asks for a purpose, a horizon and evidence before a position. Before a practice trade, estimate its round-trip cost as a percentage of the amount invested and compare it with the move you expect. If a $200 position pays $2 in total costs, it must gain 1% just to break even, and a one-month result will rarely be long enough to tell skill from luck.

### Sources for this section

- [Barber & Odean (2000) · Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00226) — *Research paper.* Household-level evidence that the most active traders earned far less than the market over 1991–1996.
- [Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti (2019) · Day Trading for a Living?](https://ideas.repec.org/p/spa/wpaper/2019wpecon47.html) — *Research paper.* Complete population of persistent Brazilian futures day traders; nearly all lost money and none showed learning.
- [Ardia, Aymard & Cenesizoglu (2023) · Fast and Furious: A High-Frequency Analysis of Robinhood Users' Trading Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11012) — *arXiv 2307.11012.* Hourly data showing retail app users reacting within an hour to extreme price drops.

modules.title: Stocks, shares, and business ownership
modules.subtitle: Understand what a stockholder actually owns
modules.objective: Explain equity ownership, market capitalization, dividends, and why share price alone does not measure value.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Imagine dividing ownership of a business into many small pieces. A share is one of those pieces. The number of pieces you own and the total number that exist determine your ownership fraction. The price of one piece is a separate question. Keeping ownership, share price, and total company value apart will make the calculations in this lesson much easier to follow.

## The idea

A share of stock is an ownership interest in a company. Common equity is a residual claim: creditors and other senior claims come first. Owners can benefit from price appreciation and dividends, but dividends are not automatic and shareholders can lose their investment. Voting rights depend on the share class.

Separate three quantities: **share price** is the market price of one share; **shares outstanding** is the number issued and held; **market capitalization** is their product. Market capitalization describes the market value of equity, not the company's cash balance or an independent estimate of what the business is worth.

## A worked example

Fictional Harbor Foods has 1,000,000 shares outstanding at $20 each. Its equity market capitalization is $20 million. Owning 100 shares means owning 100 / 1,000,000 = 0.01% of that share class, worth $2,000 at the quote. A declared $0.50 dividend per share would pay $50 on those 100 shares before taxes.

$$\text{Market capitalization} = \text{price per share}\times\text{shares outstanding}$$

Another company has 100 million shares trading at $2, so its market capitalization is $200 million. Its lower share price does not make the entire business cheaper than Harbor Foods.

### Separate the three questions

**What is the whole share class worth at the quoted price?** Multiply all 1,000,000 shares by $20. That gives the $20 million market capitalization. This is the market's total quoted value of those shares. It does not mean the company has $20 million sitting in its bank account.

**What fraction does the investor own?** Divide the investor's 100 shares by the 1,000,000 shares outstanding. The fraction is 0.0001, which is 0.01% after multiplying by 100. Owning a small fraction of the shares is different from owning a particular factory or being able to withdraw the company's cash.

**What is the investor's holding worth?** Multiply 100 shares by the $20 quote to get $2,000. If the declared dividend is $0.50 per share, multiply that amount by the same 100 shares to get $50 before taxes. The share price and the dividend answer different questions: one values the holding at a quote; the other describes a cash distribution.

Finally, compare the second company. Its $2 share price looks smaller, but there are 100 million shares. Multiplying them gives a $200 million market capitalization. You must consider both price and share count before comparing the market values of businesses.

## Splits and dilution

In a two-for-one stock split, 100 shares become 200; a theoretical $20 price becomes $10. The split itself leaves the $2,000 position value and ownership fraction unchanged. Real market prices may also move that day. A new share issuance is different: if your share count stays fixed while total shares increase, your ownership percentage falls. The company may receive new capital in exchange.

A dividend is a distribution of company resources, not free additional wealth. All else equal, distributing cash reduces the company's value. Later return calculations include both price changes and cash distributions.

## Connect to later courses

Security analysis uses diluted shares and the priority of claims to calculate per-share value. Keep the denominator and the company-wide amounts consistent.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's warning that a dividend is not free wealth has a formal version. Miller and Modigliani showed in 1961 that, in an idealized market without taxes, trading costs or information differences, dividend policy does not change what shares are worth. Cash paid out today lowers the value of the remaining claim by the same amount, and an investor who wanted cash could create a "homemade dividend" by selling a few shares. Real markets add taxes, costs and signals, which is why payout policy is still studied, but the benchmark explains why a share price normally falls when it starts trading without the right to a declared dividend.

Stock splits are a clean test of price versus value, because a split changes the share count and the per-share price without changing the business. Ikenberry, Rankine and Stice studied 1,275 two-for-one splits and reported a 3.38% return around the announcement followed by excess returns of 7.93% in the first year. Their interpretation is that managers choose to split when they expect good performance, so the decision carries information even though the arithmetic carries none. Byun and Rozeff later examined 12,747 splits from 1927 to 1996 with different benchmark methods. Splits of 25% or more showed no long-run performance significantly different from zero, and the authors concluded that the evidence against market efficiency is neither pervasive nor compelling.

Two habits follow. First, keep the arithmetic and the signal apart: a split does not create value, but the choice to split may reveal what managers believe. Second, treat a published pattern as provisional until you know how it was measured, because another team with a different sample or benchmark can reach the opposite conclusion. When you read that a stock "rose after its split", ask what it was compared with and over which period.

### Sources for this section

- [Miller & Modigliani (1961) · Dividend Policy, Growth, and the Valuation of Shares](https://doi.org/10.1086/294442) — *Research paper.* The benchmark result that, without frictions, payout policy does not change shareholder value.
- [Ikenberry, Rankine & Stice (1996) · What Do Stock Splits Really Signal?](https://doi.org/10.2307/2331396) — *Research paper.* Finds positive announcement and post-split excess returns and interprets splits as a management signal.
- [Byun & Rozeff (2003) · Long-run Performance after Stock Splits: 1927 to 1996](https://doi.org/10.1111/1540-6261.00558) — *Research paper.* A 70-year sample in which long-run post-split abnormal performance largely disappears under careful benchmarks.

modules.title: How stock markets work
modules.subtitle: Meet issuers, investors, brokers, exchanges, and indexes
modules.objective: Trace a stock transaction and distinguish the primary market, secondary market, an index, and an ETF.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A stock-market trade involves several people and several stages. The company originally issues shares, but later investors can trade those shares with each other. Your broker helps you submit an order, a trading venue helps match buyers and sellers, and settlement completes the transfer. Follow where the money goes in the example before trying to remember the names of the different institutions.

## The idea

In a primary-market offering, a company issues new securities to raise money. In the secondary market, existing securities change hands between investors. When you buy already-issued shares from another investor, your payment generally goes to that seller, not to the company.

A broker receives and routes your order. An exchange or other trading venue brings together buying and selling interest. Market makers quote prices at which they are willing to trade, subject to available size. Clearing and settlement handle the obligations after execution. A submitted order, a filled trade, and completed settlement are different stages.

Hours, settlement schedules, lot sizes, currencies, and account rules vary by market and broker. A lesson using dollar amounts does not imply those conventions apply to every exchange.

## A worked example

Harbor Foods issues 100,000 new shares at $20, raising $2 million before offering costs. Later, Maya buys 50 existing shares from Leo for $21 each through a broker. The $1,050 secondary-market payment goes to the selling side; Harbor Foods does not receive another $1,050 in capital from that trade.

### Follow the money through each trade

In the first transaction, Harbor Foods creates new shares and sells them to raise money. Multiply 100,000 shares by $20 to get $2 million before offering costs. The company receives that money because it is the issuer selling the new shares. This is the primary-market stage.

In the second transaction, the shares already exist. Maya is buying 50 of Leo's shares, so multiply 50 by $21 to get $1,050. Leo is the seller in this transaction. The payment goes to the selling side, while ownership of the shares passes to Maya through the trading and settlement process. Harbor Foods does not issue additional shares or raise additional capital through this particular trade.

The distinction explains why a company can have an actively traded stock without receiving the proceeds of every market purchase. Investors are changing who owns the existing shares. The company can still benefit or suffer from changes in market conditions, but that is a different question from who receives the payment in this example.

When reading the table, translate “claim” into “what the holder is entitled to.” A stock represents an ownership interest. A bond represents contractual obligations owed to a lender. A fund share represents an interest in the fund's portfolio. Start with that relationship before comparing the possible returns.

## Indexes, funds, and asset classes

An index is a rules-based measure of a basket of assets. An ETF is a fund whose shares trade on a market; it may seek to track an index, pursue an active strategy, or hold a narrow exposure. You buy fund shares, not the abstract index number. Fees and tracking differences can separate fund returns from index returns.

| Instrument | Basic economic claim | A question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stock | Business ownership | Can the business create durable value? |
| Bond | A debt claim with contractual terms | Can the issuer meet its obligations? |
| Fund / ETF | An interest in a pooled portfolio | What does it hold, and what does it cost? |
| Derivative | A contract tied to an underlying variable | What payoff and obligations does the contract create? |

Owning several funds does not necessarily create different exposures: their largest holdings may overlap. Likewise, an index moving up does not mean every constituent rose.

## Connect to later courses

Factor models use benchmarks; portfolio courses examine the exposures inside funds; execution courses distinguish an order's intent from what actually fills.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Most modern stock trading happens in a limit order book: a continuously updated list of buy and sell orders at different prices. Incoming orders are usually matched by price first and then by arrival time. The survey by Gould and co-authors notes that limit order books match buyers and sellers in more than half of the world's financial markets, and it summarizes statistical regularities that appear across many of them. The same review stresses that many simple models of order books fail to reproduce what real books do, a reminder that "the market" is a mechanism with rules rather than an abstract price.

After a match comes settlement, when cash and securities actually change hands. The SEC shortened the standard U.S. settlement cycle for most broker-dealer transactions from two business days after the trade date (T+2) to one (T+1), with compliance from 28 May 2024. The trade date and the settlement date are therefore different events. Other markets set their own cycles and account rules, so check the rulebook of the exchange you study rather than assuming the U.S. convention applies.

Funds add one more layer. An ETF's market price is kept close to the value of its holdings because large dealers can create or redeem fund shares in exchange for the underlying securities and profit from any gap. Ben-David, Franzoni and Moussawi found that this arbitrage also works in reverse: stocks with more ETF ownership showed higher intraday and daily volatility, and a one-standard-deviation increase in ETF ownership was associated with about 16% higher daily volatility in their sample. A fund is a claim on a basket, but trading in the fund can also move the basket.

When you trace a trade, name four stages: the order, the match, clearing and settlement. For each stage, write down which institution is responsible and what could delay or reverse it.

### Sources for this section

- [Gould et al. (2010) · Limit Order Books](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.0349) — *arXiv 1012.0349.* Survey of how limit order books work, what empirical studies find, and where popular models fall short.
- [U.S. SEC · Investor.gov (2024) · New T+1 Settlement Cycle: What Investors Need To Know](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/new-t1-settlement-cycle-what-investors-need-know-investor-bulletin) — *Official source.* Explains settlement and the U.S. move from T+2 to T+1 on 28 May 2024.
- [Ben-David, Franzoni & Moussawi (2018) · Do ETFs Increase Volatility?](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12727) — *Research paper.* Evidence that ETF arbitrage transmits trading into the underlying stocks and raises their volatility.

modules.title: Prices, quotes, and order types
modules.subtitle: Read a quote and understand the trade-off between price and execution
modules.objective: Calculate a spread, interpret OHLCV, and choose between market, limit, stop, and stop-limit orders in a hypothetical scenario.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

The price shown on a stock chart is usually the price of an earlier trade. It is useful information, but it is not a promise that you can buy or sell at that price now. To understand the choice in front of you, look at the current buyers, sellers, quantities, and the instructions attached to your order. This lesson connects those details to the price you might actually receive.

## The idea

The **bid** is a quoted buying price and the **ask** a quoted selling price. Their difference is the spread. The last traded price is a past transaction, so it is not a promise of your next fill. Available quantity matters: a large order can consume several price levels.

OHLCV records the open, high, low, close, and traded volume for a period. A candle summarizes that period; it does not reveal the sequence of every trade. Volume is shares traded, not the number of distinct people buying.

## A worked example

A fictional quote shows bid $49.90 for 100 shares and ask $50.10 for 80 shares. The spread is $0.20. A small market buy may execute near $50.10; a market sell may execute near $49.90. An immediate buy and sell of 10 shares at those prices loses $2 before fees, even if the quotes do not change. A request for 200 shares cannot assume all 200 are available at the displayed ask.

$$\text{Spread}=\text{ask}-\text{bid}$$

### Read the quote from each side

The bid of $49.90 is the displayed price on the buying side. The ask of $50.10 is the displayed price on the selling side. If you want to buy immediately, you are trying to trade with a seller, so the ask is the relevant starting point. If you want to sell immediately, you are trying to trade with a buyer, so start with the bid.

Subtract the bid from the ask: $50.10 − $49.90 = $0.20 per share. In the unchanged-quote example, buying 10 shares costs $501 and immediately selling them brings $499. The $2 difference comes from buying at the ask and selling at the bid in this unchanged-quote example. It is the same as 10 × $0.20; do not subtract a second spread charge from those already-used fill prices.

Quantity matters too. The displayed ask covers 80 shares, while the proposed order asks for 200. The quote tells us about those 80 shares, so it cannot establish the price for the remaining 120. Other sellers, updated quotes, and the order instruction determine what happens next.

A limit order makes the acceptable price explicit. It can protect that price condition, but it cannot guarantee that a willing counterparty will appear. Keep the price condition and the chance of execution separate.

## Translate an intention into an order

| Order | Instruction | Main trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market | Trade at available prices | Execution price is uncertain |
| Buy limit | Buy at the limit or lower | May fill partly or not at all |
| Sell limit | Sell at the limit or higher | May fill partly or not at all |
| Stop | Activate a market order when triggered | A gap can produce a worse fill than the stop |
| Stop-limit | Activate a limit order when triggered | The limit can prevent an exit |

For a buy limit of $50 with the best ask at $50.10, the instruction does not permit a $50.10 fill. If the market falls to $50, a fill still depends on available quantity and priority. Trigger conventions differ by venue and broker.

## Connect to later courses

The paper-trading lab demonstrates some order mechanics using hypothetical accounts. Strategy backtests use next-open fills and configurable costs. Neither a candle touching a price nor a stop instruction guarantees a fill at that price.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-14). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Why is there a spread at all? Market-microstructure research gives three broad reasons: the cost of processing orders, the risk of holding inventory, and adverse selection. Glosten and Milgrom's model isolates the third. A market maker who cannot tell an informed trader from an uninformed one expects to lose to the informed side, so even a competitive market maker earning zero profit on average sets the ask above the bid to recover those losses from everyone else. The model predicts wider spreads when informed trading is more likely, such as just before important news.

The quoted spread only prices a small order. Larger orders consume depth, and a large body of empirical work finds that price impact grows much more slowly than order size. Tóth and co-authors explain the widely reported square-root law: the average impact of a large order executed in pieces scales roughly with the square root of its size relative to traded volume,

$$
\Delta P \approx Y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{daily}}\sqrt{Q/V_{\mathrm{daily}}}
$$

where Q is the order quantity, V is daily volume, σ is daily volatility and Y is a constant of order one. Quadrupling an order roughly doubles its expected impact per share. The relation is an average across many orders, not a quote you can rely on for a single trade.

Market orders that are large relative to the available depth can also produce abrupt moves. Braun and co-authors studied ultrafast extreme events, in which prices jump within milliseconds. Large market orders were the main cause in at least 60% of the events they observed, and fewer than 40% of the moves fully recovered over the following 100 trades. A stop order that turns into a market order during such an episode can fill far from its trigger.

Before submitting a practice order, compare its size with the displayed size and with typical daily volume. When the price condition matters more than immediacy, a limit instruction states that priority explicitly.

### Sources for this section

- [Glosten & Milgrom (1985) · Bid, Ask and Transaction Prices in a Specialist Market with Heterogeneously Informed Traders](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X%2885%2990044-3) — *Research paper.* The classic adverse-selection model in which a bid-ask spread exists even without order-processing costs.
- [Tóth et al. (2011) · Anomalous price impact and the critical nature of liquidity in financial markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.1694) — *arXiv 1105.1694.* A theory of thin liquidity near the price that accounts for square-root impact, with supporting data.
- [Braun et al. (2017) · Impact and Recovery Process of Mini Flash Crashes: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.05580) — *arXiv 1707.05580.* Shows that most millisecond-scale price crashes follow large market orders and often do not fully reverse.

modules.title: Returns, compounding, and trading costs
modules.subtitle: Measure what you keep, over the time you hold
modules.objective: Calculate profit after fees, total return with dividends, and compounded returns; distinguish realized from unrealized gains.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A higher selling price is only the beginning of a return calculation. Money can also leave the account through fees or enter it through dividends. Write down every cash movement before calculating a percentage. Then ask how long the investment lasted. This approach helps you compare outcomes without confusing a price increase with the amount you actually kept.

## The idea

Profit in money and return in percent answer different questions. Include the purchase cost, sale proceeds, distributions, and fees. An unrealized gain is a change in the marked value of an open position. A realized gain results from closing it. Both affect your economic wealth, and an unrealized gain can disappear before a sale.

## A worked example

Buy 10 shares at $100 and pay a $2 entry fee: the cash outlay is $1,002. Receive $10 of dividends in total. Sell all 10 shares at $110 and pay a $2 exit fee: sale proceeds are $1,098. The net gain is $1,098 + $10 − $1,002 = $106. The return on the initial cash outlay is $106 / $1,002, approximately 10.58%, before taxes.

$$R_{\text{net}}=\frac{\text{net sale proceeds}+\text{distributions}-\text{initial outlay}}{\text{initial outlay}}$$

Zero commission does not mean zero trading cost. Spreads, slippage, fund expenses, financing, and applicable taxes can affect the outcome. Avoid double counting a spread already embedded in the actual fill prices.

### Build the return from cash movements

It helps to draw two columns: money paid out and money received. At entry, the shares cost 10 × $100 = $1,000 and the fee costs $2. The total paid out is therefore $1,002. This is the initial outlay used in the denominator.

At exit, selling 10 shares for $110 produces $1,100 before the exit fee. Subtract the $2 fee to obtain $1,098 of net sale proceeds. The investor also received $10 in dividends during the holding period. Total money received is therefore $1,098 + $10 = $1,108.

Subtract the original $1,002 from $1,108 to find the $106 net gain. Dividing $106 by $1,002 gives approximately 0.1058, or 10.58%. A calculation based only on the move from $100 to $110 would describe the share-price return and leave out the dividends and fees included here.

Once you can account for one holding period, move to a sequence of periods. The ending balance from the first period becomes the starting balance for the next. This is the key to compounding: each percentage change applies to an updated amount. The next example shows why adding the period returns can produce the wrong answer.

## Returns multiply through time

A $100 position gains 10%, reaching $110, then loses 10%, reaching $99. The combined return is −1%, although the arithmetic average of the two period returns is zero.

$$R_{\text{combined}}=(1+r_1)(1+r_2)-1$$

A decline from $100 to $80 is a 20% loss. Recovering from $80 to $100 requires a 25% gain because the new denominator is smaller. A basis point is 0.01 percentage points: 10 basis points equals 0.10%, or 0.001 as a decimal multiplier. A 10 bp fee on $1,000 is $1.

## Connect to later courses

Statistical foundations develops discounting and annualization. Backtests later separate the strategy return from the benchmark and charge costs at execution. Keep the time period, units, and cash-flow assumptions visible in every comparison.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's example of a 10% gain followed by a 10% loss is a small case of a general rule: volatility lowers compound growth. If a return series has an arithmetic mean μ and a volatility σ per period, its compound (geometric) growth rate is approximately

$$
g \approx \mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}
$$

so two assets with the same average return can grow at very different rates. A position that gains 50% and then loses 50% has an arithmetic average of zero but ends 25% lower. Ole Peters describes this as the difference between an ensemble average, taken across many parallel investors, and a time average, experienced by one investor through time. For multiplicative wealth, the time average is the one you live through. It also sets a sensible limit on leverage: beyond some point, extra exposure raises the expected return while lowering the growth rate an individual actually experiences.

Compounding also skews long-horizon results. Bessembinder studied the common stocks in the main U.S. research database since 1926 and found that most had lifetime buy-and-hold returns below one-month Treasury bills. The best-performing 4% of companies accounted for the entire net wealth the market created over Treasury bills. One implication for a beginner is that a portfolio of a few stocks can easily miss the rare, very large winners that drive the market's average.

Costs compound in the same way. The SEC's investor bulletin illustrates a $100,000 portfolio growing 4% a year for 20 years: with a 0.25% annual fee it ends near $208,000, with 0.50% near $198,000, and with 1.00% near $179,000. A fee that looks small in one year removes a growing base of future returns.

When you study any return series, report both its arithmetic mean and its compound growth rate. Report fees both as an annual rate and as a total over your horizon.

### Sources for this section

- [Peters (2009) · Optimal leverage from non-ergodicity](https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.2965) — *arXiv 0902.2965.* Distinguishes time-average from ensemble-average growth and derives an optimal leverage from the former.
- [Bessembinder (2018) · Do stocks outperform Treasury bills?](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2018.06.004) — *Research paper.* Lifetime returns of U.S. common stocks since 1926: most trailed Treasury bills while a few created the market's net gains.
- [U.S. SEC · Investor.gov · How Fees and Expenses Affect Your Investment Portfolio](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/updated) — *Official source.* Worked illustration of how annual fees of 0.25%, 0.50% and 1% compound over 20 years.

modules.title: Reading a business before buying its stock
modules.subtitle: Connect financial statements, earnings, cash, and valuation
modules.objective: Identify the three main financial statements, calculate EPS and P/E, and distinguish a low price from evidence of value.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Before buying part of a business, try to describe how it earns money. Who pays it, what does it spend, and when does the cash arrive? Financial statements organize those questions in different ways. This lesson introduces a few useful numbers, then shows why you need to read them together. A single ratio is a starting point for a question, rather than a complete judgment about the business.

## The idea

The income statement describes revenues, expenses, and profit over a period. The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity at a date. The cash-flow statement explains movements in cash from operating, investing, and financing activities. Profit and cash flow differ because recognition and payment need not happen together.

A sale on credit can increase revenue and receivables before cash arrives. Borrowing increases cash and debt without creating sales profit. Buying equipment uses cash immediately, while its accounting expense can be spread over years. Ask what caused each change before declaring the business stronger.

## A worked example

Fictional Cedar Tools reports $12 million revenue, $2 million net income available to common shareholders, and 1 million weighted-average diluted shares. Earnings per share (EPS) is $2. At a $30 share price, the price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) is 15. Its balance sheet shows $15 million assets and $9 million liabilities, leaving $6 million book equity.

$$\mathrm{EPS}=\frac{\text{net income available to common}}{\text{weighted-average diluted shares}},\qquad P/E=\frac{P}{\mathrm{EPS}}$$

Suppose operating cash flow is only $0.4 million because customers have not yet paid. That does not prove fraud, but it raises a useful question about collections and working capital. A second company with a P/E of 8 may be cheaper relative to reported earnings, or those earnings may be about to decline. The multiple alone cannot decide.

### Connect each number to the business

Revenue is the amount Cedar Tools records from sales. Net income is what remains in the stated accounting result after the relevant expenses. The two numbers describe different stages, so use the $2 million net income—not the $12 million revenue—when calculating earnings per share in this case.

Divide $2 million by 1 million weighted-average diluted shares to get $2 of earnings per share. The share-count measure accounts for the period and the dilution included in the example. At a price of $30, dividing $30 by $2 gives a P/E of 15. In ordinary language, the quoted price is 15 times this measure of annual earnings per share.

The balance sheet answers another question. Subtract $9 million of liabilities from $15 million of assets to get $6 million of book equity. Book equity is an accounting remainder. It does not automatically equal the price someone would pay for the company or the cash available for distribution.

Now compare the $2 million profit with only $0.4 million of operating cash flow. Sales may have been recorded before customers paid. The useful next step is to investigate the money owed by customers and the timing of collection. This is why you read profit, cash flow, and the balance sheet together.

## Price, value, and available evidence

Price is a current quote. Value is an estimate based on future cash flows, assets, and risk. Book equity is an accounting residual, not a guaranteed sale value. Compare several periods, examine debt and one-time items, and read the company's published reports.

When simulating a past decision, use only information available at that time. A December reporting period does not make a report released in March available in December. Treat a promotional post as a lead to verify, not as a financial statement.

## Connect to later courses

These distinctions prepare you for normalized earnings, net-current-asset value, senior claims, and margin of safety in Track 01.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks/evaluating-stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The Cedar Tools example, with $2 million of profit but only $0.4 million of operating cash flow, touches one of the best-documented findings in accounting research. Earnings can be split into a cash component and an accrual component. Accruals are the part of profit recognized before, or without, the matching cash, such as a sale on credit. Sloan examined 40,679 firm-years from 1962 to 1991 and found that the accrual part of earnings persists less into future earnings than the cash part. Stock prices, however, behaved as if investors fixated on total earnings and did not fully distinguish the two components.

A simple accrual measure scales the gap by the size of the business:

$$
\text{Accruals ratio}=\frac{\text{net income}-\text{operating cash flow}}{\text{average total assets}}
$$

A high value is a question, not a verdict, because fast-growing firms build receivables and inventory for legitimate reasons. Dechow, Ge and Schrand reviewed the many measures researchers use for earnings quality, including persistence, accruals, smoothness, timeliness, restatements and enforcement actions. They reach no single definition, because quality depends on the decision the numbers are meant to inform.

Statements can also be combined into simple scores. Piotroski built a nine-signal score from profitability, cash flow, changes in leverage and liquidity, and operating efficiency, and applied it to cheap, high book-to-market stocks. In his 1976–1996 sample, choosing the financially strong firms raised the average return of such a portfolio by at least 7.5% a year. Whether a signal keeps working after it is published and after trading costs is a separate question, examined in the strategy courses.

For Cedar Tools, use the $15 million of total assets as a stand-in for the average: the accruals ratio is ($2 million − $0.4 million) / $15 million, about 10.7%. Then compare receivables growth with revenue growth, and name the later document, such as the next cash-flow statement, that would show whether collections recovered.

### Sources for this section

- [Sloan (1996) · Do Stock Prices Fully Reflect Information in Accruals and Cash Flows about Future Earnings?](https://doi.org/10.2308/tar-9608042309) — *Research paper.* The original accrual study: cash earnings persist more than accruals, and prices do not fully reflect the difference.
- [Dechow, Ge & Schrand (2010) · Understanding earnings quality: A review of the proxies, their determinants and their consequences](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacceco.2010.09.001) — *Research paper.* A broad review explaining why no single number captures earnings quality for every decision.
- [Piotroski (2000) · Value Investing: The Use of Historical Financial Statement Information to Separate Winners from Losers](https://doi.org/10.2307/2672906) — *Research paper.* A nine-signal financial-statement score that separated stronger from weaker cheap stocks in 1976–1996.

modules.title: Risk, diversification, and position sizing
modules.subtitle: Understand what can go wrong before choosing a quantity
modules.objective: Distinguish company and market risk; calculate a hypothetical position size and explain why stops do not cap every loss.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Risk is about the ways an outcome can differ from your plan, including losses you cannot comfortably absorb. Position sizing asks how much money to commit to one idea. Diversification asks how the different ideas in a portfolio can fail together. Start with a concrete loss scenario, calculate its effect on the account, and then examine what happens if the scenario is worse than expected.

## The idea

Company risk comes from a particular issuer, such as a failed product. Market risk can affect many investments together, such as a broad repricing of discount rates. Diversification spreads exposure, but correlated holdings can decline at the same time. Ten companies in one narrow industry may share much of the same risk.

Volatility describes variability in returns. Drawdown measures the decline from a previous portfolio peak. Neither alone captures every risk: an illiquid asset can have infrequent price changes and still be hard to sell. Consider liquidity, debt, concentration, and the ability to tolerate losses.

## A worked example

In a paper account with $10,000, a hypothetical plan allocates $100 to the loss between a $50 entry and a $48 exit trigger. Planned risk per share is $2. Dividing $100 by $2 gives 50 shares, a $2,500 position. The $100 budget is 1% of this example account; it is an illustration, not a universal sizing recommendation.

$$q=\left\lfloor\frac{\text{planned risk budget}}{\text{entry price}-\text{planned exit price}}\right\rfloor$$

If a gap leads to an actual $45 exit, the loss is $250 before costs, not $100. Fees and slippage also change the result. The calculation describes a planned scenario, not a maximum loss guarantee. Check the cash required as well as the planned risk; a cash account must be able to fund the purchase.

### Distinguish the position from the planned loss

The $100 in the example is a budget for one stated loss scenario. It is not the amount being spent on shares. The assumed difference between the entry and exit is $50 − $48 = $2 per share. Dividing the $100 scenario budget by $2 gives 50 shares.

Buying those 50 shares at $50 requires $2,500 before costs. That is 25% of the $10,000 paper account. Meanwhile, the planned $100 loss is 1% of the account. Both percentages can be correct because one measures the position's purchase value and the other measures a particular planned loss.

Now change the exit price to $45. The loss per share becomes $50 − $45 = $5. Across 50 shares, that is $250 before costs. The original sizing arithmetic has not stopped working; its assumed exit price did not occur. This is the reason to examine a worse-fill scenario before deciding that a position is manageable.

Diversification asks a further question: what if several positions fall for the same reason? Holding many names helps less when they share the same underlying exposure. Consider how positions interact as well as how much is committed to each one.

## Borrowing and short selling

Margin uses borrowed money to increase exposure. If $1,000 of your money and $1,000 of borrowing buy $2,000 of stock, a 10% stock loss removes $200, or 20% of your initial equity, before financing costs. The debt still needs to be repaid. Short selling sells borrowed shares and requires buying them back; rising prices can create losses beyond the initial proceeds. Detailed rules vary by account and market.

## Connect to later courses

Portfolio construction measures co-movement. Risk management studies drawdowns and tail losses. Bot engineering turns exposure limits and stale-price checks into explicit controls.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

How many stocks make a portfolio diversified? The answer has changed over time. Campbell, Lettau, Malkiel and Xu split U.S. stock volatility into market, industry and firm-level parts. From 1962 to 1997, firm-level volatility rose relative to market volatility while correlations between individual stocks fell, so the number of stocks needed to reach a given level of diversification increased. A rule of thumb from an older sample can therefore understate the company risk left in a small portfolio.

Diversification also weakens when it is most needed. Longin and Solnik used extreme-value methods to show that correlation between international equity markets is related to the market trend rather than to volatility alone: it rises in bear markets but not in bull markets. Sandoval and Franca reached a similar picture from the correlations of world market indices around the crashes of 1987, 2001 and 2008, finding that markets tend to behave as one during large downturns. Risk estimated with calm-period correlations will overstate the protection a portfolio has in a crisis.

Stop rules have limits of their own. Kaminski and Lo derived the conditions under which stop-loss rules add or subtract value. They showed that if prices follow a random walk, a simple rule that moves entirely to cash after a loss threshold always lowers the strategy's expected return. Whether a stop helps depends on how returns actually behave, for example whether declines tend to persist, and on the details of the rule. A stop is a risk-control choice with a cost, not free insurance.

Apply this to the lesson's example. Size the position from the planned loss, then repeat the calculation twice: once with the $45 gap exit, and once assuming every position in your paper portfolio falls on the same day.

### Sources for this section

- [Campbell, Lettau, Malkiel & Xu (2001) · Have Individual Stocks Become More Volatile? An Empirical Exploration of Idiosyncratic Risk](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00318) — *Research paper.* Documents rising firm-level volatility and the growing number of stocks needed for diversification.
- [Longin & Solnik (2001) · Extreme Correlation of International Equity Markets](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00340) — *Research paper.* Shows that international correlations rise in bear markets rather than simply with volatility.
- [Sandoval & Franca (2011) · Correlation of financial markets in times of crisis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.1339) — *arXiv 1102.1339.* Correlation-matrix evidence that world markets move together during major crashes.
- [Kaminski & Lo (2014) · When do stop-loss rules stop losses?](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.finmar.2013.07.001) — *Research paper.* A framework for when stop-loss rules help or hurt, including their cost under a random walk.

modules.title: Build your first research and trading plan
modules.subtitle: Bring the fundamentals together and prepare for the advanced tracks
modules.objective: Write a testable paper-trading plan with an entry reason, order, sizing assumptions, exit conditions, costs, and review process.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

You now know the basic language of ownership, orders, returns, and risk. The next step is to connect those ideas in one written decision. A plan should be specific enough that you can review it later without relying on memory. Use a fictional trade to practise: explain what you expect, how you would act, what could prove you wrong, and when you will review the evidence.

## The idea

A plan makes a decision reviewable. Write it before observing the outcome. Specify the asset and source, the reason to enter, the evidence that would invalidate the reason, the intended holding period, the order instruction, the quantity, and the expected costs. Record actual fills separately from your intention.

Avoid evaluating a plan only by whether the last trade made money. A disciplined decision can lose; a poorly supported decision can profit by chance. Keep the record of losing trials as well as winners. Compare a strategy against a relevant benchmark over the same period using the same cost conventions.

## A worked example

In a fictional $5,000 paper account, Ari studies Harbor Foods after a published report. The hypothesis is that collections will recover; the invalidating evidence is another deterioration in receivables and operating cash flow. Ari considers 10 shares using a $20 buy limit, reserving roughly $200 plus costs. If the ask stays above $20, the order can remain unfilled.

The plan records an illustrative $18 exit trigger, a $20 planned price loss for 10 shares, and a gap scenario: an actual $15 exit would lose $50 before costs. Ari schedules a review after the next public report. There is no guarantee that the thesis works, the order fills, or the exit matches the trigger.

### Turn the example into a reviewable decision

Ari's idea is that customers will pay more promptly, improving collections. That is the hypothesis: a claim about what may happen. To make it useful, write down what evidence would support it and what evidence would weaken it. Another deterioration in receivables and operating cash flow would challenge the reason for the trade.

The order is a separate instruction. Ten shares with a $20 buy limit require roughly $200 plus costs if they fill at that limit. If sellers keep asking more than $20, Ari may receive no shares. A convincing research idea does not change that order condition.

The exit plan is also conditional. Moving from $20 to $18 would lose $2 on each of 10 shares, or $20 before costs. An actual $15 exit would lose $5 per share, or $50. Writing both cases helps Ari see the difference between an intended action and the outcome the market may allow.

When you write your own fictional plan, use full sentences before abbreviating it into a checklist. Explain why the evidence matters, what action follows from it, and what would make you wait. A later review should compare the outcome with the reasons recorded before the trade.

## Your research note

Use **Add a note** to record your own fictional plan:

1. Asset, source, and information availability date.
2. Hypothesis, holding period, and evidence against it.
3. Entry instruction, quantity, cash required, and cost assumptions.
4. Planned exit, a worse-fill scenario, and concentration check.
5. Benchmark, review date, and the result you will record even if it fails.

Confirmation bias means favoring supporting evidence and overlooking contradictions. Chasing a recent gain without checking the thesis is another common error. Add an explicit reason to wait when the evidence or data is insufficient.

### Further reading

[Investor education reference](https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investment-products/stocks/evaluating-stocks). Examples in this lesson use fictional companies and simplified amounts.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A written plan protects you against two well-studied mistakes. The first is judging a decision by its outcome. Baron and Hershey gave people descriptions of decisions made under uncertainty and varied only the result. Participants rated the same decision as worse when it turned out badly, even though those who were asked said that outcomes should not affect the evaluation. Your review rules should therefore compare a trade with what the plan knew and intended at the time, not only with what happened next.

The second mistake is the disposition effect: selling winners too soon and holding losers too long. Odean analysed 10,000 accounts at a discount broker and found a strong preference for realizing gains rather than losses. The pattern was not explained by rebalancing or by the higher trading costs of low-priced stocks, it was not justified by the later performance of the stocks sold or kept, and in taxable accounts it lowered after-tax returns. Breitmayer, Hasso and Pelster later used brokerage records for 387,993 traders from 83 countries and found large differences in the strength of the effect between countries. Cultural traits such as long-term orientation, together with age and gender, helped explain those differences. Because the tendency varies from person to person, plan for it rather than assuming you are immune.

A plan turns both findings into procedure. Decide the exit conditions before entry, record the reason for closing each position, and review a sample of winning and losing trades against the reasons you wrote in advance. Ask whether you followed the plan, whether the information you used was available when you decided, and whether you would make the same decision again with the same information. Only the last question needs judgment; the first two can be checked from your records. Keeping the losing and abandoned plans in the same journal is what makes that check honest.

### Sources for this section

- [Baron & Hershey (1988) · Outcome bias in decision evaluation](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.54.4.569) — *Research paper.* Experiments showing that people rate identical decisions worse when the outcome is bad.
- [Odean (1998) · Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00072) — *Research paper.* Account-level evidence of the disposition effect and its after-tax cost.
- [Breitmayer, Hasso & Pelster (2019) · Culture and the disposition effect](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.11492) — *arXiv 1908.11492.* Brokerage data from 83 countries showing how the disposition effect varies with culture, age and gender.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Every trading decision is made on behalf of someone: yourself, a client, an employer, or a fund's investors. Ethics in trading begins by naming that person, because the same transaction can be proper for one principal and improper for another. A duty of loyalty means placing the principal's interest ahead of your own, and placing the client's interest ahead of the firm's where the two diverge. CFA Institute's Code of Ethics expresses this as acting for the benefit of clients and placing their interests before your own; Regulation Best Interest expresses a related obligation for broker-dealers making recommendations to retail customers.

The difficulty is rarely identifying a blatant theft. It is noticing the ordinary decision where your interest quietly enters: the fund you are paid more to sell, the trade that helps your quarter, the position you already hold. Loyalty is not a feeling; it is an ordering you can write down and check afterwards.

$$
\Delta\text{cost} = (f_B - f_A)\times V,\qquad \text{adviser benefit} = r\times V
$$

## A worked example

A fictional adviser can place a client in Fund A, which charges 0.20% a year and pays the adviser nothing, or Fund B, which charges 1.20% a year and pays the adviser 0.40%. On Rp500,000,000 invested, the annual cost difference is Rp5,000,000, and the adviser receives Rp2,000,000 only in the second case. Nothing about that arithmetic decides which fund suits the client, but it does identify exactly where the adviser's interest and the client's diverge, and it is the number the client is entitled to understand.

## Put the idea into practice

Name the principal before you name the trade. Write the decision as a sentence with a subject: *I am buying this for X, whose objective is Y.* When two principals conflict, record which one you ranked first and why.

### Do and do not

- **Do** state the principal and the objective in writing before you act.
- **Do** rank interests explicitly when they conflict, and keep the reasoning.
- **Do not** rely on a recommendation being defensible; check whether it is the one you would make if you were paid identically either way.
- **Do not** treat an undisclosed benefit to yourself as harmless because the client also did well.

### Add it to your charter

Write the rule you will actually follow, the observation that would tell you the rule was broken, and the person you would tell. A rule you cannot check is a preference, not a control. Record the decision and its reasons before the outcome is known; a profitable breach is still a breach, and a loss suffered while following your rules is not evidence that the rules were wrong.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's rule has a long legal ancestry. In SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, the U.S. Supreme Court read the Investment Advisers Act as showing a congressional intent to eliminate, or at least to expose, every conflict that might incline an adviser, consciously or unconsciously, to give advice that was not disinterested. It refused to make the SEC prove an intent to injure or an actual injury to clients, the legal counterpart of the lesson's point that a client doing well does not excuse an undisclosed benefit. Regulation Best Interest is the parallel rule for broker-dealers recommending to retail customers (registered advisers answer to the Advisers Act instead): act in the customer's best interest when recommending, without putting the firm's or representative's own interest ahead. The SEC's adopting release adds a limit that the lesson's arithmetic needs: cost must be considered but is not the only factor, and the standard does not necessarily require the lowest-cost option. A dearer Fund B is therefore not automatically a breach; what is tested is whether the payment was identified and kept from driving the choice.

Evidence on how payments reach advice is uncomfortable. In an audit, Mullainathan, Noeth and Schoar sent trained auditors to advisers carrying portfolios that either served or cut against the advisers' interests. The advisers failed to de-bias clients, often reinforced biases that suited them, and pushed actively managed, higher-fee funds even when the client began with a diversified, low-fee portfolio. Surveying retirement-account research, the White House Council of Economic Advisers estimated in 2015 that conflicted advice lowers returns by roughly 1 percentage point a year, about $17 billion annually, while saying its conclusions were subject to uncertainty.

The lesson's gap is also one percentage point: 1.20% against 0.20%, or Rp5 million a year on Rp500 million, with Rp2 million going to the adviser. That shows scale only: the Council's figure is a return shortfall, the lesson's a fee difference.

Exercise: restate any recommendation as if both products paid the adviser the same. If the case for the dearer one no longer stands, the payment was doing the work.

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. Supreme Court (1963) · Securities and Exchange Commission v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc.](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/375/180) — *Official source.* The leading adviser-fiduciary decision: conflicts must be eliminated or exposed, and the SEC need not prove intent to injure or actual injury.
- [U.S. SEC (2019) · Regulation Best Interest: The Broker-Dealer Standard of Conduct](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/07/12/2019-12164/regulation-best-interest-the-broker-dealer-standard-of-conduct) — *Official source.* Rule text and adopting release for the broker-dealer best-interest standard, including its statement that cost matters but is not dispositive.
- [Mullainathan, Noeth & Schoar (2012) · The Market for Financial Advice: An Audit Study](https://doi.org/10.3386/w17929) — *Research paper.* Audit study in which advisers reinforced biases that served their own interests and pushed higher-fee active funds.
- [Council of Economic Advisers (2015) · The Effects of Conflicted Investment Advice on Retirement Savings](https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/sites/default/files/docs/cea_coi_report_final.pdf) — *Official source.* Government literature review that puts a rough annual price on conflicted retirement advice and states its own uncertainty.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Disclosure converts a hidden conflict into an informed decision by someone else. Three questions decide it: what is the conflict, is it material, and when must the other party know. Materiality is not a fixed percentage. A useful working test is whether a reasonable person would want the fact in hand before deciding, and the standards ask you to disclose all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair independence or objectivity.

Timing is where disclosure usually fails. A conflict revealed after the trade cannot inform the decision it affected, and a disclosure buried in a document nobody reads is closer to concealment than to candour. Prominence, plainness and timing are part of the obligation, not presentation preferences. Company reporting works the same way: a filing's notes often carry the scope of an issue that a headline figure hides, which is why an analyst reads the notes.

$$
w = \frac{\text{holding}}{\text{personal portfolio}},\qquad \text{disclose if a reasonable reader would want }w
$$

## A worked example

A fictional research analyst holds shares in Pelita Manufaktur and is about to publish a positive note. The holding is Rp60,000,000 against personal investable assets of Rp400,000,000, so it is 15% of their portfolio. Whether that is material to the reader does not depend on it being large to the firm; it depends on whether a reader weighing the note would want to know the author owns the share. Disclosing it in the note's first screen informs the reader; disclosing it in an appendix published a week later does not.

## Put the idea into practice

Disclose before the action the disclosure is meant to inform, in the same document, in plain language.

### Do and do not

- **Do** apply the reasonable-person test to materiality rather than a private threshold.
- **Do** put the disclosure where the decision is made, not in a separate document.
- **Do not** use volume as camouflage; a page of boilerplate that hides one relevant fact fails the purpose.
- **Do not** disclose after the fact and call it transparency.

### Add it to your charter

Write the rule you will actually follow, the observation that would tell you the rule was broken, and the person you would tell. A rule you cannot check is a preference, not a control. Record the decision and its reasons before the outcome is known; a profitable breach is still a breach, and a loss suffered while following your rules is not evidence that the rules were wrong.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson says to disclose early and in plain view. The research shows why that is necessary but not sufficient. On the rule side, the SEC's order approving FINRA Rule 2241 describes what a research report must say when it is published: whether the analyst or a household member has a financial interest in the subject company's securities, including long or short positions and options, and the nature of that interest. For the analyst's own interest the description sets no size threshold, while a firm's holding is flagged at 1% of a class of common equity, and a catch-all covers any other material conflict. The lesson's Pelita holding, 15% of the author's portfolio, would therefore be disclosable whatever its size to the firm.

Psychology adds a warning. Cain, Loewenstein and Moore showed that people generally do not discount advice from a conflicted adviser enough even when the conflict is disclosed, and that disclosure can increase the bias because advisers feel morally licensed to exaggerate. Sah, Loewenstein and Cain reported six experiments in which disclosure also raised the pressure to comply, because advisees felt obliged to satisfy the adviser's personal interests. That pressure fell when the disclosure came from an external source rather than the adviser, when it was not common knowledge between the two, or when the advisee could change their mind later. Onuchic's theoretical model adds a design problem: mandated transparency about a seller's motives can discourage the seller from sharing, or even acquiring, information about the product's value.

These are laboratory and model results, not measurements of real research notes, so read them as cautions. An inference, not a finding, is that a disclosure line is a minimum: who delivers it, and whether the reader can still act differently afterwards, matter as much as where it sits.

Exercise: write the first sentence of a Pelita Manufaktur note so that it states the long position, its weight in the author's portfolio and the purchase date before any recommendation. Then add a pointer to a public source the reader can check without relying on you.

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. SEC (2015) · Order Approving a Proposed Rule Change, as Modified by Amendment No. 1 Thereto, To Adopt FINRA Rule 2241 (Research Analysts and Research Reports) in the Consolidated FINRA Rulebook](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2015/07/22/2015-17971/self-regulatory-organizations-financial-industry-regulatory-authority-inc-order-approving-a-proposed) — *Official source.* Describes the research-report disclosures FINRA Rule 2241 requires, including the analyst's financial interest, the 1% firm-ownership trigger and the catch-all for other material conflicts.
- [Cain, Loewenstein & Moore (2005) · The Dirt on Coming Clean: Perverse Effects of Disclosing Conflicts of Interest](https://doi.org/10.1086/426699) — *Research paper.* Shows that recipients under-discount disclosed conflicts and that disclosure can make advisers' advice more biased.
- [Sah, Loewenstein & Cain (2013) · The burden of disclosure: Increased compliance with distrusted advice](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0030527) — *Research paper.* Six experiments showing disclosure can raise pressure on advisees to comply, and which arrangements reduce that pressure.
- [Onuchic (2021) · Advisors with Hidden Motives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07446) — *arXiv 2103.07446.* A model of an adviser whose payoff depends on which product is sold, with a result on how mandated transparency about motives changes what the adviser shares.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An inducement is any benefit that could influence a recommendation: commission, a revenue share, a platform payment, research paid for by order flow, a sales target, hospitality. The ethical problem is not that money exists; it is that the person acting on the recommendation cannot see the arrangement and therefore cannot discount it. Fee disclosure exists because small recurring percentages compound into large amounts that investors routinely underestimate.

The practical discipline is to compute total cost of ownership rather than compare headline rates. Add the ongoing charge, the transaction costs you cause by trading, and any spread or platform fee, then express the total in money over a realistic holding period. A small business owner understands this instinctively: sales are not cash, and an obligation you have not written down still has to be paid.

$$
C = f\cdot V + n\cdot c\cdot V + F
$$

## A worked example

A fictional portfolio of Rp250,000,000 is charged 0.9% a year, turns over twice a year at a round-trip cost of 0.3%, and pays a Rp600,000 annual platform fee. The ongoing charge is Rp2,250,000, the trading cost is 2 x 0.003 x 250,000,000 = Rp1,500,000, and the platform fee is Rp600,000: Rp4,350,000 in total, or 1.74% of the portfolio. A recommendation that raises turnover to four times a year adds another Rp1,500,000 without changing the headline fee at all.

## Put the idea into practice

Quote costs in money over a holding period, not in basis points in isolation. Separate the costs the investor chose from the costs your activity creates.

### Do and do not

- **Do** total the ongoing charge, the trading cost and the platform fee before comparing products.
- **Do** state who receives each payment.
- **Do not** describe a recommendation as free because the fee is deducted rather than invoiced.
- **Do not** increase turnover without being able to show the expected benefit exceeds the cost you just added.

### Add it to your charter

Write the rule you will actually follow, the observation that would tell you the rule was broken, and the person you would tell. A rule you cannot check is a preference, not a control. Record the decision and its reasons before the outcome is known; a profitable breach is still a breach, and a loss suffered while following your rules is not evidence that the rules were wrong.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Regulators already ask for the discipline this lesson teaches. Article 24 of the EU's MiFID II directive says information on all costs and charges, including third-party payments, must be aggregated so that the client can see the overall cost and its cumulative effect on return. An inducement is allowed only if it is designed to enhance the quality of the service and does not impair the duty to act in the client's best interest, and its existence, nature and amount must be disclosed before the service is provided. Firms giving independent advice or managing portfolios may not keep third-party payments at all, apart from minor non-monetary benefits that are disclosed.

The research shows why visibility matters. Barber, Odean and Zheng studied 30 years of mutual fund flows. Flows fell with front-end loads but showed no relation to operating expenses, a result they attribute to marketing and advertising costs often embedded in those expenses. Christoffersen, Evans and Musto found that brokers' shares of sales loads and other revenue had significant effects on funds' inflows, particularly for unaffiliated brokers, and that load sharing, but not revenue sharing, predicted poor performance. Read together, these studies suggest that investors respond to the charges they can see, and that payments to intermediaries can steer money whether or not the client has understood them.

The cumulative effect is easy to compute. Levine shows that an annual fee of ε% of assets for N years costs almost N×ε% of the final value, compared with an identical investment paying no fee:

$$
1-(1-\varepsilon)^{N} \approx N\varepsilon
$$

For the lesson's 1.74% a year and N = 10, the shortcut gives 17.4% and the exact figure is 16.1%. If turnover rises to four times a year, total cost becomes 2.34% and the ten-year shortfall about 21.1%. These are illustrations rather than findings, and they treat every cost as a yearly share of assets.

Exercise: put your own total cost and horizon into the formula, then compare the shortfall with the benefit you expect from the extra turnover or the dearer product.

### Sources for this section

- [European Parliament & Council of the EU (2014) · Directive 2014/65/EU (MiFID II), Article 24: General principles and information to clients](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2014/65/article/24) — *Official source.* Article 24 of MiFID II, as reproduced by legislation.gov.uk: aggregated cost disclosure, the conditions for inducements, and the ban on keeping third-party payments in independent advice and portfolio management.
- [Barber, Odean & Zheng (2005) · Out of Sight, Out of Mind: The Effects of Expenses on Mutual Fund Flows](https://doi.org/10.1086/497042) — *Research paper.* Thirty years of fund flows: investors respond to salient front-end loads but not to operating expenses.
- [Christoffersen, Evans & Musto (2013) · What Do Consumers’ Fund Flows Maximize? Evidence from Their Brokers’ Incentives](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2012.01798.x) — *Research paper.* Shows that the payments brokers receive from funds influence where investor money goes, and that load sharing and revenue sharing predict performance differently.
- [Levine (2021) · Investment AUM Fee Costs: Evaluating a Simple Formula](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.00837) — *arXiv 2107.00837.* Derives and tests the shortcut that an annual percentage fee over N years costs almost N times the fee rate in final value.
