exams.title: Unit 1: Duty, conflict and disclosure
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: The most useful first step when two principals' interests conflict is:
options: Postpone the decision until prices move
Write down which interest you ranked first and the reason
questions.explanation: An explicit, recorded ranking is what allows the decision to be reviewed later.

questions.question: Burying a relevant conflict inside lengthy boilerplate is best described as:
options: Required, since legal text belongs in an appendix
A failure of prominence that works against the purpose of disclosing
Acceptable, because the fact was technically published
questions.explanation: Prominence and plain language are part of the obligation, not formatting taste.

questions.question: Calling advice 'free' because the fee is deducted from assets is:
options: Misleading, since the cost is borne by the investor either way
Accurate, because no invoice is issued
questions.explanation: A deducted cost is still a cost; the description misstates what the investor pays.

questions.question: Allocating the better fills to one account after seeing the prices is:
options: Acceptable where all accounts had the same strategy
Required, so the largest account is not disadvantaged
A breach of fair dealing, even if every account received something
questions.explanation: Allocation must follow a rule fixed before the outcome is known.

exams.title: Unit 2: Market integrity
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: On inadvertently receiving inside information, the correct first step is:
options: Wait to see whether the price moves on its own
Report it so the firm can restrict the security and record the event
Trade quickly before the information spreads
questions.explanation: Prompt reporting lets the firm restrict trading and preserves a record of the receipt.

questions.question: Two accounts under common control trading with each other to show volume is:
options: A wash trade, because no genuine change of beneficial ownership occurs
Acceptable, because both sides were willing
Permitted if the price used is the prevailing market price
questions.explanation: Transactions without a real change in beneficial ownership create a false impression of activity.

questions.question: The most checkable element of a promotional message is usually:
options: The confidence of the person sending it
The promoter's holding and the security's traded volume
questions.explanation: Holdings and volume are verifiable facts; a target is an unverifiable forecast.

questions.question: A routing arrangement that pays the firm:
options: Needs no review if customers do not complain
Requires documented evidence that the customer's result was still served
questions.explanation: The incentive runs against the customer, so the diligence behind the routing must be evidenced.

exams.title: Unit 3: Conduct in automated and quantitative work
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: A pre-trade control should:
options: Reject the order before it reaches the market
Log a warning for later review
Notify the trader after the fill is received
questions.explanation: A control that only warns does not prevent the exposure it was designed to stop.

questions.question: Re-using a holdout segment after a disappointing result:
options: Is fine as long as the model is not changed afterwards
Improves the estimate by adding data
Destroys its value as an untouched test and must be disclosed
questions.explanation: Once a segment informs a choice it is no longer an independent test, and the reader must be told.

questions.question: Using the latest revised value at an earlier decision date:
options: Introduces information that did not exist then, even though no value is incorrect
Is acceptable because revisions improve accuracy
questions.explanation: The file is accurate but the value is attached to a date on which it was not knowable.

questions.question: Showing simulated results beside live results without labelling them is:
options: An omission that makes the presentation misleading
Acceptable if the simulation used the same rules
Required, so the reader sees the full history
questions.explanation: The reader cannot evaluate the record without knowing which figures were actually earned.

exams.title: Unit 4: Care, refusal and record
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Where tolerance exceeds capacity, the recommendation should follow:
options: Tolerance, because the client accepted the risk in writing
Capacity, because the obligation exists regardless of preference
questions.explanation: The binding constraint is the loss the circumstances can actually absorb.

questions.question: Urgency in a payment request should:
options: Be resolved by asking the requester to confirm in the same thread
Increase verification, because it is a common pressure tactic
Justify skipping a step to avoid a missed deadline
questions.explanation: Pressure to act quickly is a warning sign, and confirmation in the same channel proves nothing.

questions.question: Investigating alone by altering the underlying records:
options: Damages the evidence others will need
Is the fastest way to confirm a concern
questions.explanation: Preserving the record matters more than personally confirming the suspicion.

questions.question: The best time to write a charter is:
options: During a drawdown, when the risks are vivid
After a profitable run, when confidence is high
Before the situation arises, when no position is at stake
questions.explanation: Deciding in advance is the entire mechanism; pressure is what the charter is meant to survive.

exams.title: Trading ethics & market conduct final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: A recommendation pays the adviser more and also suits the client. The conflict:
options: Still requires disclosure, because the client cannot weigh what they cannot see
Disappears, because the outcome was good for the client
Is resolved by the adviser's confidence in the product
questions.explanation: Suitability and disclosure are separate obligations; a good outcome does not retire the second.

questions.question: A conflict disclosed a week after the research note was published:
options: Satisfies the obligation, since it was eventually disclosed
Is adequate if the note later proved accurate
Failed its purpose, because it could not inform the decision it affected
questions.explanation: Disclosure must precede or accompany the action it is meant to inform.

questions.question: Doubling turnover while leaving the management fee unchanged:
options: Reduces cost by spreading it over more transactions
Raises the investor's total cost even though the headline rate did not move
Has no cost effect, since the fee is what the investor agreed to
questions.explanation: Trading costs scale with turnover and are borne by the investor regardless of the headline fee.

questions.question: A small personal trade placed just before a large client order is objectionable because:
options: It uses knowledge of a pending client order, regardless of its size
It reduces the firm's commission income
questions.explanation: The wrong is the use of the order information, not the size of the resulting position.

questions.question: Assembling many non-material public and non-public pieces into a material conclusion is:
options: Prohibited, because the conclusion is material
Permitted only after the issuer approves the conclusion
Legitimate analysis, because the conclusion is the analyst's own work
questions.explanation: The mosaic is the analyst's product; the prohibition attaches to a single material non-public fact.

questions.question: A high order-to-trade ratio on its own:
options: Is irrelevant to any manipulation question
Identifies an outlier to investigate, not proof of intent
questions.explanation: Genuine strategies can cancel heavily; the ratio is a signal that requires explanation.

questions.question: Repeating an unverified claim framed as a question is:
options: Still a communication that induces action and must meet the same standard
Acceptable, because a question asserts nothing
Only a problem if the sender holds the security
questions.explanation: Framing does not change the effect on a reader or the obligation not to mislead.

questions.question: Implementation shortfall is measured against:
options: The best price printed at any point in the session
The price when the decision was made, including costs
questions.explanation: The decision price is the benchmark, and costs form part of the shortfall.

questions.question: Per-order value limits failed here because:
options: Every individual order was compliant while the cumulative total was not
The limit was set too low
questions.explanation: Individually acceptable orders can breach a cumulative exposure that nothing was measuring.

questions.question: Across 40 independent null tests, the chance of at least one p-value below 0.05 is about:
questions.explanation: 1 - 0.95^40 is approximately 0.871.

questions.question: Data being commercially available means:
options: That any licensing question has been settled by the vendor
That the data must be point-in-time
Nothing by itself about whether you are permitted to use it
questions.explanation: Availability is not permission; terms, collection method and confidentiality duties still apply.

questions.question: Twelve months of results represent:
options: A sufficient sample once the return exceeds the benchmark
One observation of an annual outcome, not a sustained rate
Twelve independent pieces of evidence about annual performance
questions.explanation: A single year is one draw; monthly observations do not multiply the annual evidence.

questions.question: A 30% decline on the risky portion costs, as a share of total assets:
An instruction found inside a document submitted for processing is:
options: A valid instruction if the document is genuine
Authoritative once the sender confirms by replying
Untrusted content, not authority to act
questions.explanation: Authority must be verified through a channel independent of the message carrying the request.

questions.question: An escalation is most useful when it describes:
options: Observations with dates and identifiers, rather than conclusions
The motive you believe explains the behaviour
questions.explanation: Observations can be checked; an attributed motive cannot, and it invites dismissal.

questions.question: A breach of the position limit that turned out profitable should be:
options: Recorded and corrected, because the outcome does not amend the rule
Left alone, since no harm resulted
Used to raise the limit to the size that worked
questions.explanation: A rule that bends after a good outcome provides no constraint when it matters.

modules.title: Start a paper run: account type, seed and a fictional market
modules.subtitle: Create a paper account whose settings you can explain, and know what a new run keeps, archives and replaces.
modules.objective: Create a paper account whose settings you can explain, and know what a new run keeps, archives and replaces.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A paper run is a small experiment, and its settings are the conditions of the experiment. The account type decides whether you can only sell shares you own or may also borrow shares to sell. The market seed is a whole number that fixes the entire generated world: with the same seed the terminal produces the same bars, headlines, reporting calendar and company accounts, so you can repeat a decision under identical conditions. Left empty, the seed is chosen for you and every new account meets a different market.

The four cost fields turn trading friction into numbers you can inspect: a flat commission per order, slippage and spread in basis points (one basis point is 0.01%), and volume participation, the share of each bar's volume your orders may take. The defaults ($1, 2 bps, 2 bps and 1%) are teaching assumptions, not any broker's price list. A new run is always a new $100,000 account, never a reset in place, and earlier runs stay in the run history for review. Every company is fictional and every price is generated, so nothing in the terminal is a statement about a real security.

$$
f=\frac{s+\sigma/2}{10^{4}},\qquad \text{round-trip cost}=2c+Q\,(P_{\text{buy}}-P_{\text{sell}})
$$

## A worked example

Suppose the next bar opens at 148.50 and you buy 10 shares at market with the default costs. Friction is (2 + 2 ÷ 2) ÷ 10,000 = 0.0003, which is 3 basis points. The buy fills at 148.50 × 1.0003 = 148.54455, rounded to the cent: 148.54. You pay 10 × 148.54 = $1,485.40 plus the $1 commission, so cash falls from $100,000.00 to $98,513.60.

Now suppose the price has not moved when you sell. The sale fills at 148.50 × 0.9997 = 148.45545, which rounds to 148.46, so you receive $1,484.60 less the $1 commission and cash ends at $99,997.20. The price did not change, yet the round trip cost $2.80: $0.80 from the gap between the two fills on 10 shares, and $2.00 in commissions.

Raise slippage and spread to 10 bps each and friction becomes 0.0015. The same round trip now fills at 148.72 and 148.28 and costs $6.40. The market is identical and only the settings differ, which is why a result means little unless its seed and costs are written beside it.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the terminal.** Choose **Trading simulator** in the left navigation. On a first visit the terminal creates a default run for you: a cash account with $100,000, 32 fictional companies and a seed taken from the run's identifier. The account bar shows **PAPER TRADING**, **Equity**, **Cash** and **Realized P&L**. The replay bar should read "Day 2 · bar 110/390" with the clock at "Jan 7, 11:19 AM ET". In the status bar, "Guest · saved for this browser" means a 30-day browser cookie holds your run, and "Account synced" means it belongs to your signed-in account. Runs created as a guest never merge into an account later.

**Open the dialog.** Click the **New simulation run** icon (the circular arrows) at the right end of the replay bar. The dialog **Start a new simulation** opens. Leave **Practice mission (optional)** on "No mission · free practice" for now.

**Choose the account type.** **Account type** offers "Cash · long only" (the default) and "Margin · may sell short". Keep Cash for now; lesson 13.8 uses Margin. If the small print at the foot of the dialog still says long-only after you choose Margin, trust the help text under **Account type**, and the MARGIN badge that appears in the account bar once the run exists.

**Choose the market.** **Market data** is "Seeded synthetic market". "Historical replay" is disabled and labelled "· no imported datasets", because no historical data ships with the course.

**Set the seed.** In **Market seed (optional)** type a whole number from 0 to 1,000,000, such as 4242, or leave the box empty to see the placeholder "Automatic". A mission overrides this field with its own fixed seed.

**Check the costs.** The four numeric fields start at **Commission / order ($)** 1, **Slippage (bps)** 2, **Spread (bps)** 2 and **Volume participation (0–1)** 0.01. They accept 0 to 100, 0 to 100, 0 to 100 and 0.001 to 1. Leave them alone for this first run.

**Create the account.** Click **Create new paper account**. The notice reads "New $100,000 paper account ready. Prior runs remain in your run history." and the status bar shows the seed you typed. If a creation attempt fails, the terminal keeps the saved request and resends it unchanged on your next click, so check the seed in the status bar and the costs under **Execution model** before you rely on the new run.

**Find the old run.** Open the select **Simulation run history** in the status bar. The newest entry reads "Current · {date}" and the others "Archived · {date}". Choose an archived run and the terminal shows "Archived run · review and export only"; click **Return to current run** to trade again. A new run keeps your layout, symbol, indicators and watchlist, but not your drawings or your order ticket.

**Check.** Create a second run with the same seed. The first chart and the watchlist prices should match the first run. Create a third run with the seed left empty and they should differ.

### Practise in the terminal

Create a run with seed 4242 and the default costs, and write the seed and the four cost settings in your notebook. Create a second run with seed 4242 and compare the watchlist prices with the first. Then create a third run with **Slippage (bps)** 10 and **Spread (bps)** 10 and keep it for lesson 13.5, where you will measure a round trip yourself. No practice mission is needed yet: missions start in the same dialog, and lessons 13.4, 13.5, 13.7, 13.9, 13.11 and 13.12 each link one.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.
modules.code:
from math import floor

def to_cent(x):
    return floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100

def round_trip(open_price, shares, commission, slippage_bps, spread_bps):
    friction = (slippage_bps + spread_bps / 2) / 10000
    buy = to_cent(open_price * (1 + friction))
    sell = to_cent(open_price * (1 - friction))
    print("Friction:", friction)
    print("Buy fill:", buy)
    print("Cash after the buy:", round(100000 - shares * buy - commission, 2))
    print("Sell fill:", sell)
    print("Cash after the sale:", round(100000 - shares * buy - commission + shares * sell - commission, 2))
    print("Round-trip cost:", round(2 * commission + shares * (buy - sell), 2))

print("Default costs")
round_trip(148.50, 10, 1, 2, 2)
print("Slippage 10 bps and spread 10 bps")
round_trip(148.50, 10, 1, 10, 10)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: In your notebook, write the seed and the four cost settings of your run. Then compute the round-trip cost of buying and selling 20 shares at an unchanged open of 96.40, first with the default costs and then with Slippage 10 bps and Spread 10 bps, and say which settings you would use for a first week of practice and why.
assignment.solution: With the defaults, friction is 0.0003: the buy fills at 96.43 and the sale at 96.37, so the round trip costs 2 × $1 plus 20 × $0.06 = $3.20. With Slippage 10 and Spread 10, friction is 0.0015: the fills are 96.54 and 96.26, so the cost is $2 plus 20 × $0.28 = $7.60. Neither setting is correct in itself. The defaults are mild teaching assumptions and the higher settings are a harsher test; whichever you choose, write the settings next to every result so that the numbers can be compared and repeated.

realWorld.task: A fictional learner clicks Create new paper account, loses the connection before the confirmation arrives, and clicks again after changing the Market seed (optional) field from 4242 to 5151 (illustrative values). Decide which run exists afterwards and what the learner should check.

modules.title: Read the terminal: chart, panels and command codes
modules.subtitle: Find every panel and shortcut used in later lessons, and read the chart header, timeframes and indicators correctly.
modules.objective: Find every panel and shortcut used in later lessons, and read the chart header, timeframes and indicators correctly.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 7 minutes reading the idea and the example, 15 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A trading terminal shows several views of one account and one clock. Some panels carry information about the market (the chart, News, Company and Desk) and some carry the state of your account (Positions, Open orders, Order history, Trade history and Account history). Keep the two groups apart in your head: a chart can tempt you, but only the state panels tell you what you own, what is waiting and what you paid. Everything on screen is bounded by the replay clock, because the server never sends a bar, headline or result dated after it.

The chart header says exactly what you are looking at: the symbol, the timeframe, the time zone (ET, the New York exchange clock), the label SYNTHETIC, and the open, high, low, close and volume of the bar under the pointer. Indicators are calculated by the server from the bars you can already see, and each one needs a warm-up, because a 20-bar average cannot exist until 20 bars have formed. An indicator's period counts bars of the timeframe you are viewing, so the same setting means 20 minutes on the 1m chart and 20 hours on the 1h chart. The Command dialog is the keyboard route through all of this.

$$
\text{SMA}_{n}(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C_{t-k}
$$

## A worked example

At the default start the market has 500 one-minute bars behind the clock: all 390 bars of Day 1 and the first 110 of Day 2. The 1m chart therefore holds 500 bars. Group them by the hour and the 1h chart holds 9 bars: Day 1 gives six full hours and a last half hour (7 bars), and Day 2 gives 2 so far. The 1D chart holds just 2.

A 20-bar simple moving average needs 20 bars. On the 1m chart it exists almost everywhere. On the 1h chart the legend shows "SMA 20 · warming up", because 9 bars are fewer than 20, and 11 more hourly bars are needed. On the 1D chart no value can exist for another 18 sessions.

To see the arithmetic of an average, take five closes of 148.50, 148.56, 148.62, 148.58 and 148.64 (illustrative). Their sum is 742.90 and a 5-bar average is 742.90 ÷ 5 = 148.58. An average lags the price by design: it tells you where the price has been, not where it will go.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the Command dialog.** Click the symbol button at the left of the toolbar; it shows the current symbol, NVRA by default. The dialog **Command** opens with the box **Search stocks**. Type a ticker alone to choose a company, a function code alone to open a view, or both: `NVRA N` selects Novara Microsystems and opens its news. Press Enter. The codes are GP (chart), N or NEWS (news), MOV or DESK (the Desk tab), FA or DES (company financials), RV or PEER (the peer table), CAL, ECO or EARN (the calendar), PORT (performance), POS (positions), OMON (open orders), BLOT (trade history), W (watchlist), BUY and SELL (tickets) and HELP (the execution model). The code buttons in the dialog act on the current symbol. Tickers must match exactly: pressing Enter on a company name leaves the dialog open, so click a result instead.

**Set the chart.** In the toolbar, the group **Chart timeframe** offers 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h and 1D, and the select **Chart type** offers Candles, OHLC bars and Line. Click 1h and notice how few bars the chart holds, then click 1m again. The icons **Fit chart** and **Return to latest bar** reset the view.

**Read the header.** At the top left of the chart find "NVRA · 1m · ET · SYNTHETIC" followed by O, H, L, C and Vol for the bar under the pointer, or for the latest bar when the pointer is away. Vol matters later: it limits how many shares your orders can fill in one bar.

**Add an indicator.** Click **Indicators**. The dialog starts with Volume and SMA 20 and says "At most eight indicators." Under **Add indicator** choose RSI, whose period starts at 14. The eye icon (**Hide SMA** or **Show SMA**) and the cross (**Remove SMA**) hide and remove an indicator. Periods run from 2 to 200, and MACD has a **Fast period**, a slow period and a signal period.

**Draw on the chart.** In the left rail **Chart tools**, choose **Trend line** and click two points on the chart; the hint reads "Click two points on the chart · Esc to cancel". **Horizontal line** and **Text annotation** need one click, and **Rectangle** and **Price measurement** need two. **Undo drawing** and **Redo drawing** step back and forward, and so do Ctrl or Cmd with Z, plus Shift to redo, outside text boxes. **Objects** in the toolbar opens the Drawings tab, where a form edits a drawing by price and time; the form lists times in UTC while the chart uses ET.

**Find the panels.** The right sidebar has five tabs: **Watchlist**, **News**, **Desk**, **Trade** and **Drawings**. The bottom panel has eight: **Positions**, **Open orders**, **Order history**, **Trade history**, **Account history**, **Company**, **Performance** and **Calendar**. Drag the separators **Watchlist width** and **Trading panel height**, or press the arrow keys while one has focus. **Collapse watchlist** and **Collapse trading panel** hide a panel, and **Open watchlist** and **Open trading panel** bring it back. On a narrow screen the same views appear as the tabs Chart, Watchlist, News, Trade and Portfolio.

**Right-click for a limit ticket.** Right-click the chart at a price. The **Trade** tab opens with the ticket set to **Limit** at that price. Nothing is placed until you preview and confirm, as lesson 13.5 shows.

**Open the guide.** The question-mark icon **Simulator walkthrough**, or the **Execution model** button in the status bar, opens a five-step guide and a collapsible description of the execution and accounting model. It never opens by itself.

**Check.** Typing POS, OMON, BLOT and PORT should open four different bottom tabs, and the 1h chart should show SMA 20 as warming up until 20 hourly bars exist.

### Practise in the terminal

Run POS, OMON and BLOT from the Command dialog and note which tab each opens. Set the 1h timeframe and record how many bars you can see. Add RSI and write down its default period. Then write one line for each of the eight bottom tabs saying whether it shows market information or the state of your account. No practice mission fits this lesson, because it asks you to look rather than trade.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.
modules.code:
from math import ceil

day1 = 390
day2 = 110
hourly = ceil(day1 / 60) + ceil(day2 / 60)
print("One-minute bars at the start:", day1 + day2)
print("Hourly bars at the start:", hourly)
print("Daily bars at the start:", 2)
print("Hourly bars still needed for a 20-bar average:", 20 - hourly)

closes = [148.50, 148.56, 148.62, 148.58, 148.64]
total = 0
for close in closes:
    total = total + close
print("Sum of the five closes:", round(total, 2))
print("5-bar simple moving average:", round(total / len(closes), 2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: In your notebook, build a one-page map of the terminal: the five right-sidebar tabs and the eight bottom-panel tabs, the command code that opens each one you can reach by code, and whether each shows market information or the state of your account. Then work out how many bars the 1h chart holds when a run starts and how many more an SMA 20 needs.
assignment.solution: The right sidebar has Watchlist (W), News (N), Desk (MOV), Trade (BUY or SELL) and Drawings (opened with Objects). The bottom panel has Positions (POS), Open orders (OMON), Order history, Trade history (BLOT), Account history, Company (FA), Performance (PORT) and Calendar (CAL). Positions, Open orders, Order history, Trade history and Account history are the state of your account; News, Desk, Company and Calendar describe the market, and Performance compares the two. At the start the 1h chart holds 9 bars (7 from Day 1 and 2 from Day 2), so an SMA 20 needs 11 more hourly bars, a little under two sessions.

modules.title: Move the replay clock without hindsight
modules.subtitle: Advance the replay clock deliberately, convert bars into sessions, and write each decision down before every jump.
modules.objective: Advance the replay clock deliberately, convert bars into sessions, and write each decision down before every jump.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

In the terminal the replay clock is the only moment that exists. The server answers every request with data dated at or before the clock: bars, headlines, statements, calendar outcomes and analytics. That makes hindsight impossible inside the terminal, but not inside your head. Once you have advanced the clock you can no longer remember what you honestly thought before, so write the decision, the reason and what would change your mind first, and advance afterwards.

The controls move the clock in bars, not in seconds. A session is 390 one-minute bars, from 09:30 to 16:00 ET, and a week is 5 sessions, 1,950 bars. The jump buttons 15m, 1h, 1D and 1W move 15, 60, 390 and 1,950 bars at once. Replay speed (1×, 5×, 30× and 390×) is the number of bars advanced about every 0.8 seconds while Play is on; it is a bar rate, not a time multiplier. A large jump is processed bar by bar on the server, so orders can fill and stops can trigger inside it, but you are not there to react, as if you had left your desk.

$$
\text{session}=\left\lfloor \frac{c}{390}\right\rfloor+1,\qquad \text{bar}=(c \bmod 390)+1
$$

## A worked example

A new run starts at bar index 499, which the replay bar shows as Day 2, bar 110. For any index c, the session is c ÷ 390 rounded down, plus 1, and the bar number is the remainder of c ÷ 390, plus 1. The clock time is 09:30 plus one minute for each bar after the first.

Click Next replay bar: c = 500, so Day 2, bar 111, 11:20 AM ET. Then the 1h jump adds 60 bars: c = 560, which is Day 2, bar 171, 12:20 PM ET. The 1D jump adds 390: c = 950, which is Day 3, bar 171, the same time on the next day. The 1W jump adds 1,950, which is five sessions: c = 2,900, which is Day 8, bar 171. Day numbers count sessions, so weekends never appear as days.

Speed works the same way. At 1× each tick advances 1 bar, so a session of 390 bars takes 390 × 0.8 = 312 seconds, about five minutes. At 30× a session takes 13 ticks, 10.4 seconds. At 390× a session passes in a single tick.

## Put the idea into practice

**Find the replay bar.** Under the chart, from left to right: **Play replay** (which becomes **Pause replay**), **Next replay bar**, the group **Jump replay** (15m, 1h, 1D and 1W, with hover text such as "Jump forward by one hour"), the newspaper icon **Mark scored headlines on the chart**, the group **Monitor windows** (1, 2, 3), the select **Replay speed**, the clock text, the bar **Progress through the session**, the counter ("Day 2 · bar 110/390") and the **New simulation run** icon.

**Write before you step.** In your notebook write one line: the company, what you expect over the next hour, and why. Then click **Next replay bar** once. The counter moves to bar 111, the clock to 11:20 AM ET, and the notice reads "Replay advanced by one bar."

**Jump an hour.** Click **1h**. The notice reads "Replay advanced by one hour." and the counter reads bar 171, 12:20 PM ET. Compare the chart with your line.

**Play and pause.** Choose 5× in **Replay speed**, click **Play replay** and watch the counter move in steps of five bars. Click **Pause replay**, or press Esc, to stop. Esc also cancels a drawing tool. Opening an order preview, cancelling or editing an order, and any error message also pause the replay.

**Cross the close.** Click **Next replay bar** until the clock reads 3:59 PM ET. The clock text now adds "Market closed · next session on step". One more click moves to 9:30 AM the next morning, where the price can open away from the previous close: an overnight gap.

**Check.** After each jump, the counter and clock should match your own arithmetic, the News tab should list nothing dated after the clock, and your notebook line should have been written before the step.

### Practise in the terminal

Use a free-practice run. Before each of three jumps (**15m**, **1h** and **1D**), write your expected direction for NVRA at the end of the jump and one sentence of reasoning. After the jump, mark whether you were right and whether your reasoning was. Three notes prove nothing about skill. The aim is to notice how easily the reasoning rewrites itself once the answer is visible. No practice mission is needed here.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.

The 1W jump gives Day 8, bar 171 (12:20 PM), because each jump adds to the clock the one before left. Your decision note should name the company, the expected direction over a stated period, the reason and what would change your view, and it must be written before the jump. The comparison afterwards should judge the reasoning as well as the result: a correct guess for a poor reason is luck, and a wrong guess for a good reason may be fine.

modules.title: Read the simulated newsroom: scores, tone and chart markers
modules.subtitle: Read a headline's scope, impact tier and score, interpret the tone gauges, and trace a price move to its scored headline without over-reading the chart.
modules.objective: Read a headline's scope, impact tier and score, interpret the tone gauges, and trace a price move to its scored headline without over-reading the chart.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The simulated newsroom is generated before the prices, and the price engine then applies each headline's score. In this market, therefore, a move can be traced to a cause. One point is one basis point (0.01%), so a +250 point item is a modelled move of +2.50%, of which 58% lands on the bar the item is dated and the rest drifts over the bars that follow. A company item applies its score to one company. A sector item reaches its members through their sector loading and a macro release reaches every company through its beta, so the same score does not move every stock by the same amount. Each item is tagged by scope (CO for one company, SEC for a sector, ECO for a macroeconomic release, MKT for the whole market) and by impact: H for 400 points or more, M for 120 or more, L below that, and a dot for routine chatter, which carries no score and moves nothing.

Real markets give you no such score. You never see how much a real headline is worth, and prices move for many reasons at once. Use this tool to practise asking what a headline implies and for whom, not to conclude that headlines predict prices. Not every candle has a story either, because noise moves prices on its own, and an invented headline is not evidence about any real company. Tone summarises the tape. It is the weight of the released items, counted as 3 for high, 2 for medium and 1 for low, signed plus or minus for positive or negative news, divided by the total weight. It therefore sits between −1 and +1 however much chatter there is.

$$
\frac{\Delta P}{P}=\frac{\text{points}}{10\,000},\qquad \text{tone}=\frac{\sum_{i} w_{i}\,d_{i}}{\sum_{i} w_{i}}
$$

## A worked example

Suppose a company item on NVRA is scored +250 points. That is a modelled move of 250 × 0.0001 = 2.50%. With the stock at 148.50 the total is about $3.71, of which 58% (about $2.15) lands on the dated bar and the other 42% (about $1.56) drifts over the following bars. Since 250 is at least 120 and below 400, the item is tagged M.

Now read the tone. Suppose three scored items were released in the last session: a high positive item (weight 3), a medium negative item (weight 2) and a low positive item (weight 1). The signed weight is 3 − 2 + 1 = 2 and the total weight is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6, so the tone is 2 ÷ 6 = +0.33, shown as a market tone of 33%. Add ten chatter items and the tone does not change, because chatter has weight zero, although the item count rises.

One bar can hold several items. If a +250 item and a −130 item land in the same 5-minute bar, the chart marker shows their net, +120, followed by (2) for two items. A single circle on the chart can therefore hide two opposite stories.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the newsroom.** In the right sidebar click **News**, or type `NVRA N` in the Command dialog. The panel is headed **Newsroom** with a **SIMULATED** badge. The group **News scope** has **All markets** and the current ticker. With the ticker selected you see that company's own items plus the sector and macro items that move it.

**Read an item.** Each item shows a time, a scope tag (CO, SEC, ECO or MKT), the ticker if there is one, an impact letter (H, M, L or a dot), the headline, its source and category, and a score such as "+250 pts" or "0 pts". Hover the score for the arithmetic: one point is one basis point, 58% of it on this bar and the rest drifting.

**Read the gauges.** The gauges **Session** (the last 390 bars) and **5 sessions** (the last 1,950) run from −1 to +1 and read 0.00 when nothing has been released. Under them the text reads "N items this session · P positive · Q negative · R neutral · market tone X%". The scope buttons change the two gauges and the item counts, while the market tone always covers the whole market.

**Use the headline strip.** Above the chart the **SIM NEWS** strip carries the 12 newest items. Click one to select its company and open the News tab.

**See the markers.** On the chart, scored headlines appear as circles labelled with their points, for example "+250", or "+120 (2)" when two items fall in one bar and net to +120. Your own fills appear as arrows such as "BUY 10 @ 148.54". Click the newspaper icon **Mark scored headlines on the chart** to hide or show the circles.

**Trace a move.** Step with **Next replay bar** or the **15m** jump until a new item appears for your company. Find its circle on the chart and compare the bar's move with the score. Remember that 58% of the modelled move lands on the dated bar, that noise is added to every bar, and that sector and macro items reach a company through loadings.

**Check.** For one item write its scope, its impact tier, its points, the modelled percentage move (points ÷ 100) and the share on the dated bar (58%).

### Practise in the terminal

Try the mission [Trade what the tape actually said](/simulator?mission=read-the-tape). The link only preselects it: open the terminal, click the **New simulation run** icon, check that **Practice mission (optional)** shows "Trade what the tape actually said · VLOC", and click **Create new paper account**. Click the collapsed **Practice mission** bar under the toolbar to read the brief and the three objectives. VLOC is in your watchlist, but the terminal does not switch to a mission's company for you, so click VLOC yourself and select the VLOC scope in the News tab. The objectives are to make your first VLOC entry within one session after an item of 150 points or more on VLOC (the time must be within 390 clock minutes, and overnight does not count), to write a thesis on every order that names the headline, and to keep the position under 10% of opening equity, which is $10,000. A qualifying item can take a couple of sessions to appear, so move the clock in small steps and stop when one arrives. The objectives judge what you did and wrote, never your profit.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.

modules.title: Market and limit orders: preview, reservations and the next bar
modules.subtitle: Place, preview, amend and cancel a market order and a limit order, and explain why neither can fill until the next bar.
modules.objective: Place, preview, amend and cancel a market order and a limit order, and explain why neither can fill until the next bar.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 7 minutes reading the idea and the example, 15 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An order is an instruction, not a trade. In the terminal it passes through states you can see: drafted on the ticket, previewed (nothing is committed yet), accepted (cash is reserved but nothing is owned) and filled on a later bar. The preview shows estimates built from the last close, while the fill uses the next bar's open. An order placed after bar c is first tested on bar c + 1, so acceptance never changes your holdings, and the gap between the two prices is the price of acting without knowing the next bar.

A buy order reserves the estimated cost of its unfilled shares plus its unpaid commission, rounded up to the cent, so the same cash cannot be committed twice. If a gap makes a fill unaffordable, the order is cut back or rejected rather than creating debt. A market order accepts whatever the next bar offers, with slippage and half the spread against you. A limit order names the worst price you will accept. It fills at the open if the open is already at or better than the limit, and otherwise only if the price trades strictly through the limit. A touch alone is not enough, because the simulator never assumes your order was first in a queue. The price of that caution is that a limit may never fill, and that is a result too.

$$
R=q\,P_{\text{res}}+c,\qquad P_{\text{res}}=\begin{cases}\lceil P_{\text{last}}(1+f)\rceil_{0.01} & \text{market buy}\\ L & \text{buy limit}\end{cases}
$$

## A worked example

Suppose the last close is 148.50 and you preview a market buy of 10 shares with the default costs. The ticket prices it from the last close plus friction, rounded up: 148.50 × 1.0003 = 148.54455, which rounds up to 148.55. The estimated value is 10 × 148.55 = $1,485.50, and with the $1 commission the estimated debit is $1,486.50. After you place the order, Reserved cash shows $1,486.50 and Available cash falls to $98,513.50. You own nothing yet.

Now suppose the next bar opens at 148.62. The order fills at 148.62 × 1.0003 = 148.66 after rounding to the nearest cent. That is 10 × 148.66 = $1,486.60, plus the $1 commission, so $1,487.60 leaves your cash, which becomes $98,512.40, and the reservation is released. Your average cost is $1,487.60 ÷ 10 = $148.76, because the commission is part of what you paid. The estimate was $1.10 too low because the market opened above the last close.

Compare a buy limit at 148.20 for the same 10 shares. It reserves 148.20 × 10 + $1 = $1,483.00. If the next bar opens at 148.45 and trades down to 148.10, the price traded strictly through the limit, so the order fills at the limit: friction would make it 148.24, but a buy never pays more than its limit, so the fill is 148.20 and cash falls to $98,517.00. If that bar had traded down only to 148.20, the limit would have been touched but not passed, and nothing would fill. If the bar had opened at 148.10, the order would fill at the open plus friction, 148.14.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open a ticket.** Click **Trade** in the right sidebar, or use the quick **Buy** and **Sell** buttons under the selected company in the **Watchlist** tab, or type `NVRA BUY` in the Command dialog. The section **Order ticket** shows **Buy** and **Sell** buttons, **Order type** (Market by default), **Shares** (10) and **Duration** (GTC).

**Write the reason first.** Open **Trade thesis & lesson** and, in **Trade thesis**, answer the prompt "Why this trade? What would change your view?" in a sentence or two. **Linked lesson** offers only 0.4, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.8, so leave it on "No lesson".

**Preview.** Click **Preview buy order**. The preview pauses the replay and shows Estimated notional, Estimated debit, Available cash / reserved, Available shares and Position after full fill. If the button is disabled, read the line under the ticket, for example "Enter a positive whole number of shares." or "Insufficient available cash, including working orders and fees."

**Place.** Click **Place buy order**. The panel jumps to **Open orders** and the notice reads "Order accepted. Advance replay to observe its fill." The ticket's **Reserved cash** now shows the reservation, and **Positions** is still empty because nothing has filled.

**Advance.** Click **Next replay bar**. The order fills at that bar's open plus friction. **Trade history** shows Filled at, Symbol, Side, Shares, Fill price, Fee and Realized P&L. The chart marks the fill, for example "BUY 10 @ 148.66", **Positions** lists the shares with their Average cost, and a dashed line on the chart reads "LONG 10 · average 148.76".

**Place a limit order.** Change **Order type** to **Limit**, type a **Limit price**, then preview and place as before. The row in **Open orders** offers **Cancel**, **Edit** and **Journal**, and the chart draws a draggable line such as "BUY 10 · LIMIT 148.20". **Edit**, or dragging that line, opens **Confirm order amendment** with **New limit price** and **Confirm amendment**. **Cancel** shows "Order remainder canceled." Market orders have no **Edit**, because they have no price to change.

**Choose a duration.** **DAY** orders expire at the last bar of the session, and an order placed on that last bar belongs to the next session. **GTC** orders keep working until they fill or you cancel them.

**If the notice says "Unconfirmed action saved; recover it before placing another trade."** the terminal could not confirm that the order reached the server. Click **Reconnect & retry action**. It reloads your account and resends the same request, so the order can exist only once. Do not place the order again by hand.

**Check.** Compare the Estimated debit in the preview with the cash actually spent after the fill. They differ because the preview prices the order from the last close and the fill uses the next open.

### Practise in the terminal

Try the mission [Place your first paper order](/simulator?mission=first-order). The link only preselects it: open the terminal, click the **New simulation run** icon, check that **Practice mission (optional)** shows "Place your first paper order · NVRA", and click **Create new paper account**. Decide the price you are willing to pay before you look at the chart again, enter a buy limit at that price, and write your reason in **Trade thesis**; the box is already open on mission runs. Then advance by a full session with the **1D** jump. The three objectives are a limit entry, a thesis on every order and a session advanced after your first order. They say nothing about profit, and a limit that never fills is a result too: it tells you the market did not come to your price.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.
modules.formula: R=q\,P_{\text{res}}+c,\qquad P_{\text{res}}=\begin{cases}\lceil P_{\text{last}}(1+f)\rceil_{0.01} & \text{market buy}\\ L & \text{buy limit}\end{cases}
modules.code:
from math import ceil, floor

def to_cent(x):
    return floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100

def limit_buy_fill(open_price, low, limit, friction):
    if open_price <= limit:
        return min(to_cent(open_price * (1 + friction)), limit)
    if low < limit:
        return limit
    return 0

friction = (2 + 2 / 2) / 10000
shares = 10
commission = 1
last_close = 148.50

reserve_price = ceil(last_close * (1 + friction) * 100) / 100
reserved = round(shares * reserve_price + commission, 2)
print("Reserve price per share:", reserve_price)
print("Estimated debit and reserved cash:", reserved)
print("Available cash after placing:", round(100000 - reserved, 2))

next_open = 148.62
fill = to_cent(next_open * (1 + friction))
paid = round(shares * fill + commission, 2)
print("Fill price:", fill)
print("Cash after the fill:", round(100000 - paid, 2))
print("Average cost per share:", round(paid / shares, 2))

limit = 148.20
print("Cash reserved by the limit order:", round(limit * shares + commission, 2))
print("Bar trades through the limit:", limit_buy_fill(148.45, 148.10, limit, friction))
print("Bar only touches the limit (0 means no fill):", limit_buy_fill(148.45, 148.20, limit, friction))
print("Bar opens below the limit:", limit_buy_fill(148.10, 148.00, limit, friction))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: The last close is 96.40 and the costs are the defaults. Compute the reserve price and the reserved cash for a 20-share market buy and for a 20-share buy limit at 95.90. Then say what happens to each if the next bar opens at 96.55 and its low is 96.30.
assignment.solution: The market buy reserves a price of ceil(96.40 × 1.0003) = 96.43, so 20 × 96.43 + $1 = $1,929.60. The limit order reserves 20 × 95.90 + $1 = $1,919.00. If the next bar opens at 96.55, the market order fills at 96.55 × 1.0003 = 96.58 and costs 20 × 96.58 + $1 = $1,932.60, which is $3.00 more than it reserved. The limit does not fill: the open is above 95.90 and the low of 96.30 never traded below it, so the order keeps working and keeps its reservation of $1,919.00.

modules.title: How fills are priced: slippage, spread, participation and partial fills
modules.subtitle: Compute a fill from a bar's open and volume, and explain slippage, half the spread, the participation cap, first-in-first-out sharing and partial fills.
modules.objective: Compute a fill from a bar's open and volume, and explain slippage, half the spread, the participation cap, first-in-first-out sharing and partial fills.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 7 minutes reading the idea and the example, 15 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The simulator cannot see an order book or the path of prices inside a minute, so it prices a fill from numbers in the bar (open, high, low and volume) and from four settings you chose. Slippage and half the spread move a market order's price against you. Participation sets how much of the bar's volume your orders may take: capacity is the whole-number part of volume × participation, shared by all your orders in that symbol in the order they arrived, and what does not fill keeps working on later bars. The commission is charged once, on an order's first fill.

These rules are cautious on purpose, and they are still simplifications. A real fill depends on queue position, hidden liquidity and your own market impact, none of which is modelled here. The tape and order book windows in lesson 13.10 are illustrations that never touch a fill. Treat the rules as a way to see why size and liquidity matter: a 1% cap makes a large order take several bars, while a higher participation setting makes fills easier than a real market is likely to give you.

$$
\text{fill}_{t}=\min\big(\text{remaining}_{t},\ \lfloor V_{t}\,\pi\rfloor-\text{used}_{t}\big),\qquad P_{t}=\operatorname{round}\big(O_{t}\,(1\pm f)\big)
$$

## A worked example

Suppose you place a 600-share market buy with the default costs, and the next three bars have opens of 148.50, 148.60 and 148.55 and volumes of 26,000, 18,000 and 22,000 shares (hypothetical numbers). Capacity is the whole-number part of volume × 0.01: 260, 180 and 220 shares.

Bar one fills 260 shares at 148.50 × 1.0003, which is 148.54, and charges the $1 commission. Bar two fills 180 at 148.60 × 1.0003 = 148.64 with no commission. Bar three has room for 220 but only 160 shares remain, so it fills 160 at 148.55 × 1.0003 = 148.59. The total is 260 × 148.54 + 180 × 148.64 + 160 × 148.59 = 38,620.40 + 26,755.20 + 23,774.40 = $89,150.00, an average of 148.58 per share, plus one commission: $89,151.00.

A second order in the same stock queues behind yours and receives only the capacity left after yours has been served on each bar. In this example it would get nothing on bars one and two, and up to 60 shares on bar three. Arrival order decides, not size or urgency.

## Put the idea into practice

**Make capacity visible.** Click the **New simulation run** icon. Set **Volume participation (0–1)** to 0.001, its minimum, and leave the other fields at their defaults. Click **Create new paper account**.

**Read the bar's volume.** Hover the latest bar, or look at the chart header with the pointer away from the chart: the readout ends with "Vol …". At 0.001 the capacity is the whole-number part of Vol × 0.001, so 26,000 shares gives 26. The bar that fills your order will have its own volume, so treat this as a guide and check the fill bar afterwards.

**Place an order that is too big for one bar.** Choose a liquid company such as NVRA, open the **Trade** tab, enter 100 in **Shares**, keep Market and GTC, write a short reason in **Trade thesis**, then click **Preview buy order** and **Place buy order**.

**Step one bar at a time.** Click **Next replay bar**. In **Open orders** the row reads BUY · market, **Shares / filled** shows the order's quantity and what has filled, the status reads "partially filled", and the small text shows how many shares remain. Repeat until the order is filled, and watch **Reserved cash** shrink as it fills.

**Read the fills.** Open **Trade history**. Each partial fill is its own row. Only the first row carries the Fee of $1.00, and each Fill price is that bar's open plus 3 basis points, rounded to the cent. Hover a fill bar on the chart and check that the shares filled equal the whole-number part of Vol × 0.001, or the shares that remained, whichever is smaller.

**Queue a second order.** Place a second market buy of 10 shares in the same symbol straight after the first, before advancing. On the next bar the first order takes all the capacity, so the second shows 0 filled until the first is complete: first in, first out.

**Cancel the rest.** Click **Cancel** on a partly filled order. The notice reads "Order remainder canceled." Only the unfilled part is released, and the shares already filled stay in **Positions**.

**Check.** The sum of the filled shares in Trade history equals the quantity less the remainder, the Fee column has one non-zero entry per order, and the average price is the notional divided by the shares filled.

### Practise in the terminal

Repeat the exercise with the default participation of 0.01 and the same 100 shares. Note that the whole order now fills on the first bar whenever that bar has a volume of at least 10,000 shares. Write down the Fill price, the Fee and the average price for each run, and explain the difference using the participation setting. Then sell the shares again and check that sells fill at the open minus 3 basis points. No practice mission is needed for this lesson, because it changes a cost setting and a free-practice run keeps the market simple.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.

from math import floor

def to_cent(x):
    return floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100

friction = (2 + 2 / 2) / 10000
opens = [148.50, 148.60, 148.55]
volumes = [26000, 18000, 22000]
remaining = 600
notional = 0
commission = 1
for i in range(3):
    capacity = volumes[i] // 100
    fill = min(remaining, capacity)
    price = to_cent(opens[i] * (1 + friction))
    notional = notional + fill * price
    remaining = remaining - fill
    print("Bar", i + 1, "capacity", capacity, "fill", fill, "price", price, "remaining", remaining)
print("Shares bought:", 600 - remaining)
print("Notional:", round(notional, 2))
print("Average price:", round(notional / 600, 2))
print("Total cash paid including one commission:", round(notional + commission, 2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

modules.title: Stops, trailing stops and attached exits
modules.subtitle: Place stop, stop-limit, trailing-stop and attached-exit orders, and predict how each behaves when a price gaps.
modules.objective: Place stop, stop-limit, trailing-stop and attached-exit orders, and predict how each behaves when a price gaps.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A stop order is a trigger, not a price. A sell stop waits until a bar trades at or below the stop price and then becomes a sell at the market, so when a bar opens below the stop the fill comes at that worse open. A stop-limit triggers in the same way but then needs a later bar inside its limit, so it can protect the price and still leave you holding the shares. A trailing stop, offered for sells only, starts from the close when you place it and sits a percentage below it; after each bar it moves up to follow the new high, and it never moves down.

Attached exits let a buy carry its own plan out. Ticking **Attach exits to this entry** adds a take-profit above the entry, a stop-loss below it, or a trailing stop instead of the stop-loss. The exits wait, holding nothing in reserve, until the entry fills, then cover exactly the shares that filled. They are one-cancels-other: when one trades, the other shrinks or is cancelled. If a single bar reaches both, the terminal takes the stop first, because it cannot see the order of prices inside the bar and refuses to assume the flattering one.

$$
P_{\text{fill}}=\operatorname{round}\big(\min(O_t,S)\,(1-f)\big),\qquad S_{t+1}=(1-\tau)\,\max(A_t,H_t)
$$

## A worked example

You hold 10 shares and place a sell stop at 145.00 with the default 3 basis points of friction. The next bar opens at 146.10 and trades down to 144.80, which triggers the stop. The fill is the lower of the open and the stop, 145.00, less 3 basis points: 145.00 × 0.9997 = 144.9565, which rounds to 144.96.

Now suppose bad news arrives overnight and the next bar opens at 142.00. The stop is still triggered, but the fill is the lower price, 142.00 × 0.9997 = 141.9574, which rounds to 141.96. That is 3.04 below your stop, or $30.40 on 10 shares. A stop decides when an exit is attempted, not the price it receives.

A 5% trailing stop placed when the close is 150.00 starts at 150.00 × 0.95 = 142.50. The next bar trades between 149.00 and 153.00. It is tested against 142.50 and does not trigger, then the anchor rises to the 153.00 high and the stop becomes 145.35. When the following bar opens at 146.00 and dips to 144.90, it triggers at 145.35 and fills at 145.35 × 0.9997, rounded to 145.31.

## Put the idea into practice

**Protect shares you own.** Buy 10 shares of any company and advance one bar so that they fill. Open the **Trade** tab, click **Sell**, choose **Stop** in **Order type**, type a price below the last trade in **Stop price**, keep **Duration** at GTC and write why the stop sits there in **Trade thesis**. Click **Preview sell order**, read the estimates and click **Place sell order**. The working order draws a line on the chart that you can drag to a new price; dragging opens **Confirm order amendment**, where **Confirm amendment** applies it.

**Compare a stop-limit.** Place a second sell with **Order type** Stop-limit and both **Stop price** and **Limit price** filled in. Note in your notebook that after it triggers it can fill only on a later bar, and only at your limit or better.

**Use a trailing stop.** Choose **Trailing stop**, which appears for sells, and enter a percentage in **Trail (% below the high)** between 0.25 and 50. Advance a few bars with **Next replay bar** and watch the order's stop rise as new highs print.

**Attach exits to an entry.** On a **Buy** ticket with Market or Limit, tick **Attach exits to this entry** and fill **Take profit** and **Stop loss**, or **Or trail the stop (%)** instead of the stop loss. The ticket shows "Risking $X to make $Y · R:1". A take-profit below the entry or a stop-loss above it is refused with "A take-profit has to sit above the entry it protects." or "A stop-loss has to sit below the entry it protects." In **Open orders** the legs show only a **Journal** button until the entry fills, and cancelling the entry cancels them.

**Check.** In **Trade history**, a triggered stop's **Fill price** is never above the lower of the bar's open and the stop, less friction. A stop-limit that triggered on a bar has no fill on that same bar.

### Practise in the terminal

Try the mission [Protect a position before you need to](/simulator?mission=stop-discipline). No other lesson links it, so start it here: open the terminal, click the **New simulation run** icon, check that **Practice mission (optional)** shows "Protect a position before you need to · QBIT", and click **Create new paper account**. QBIT is not in the default watchlist, so click the symbol button, type QBIT and press Enter. Open a position, then place a protective sell stop while the price is still calm, writing a reason on every order. If you use attached exits, open **Journal** on each exit leg and write its reason too, then confirm in the mission panel that the thesis objective is met.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.

def to_cent(x):
    return floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100

friction = (2 + 2 / 2) / 10000
stop = 145.00
for bar_open in [146.10, 142.00]:
    fill = to_cent(min(bar_open, stop) * (1 - friction))
    print("Open", bar_open, "-> stop fill", fill, "gap below stop", round(stop - fill, 2))

trail = 0.05
anchor = 150.00
trailing_stop = anchor * (1 - trail)
print("Trailing stop placed at", round(trailing_stop, 2))
anchor = max(anchor, 153.00)
trailing_stop = anchor * (1 - trail)
print("After a 153.00 high the stop is", round(trailing_stop, 2))
print("Fill when the next bar dips through it:", to_cent(trailing_stop * (1 - friction)))

entry = 148.54
risk = (entry - 144.00) * 10
reward = (156.00 - entry) * 10
print("Bracket risk:", round(risk, 2), "reward:", round(reward, 2), "R:", round(reward / risk, 2))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: You hold 20 shares bought at 97.40 and place a sell stop at 95.00 with default costs. Work out the fill if the next bar opens at 96.20 and trades to 94.80, and again if it opens at 93.50. Then say what a stop-limit at 95.00 / 94.90 would have done in the second case.
assignment.solution: In the first case the bar trades through 95.00, so the fill is the lower of the open and the stop, 95.00, less 3 basis points: 95.00 × 0.9997 = 94.97 after rounding, a loss of (97.40 − 94.97) × 20 = $48.60 before commissions. In the second case the open is below the stop, so the fill is 93.50 × 0.9997 = 93.47, a loss of $78.60. A stop-limit at 95.00 / 94.90 would trigger on the gap bar but could only fill on a later bar at 94.90 or better, so if prices stayed lower it would leave all 20 shares unsold.

modules.title: Margin accounts and short selling
modules.subtitle: Open a margin run, sell short, and compute buying power, the borrow fee and the price at which a short is bought in.
modules.objective: Open a margin run, sell short, and compute buying power, the borrow fee and the price at which a short is bought in.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A margin account lets you sell shares you do not own. You borrow them, sell them now, and must buy them back later; if the price rises in between, the loss has no ceiling, because a price has no upper limit. In the terminal a margin account is chosen when the run is created, with **Account type** set to "Margin · may sell short". Practice missions always use cash accounts so that every attempt meets the same rules.

Three numbers govern the account. Buying power is twice equity less gross exposure, never below zero, and a short uses it at the full value of the shares borrowed, just like a purchase of the same size. Borrowed shares cost a fee of 5% a year, charged once per session as its own line in **Account history**. When equity falls below 30% of gross exposure, the terminal buys the short back with a real order that queues like any other. Buying back borrowed shares is never refused for lack of cash, because closing a short reduces risk. Dividends are not modelled, which a real short seller would have to pay.

$$
\text{BP}=\max\big(0,\;2E-G\big),\qquad \text{buy-in when } E<0.3\,G
$$

## A worked example

Start a margin run with $100,000 and sell short 600 shares at a fill of 150.00, ignoring fees. The sale adds $90,000, so cash is $190,000, while you owe 600 shares worth $90,000. Equity is 190,000 − 90,000 = $100,000, gross exposure is $90,000 and buying power is 2 × 100,000 − 90,000 = $110,000.

If the price rises to 200.00, the shares you owe are worth $120,000. Equity falls to 190,000 − 120,000 = $70,000, gross exposure is $120,000 and buying power shrinks to 2 × 70,000 − 120,000 = $20,000. The buy-in comes when equity is below 30% of gross: 190,000 − 600P < 0.3 × 600P, so P must exceed 190,000 ÷ 780 = 243.59, a rise of about 62% from the short price.

While the position is open, the borrow fee at a price of 150.00 is 90,000 × 0.05 ÷ 252 ≈ $17.86 per session, or about $89.29 over a five-session week if the price does not move.

## Put the idea into practice

**Create a margin run.** Click the **New simulation run** icon, leave **Practice mission (optional)** on "No mission · free practice", set **Account type** to "Margin · may sell short" and click **Create new paper account**. Read the help text under **Account type** rather than the small print at the foot of the dialog. The account bar now shows **MARGIN**, **Buying power** and **Gross** next to **Equity** and **Cash**.

**Sell short.** Choose a company you do not own, open the **Trade** tab and click **Sell**. Enter a small quantity in **Shares**, keep Market and GTC, and write why you expect the price to fall in **Trade thesis**. The preview shows **Buying power** where a cash account shows available cash. Click **Preview sell order** and then **Place sell order**, and advance one bar.

**Watch the numbers.** After the fill, check that **Cash** rose by the proceeds less the commission and that **Gross** shows the value of the borrowed shares. Advance by a session with the **1D** jump, then open **Account history** and find the line "Stock borrow fee on short positions".

**Cover.** In **Positions**, click **Close** on the short. It prefills a **Buy** ticket for the full quantity; preview and place it, then advance one bar.

**Check.** Your realized result is the sale proceeds less the purchase cost, the two commissions and every borrow fee line, and the borrow fee lines match the formula above for the prices at which they were charged.

### Practise in the terminal

There is no practice mission for this lesson, because missions use cash accounts. In a free margin run, short 100 shares of a calm company and record the fill, the buying power before and after, and each session's borrow fee for a week. Compute the buy-in price for your position with the formula in this lesson, and write down what you would do long before the price got near it. Then cover, and compare the total borrow fee with your estimate.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.

print("Borrow fee per session at 150:", round(fee_per_session, 2))
print("Borrow fee over five sessions:", round(fee_per_session * 5, 2))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

modules.title: Company accounts, consensus and the earnings calendar
modules.subtitle: Read a fictional company's statements, ratios, consensus and reporting date, and compute a surprise and a trailing P/E without hindsight.
modules.objective: Read a fictional company's statements, ratios, consensus and reporting date, and compute a surprise and a trailing P/E without hindsight.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Every fictional company has generated quarterly accounts that tie together: equity is assets less liabilities, and each quarter's closing cash equals the previous cash plus that quarter's operating, investing and financing flows. A company that would run short of cash borrows the difference, so short-term debt and external financing tell you when a business needed help. Before a print you can see only the expectation: the quarter's label, its date and the published consensus. The reported figures leave the server only once the clock reaches the bar that prints them.

Prints land at a session open, so the result arrives with the price gap it causes. The ratios are computed from quarters already reported and the current price, and a ratio whose denominator is zero or negative shows "—" rather than a misleading number. Five companies are development-stage businesses that lose money and are valued on sales, so their P/E is "—" by design. Nothing in these accounts describes a real company.

$$
\text{surprise}=\text{EPS}_{\text{reported}}-\text{EPS}_{\text{consensus}},\qquad P/E=\frac{P}{\sum_{k=0}^{3}\text{EPS}_{t-k}}
$$

## A worked example

A company's consensus EPS for the quarter is $1.20 and it reports $1.26. The surprise, stated as a distance, is 1.26 − 1.20 = +$0.06; as a share of consensus that is 0.06 ÷ 1.20 = 5.0%. Its last four quarters, including this one, are $1.10, $1.15, $1.18 and $1.26, so trailing EPS is $4.69. At a price of 148.50 the trailing P/E is 148.50 ÷ 4.69 ≈ 31.66.

The quarter's net income is $26.0 million but operating cash flow is only $18.5 million, so cash conversion is 18.5 ÷ 26.0 ≈ 71%. If short-term debt also rose, the beat leaned partly on borrowing. All of these figures are illustrative; your run will show different ones.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the accounts.** Click the symbol button and type `NVRA FA`, then press Enter; Enter works even though the dialog says "No matching stock is available in this run." for the combined text. The **Company** tab opens with the badge "SIMULATED" and either "Next report …" with consensus or "… reported" with the surprise.

**Read the statements.** In the **Statements** group, start with **Ratios**: the groups are Valuation, Profitability, Growth & distribution, Balance sheet and Value screens. Then open **Income statement**, **Balance sheet** and **Cash flow**. Compare net income with operating cash flow, and look for rising short-term debt or external financing. **Peers** lists the sector's other companies with a **Sector median** row.

**Find the date.** Open the **Calendar** tab. **Company results** shows When, Symbol, Period, Consensus EPS and Reported; before the print, Reported reads "in N bars", and Consensus EPS may read "not yet set" until it is published. **Economic releases** lists the macro calendar, marked "Scheduled" until each item is released.

**Watch a print.** Write your expectation in your notebook, then advance with the **1D** jump until Reported changes to the EPS figure with its surprise in brackets. Look at the opening bar of that session on the chart.

**Check.** Recompute the surprise from the published consensus and the reported EPS, and the trailing P/E from the last four reported quarters and the price, and compare them with the terminal.

### Practise in the terminal

Try the mission [Hold a company through its results](/simulator?mission=earnings-gap). The link only preselects it: open the terminal, click the **New simulation run** icon, check that **Practice mission (optional)** shows "Hold a company through its results · NVRA", and click **Create new paper account**. NVRA's print falls at the open of Day 5. Read the accounts and consensus first, write what you expect and why in **Trade thesis**, hold at least 25 shares into the print, and stay for the session after it. The mission judges the order of these steps, not whether the result made money.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.

After the print, compute the surprise and the new trailing P/E, and describe the opening gap.
assignment.solution: A complete answer records the published expectation before the print and the reported figures after it, so nothing depends on hindsight. The surprise is reported EPS minus consensus EPS, stated as a distance (and optionally as a share of consensus). The trailing P/E divides the current price by the sum of the last four reported EPS figures; if that sum is zero or negative the ratio is undefined, as the terminal's '—' shows. A good answer also compares cash flow with net income, notes any new short-term debt, and treats the gap as one observation from a simulated market, not a rule.
