modules.title: Desk analytics and monitor windows
modules.subtitle: Read the Desk tab's quant sheet and lists, split the chart into monitor windows, and use a named screen as a hypothesis you test before trusting.
modules.objective: Read the Desk tab's quant sheet and lists, split the chart into monitor windows, and use a named screen as a hypothesis you test before trusting.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The **Desk** tab carries the badge "API CALCULATED": every figure on it is computed on the server from bars the clock has already reached, never from the future. The quant sheet for the selected company lists Last, SMA 20, SMA 50, EMA 20, RSI 14, MACD hist., Volatility (ann.), Beta, Correlation, Session move, Since open and Relative volume, and the lists below rank Top gainers, Top losers, Most active and Sectors.

Monitor windows split the chart area into two or three panes, each showing a tool: Time & sales, Order book, Heat map, Screener, Sessions, Quotes or News. The tape in Time & sales is invented, but it is constrained by each bar: it opens at the open, closes at the close, touches the high and the low and its sizes add up to the volume. The order book shows indicative size at the run's spread. Neither ever affects a fill. The Screener offers named screens such as Oversold (RSI under 30) rather than adjustable thresholds, because a screen chosen in advance is a hypothesis, while a threshold tuned after seeing the winners simply fits the answer.

$$
\text{RSI}=100-\frac{100}{1+RS},\qquad RS=\frac{\overline{\text{gain}}_{14}}{\overline{\text{loss}}_{14}}
$$

## A worked example

RSI compares average gains with average losses over 14 bars. With an average gain of 0.60 and an average loss of 0.40, the ratio is 1.5 and RSI = 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + 1.5) = 60, comfortably between the Oversold (30) and Overbought (70) screens. A company trading 2,400,000 shares when its average is 1,600,000 has a relative volume of 1.5.

Suppose you run the Oversold screen for several sessions and 9 of the 16 names it listed rose the next session, while 17 of 32 names in the Whole listing rose. That is 56% against 53%, a gap of three points on very few observations: not yet evidence that the screen picks winners. These numbers are illustrative.

## Put the idea into practice

**Read the desk.** Open the **Desk** tab in the right sidebar. Check the quant sheet for the selected company and click a name in **Top gainers** to select it everywhere in the terminal.

**Split the chart.** In the replay bar's **Monitor windows** group, click **2** or **3**. Each new window has a select **Tool for monitor 2** or **Tool for monitor 3**; the defaults are Time & sales and Heat map. Windows are hidden when the screen is 900 pixels wide or less.

**Read the tape.** With Time & sales showing, advance one bar. Its summary reads "N prints · M shares · X% lifted the offer"; check that the prints start at the bar's open and end at its close. Then switch the window to **Order book** and note that it shows indicative size, not a queue you can join.

**Run a screen.** Set a window to **Screener** and choose a screen in **Screen**: Trending up, Oversold, Overbought, Unusual volume, Low earnings multiple, Widest ranges or Whole listing. The columns are Symbol, Last, Chg, RSI, Rel vol, P/E and Vol. Write your prediction for the listed names before you advance.

**Check.** Click a symbol in any tool and confirm that the chart and ticket switch to it; then compare the RSI in the Screener with the quant sheet's RSI 14 for the same company.

### Practise in the terminal

There is no mission for this lesson. Choose one named screen, write down your prediction for its names, and advance one session at a time for at least ten sessions. Record how many of its names rose and how many in the Whole listing rose, and keep the screen unchanged throughout. At the end, decide whether the difference is large enough, over enough observations, to mean anything.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.
modules.code:
average_gain = 0.60
average_loss = 0.40
rs = average_gain / average_loss
rsi = 100 - 100 / (1 + rs)
print("RS:", rs, "RSI:", round(rsi, 1))
print("Relative volume:", 2400000 / 1600000)
screen_hits = 9
screen_names = 16
listing_hits = 17
listing_names = 32
print("Screen hit rate:", round(screen_hits / screen_names * 100, 1), "%")
print("Whole listing hit rate:", round(listing_hits / listing_names * 100, 1), "%")

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Run one named screen for ten sessions without changing it. Record each session's listed names, how many rose the next session, and the same count for the Whole listing. Report both hit rates and explain whether the difference supports the screen.
assignment.solution: A good answer fixes the screen before the first session and keeps it unchanged, records the prediction before each advance, and reports both hit rates with their counts. With a few dozen observations in a generated market, a difference of a few percentage points is well within what chance alone produces, so the honest conclusion is usually that the screen is untested rather than proven. Tuning the RSI threshold after seeing which names rose would make the hit rate look better by construction and is not evidence.

modules.title: Performance against the QX-200, journals and exports
modules.subtitle: Read the Performance tab against the QX-200 benchmark, journal each order's reasoning, and export your records safely.
modules.objective: Read the Performance tab against the QX-200 benchmark, journal each order's reasoning, and export your records safely.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the idea and the example, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The **Performance** tab marks your account on every observed bar and compares it with the QX-200, an equal-weighted index of every company in the run rebased to the bar your account opened on. Measuring against the market rather than against zero separates what the market did from what your decisions added. Beta and alpha describe that split, and Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, CAGR, daily VaR and CVaR come from session closes at 252 sessions a year. Below 20 closed sessions the panel warns that annualizing so few returns "produces a number, not a measurement".

The trade statistics are simple counts you can check: a closing trade is a fill that realized a gain or a loss, win rate is winning closing trades divided by all closing trades, and profit factor is gross wins divided by gross losses ("—" when there is no loss). Your journal, the thesis written on each order and its fills, is the other half of a review: it records what you expected before you knew the outcome. Exports keep both. CSV cells that start with =, +, − or @ gain an apostrophe so that a spreadsheet cannot run them as formulas.

$$
\text{win rate}=\frac{n_{\text{win}}}{n_{\text{closing}}},\qquad \text{PF}=\frac{\sum \text{wins}}{\left|\sum \text{losses}\right|},\qquad \text{excess}=R_p-R_{\text{QX-200}}
$$

## A worked example

Four closing trades realize +$120, +$80, −$50 and −$150. Two of four won, so the win rate is 50%. Gross wins are $200 and gross losses are $200, so the profit factor is 200 ÷ 200 = 1.00: the account broke even on its closed trades. The average win is $100 and the average loss is −$100.

The equity path runs $100,000, $101,200, $99,800 and $100,600. The deepest fall from a peak is 101,200 − 99,800 = $1,400, a maximum drawdown of 1,400 ÷ 101,200 ≈ 1.38%. If the account returned +0.6% while the QX-200 returned +0.9%, the excess return is −0.3 percentage points: the market did better than your choices over the same bars.

## Put the idea into practice

**Read performance.** Open the **Performance** tab in the bottom panel. Note **Equity**, **Total return**, **Max drawdown**, **Realized P&L** and **Unrealized P&L**, then **Closing trades**, **Win rate**, **Profit factor**, **Average win**, **Average loss**, **Average exposure**, **Bars observed** and **Sessions**. The chart **Equity path vs QX-200** sets your account against the benchmark, with **Your return**, **QX-200 return**, **Excess return**, **Beta** and **Alpha (annualized)** beside it. **Attribution by company** shows where results came from.

**Journal an order.** In **Open orders**, **Order history** or **Trade history**, click **Journal** on a row. The **Trade journal** dialog has **Trade thesis** and **Linked lesson**; write what you expected and what would have changed your mind, then click **Save journal** and look for "Trade journal saved."

**Export.** On any bottom-panel tab, click **Export table as CSV** to save it as a file such as quanta-open-orders.csv. For the whole run, click **Export simulation** in the status bar and choose "Run, chart settings & journal (JSON)".

**Check.** Recompute win rate and profit factor from the realized P&L column of your exported trade history, and confirm that they match the panel.

### Practise in the terminal

Try the mission [Size a position you could survive](/simulator?mission=position-size). The link only preselects it: open the terminal, click the **New simulation run** icon, check that **Practice mission (optional)** shows "Size a position you could survive · ZEPH", and click **Create new paper account**. Keep every position under 5% of opening equity, place at least three orders and advance a full week. Then read the Performance tab, journal every order, export the trade history and recompute the statistics yourself.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.
modules.code:
trades = [120, 80, -50, -150]
wins = 0
gross_win = 0
gross_loss = 0
for result in trades:
    if result > 0:
        wins = wins + 1
        gross_win = gross_win + result
    if result < 0:
        gross_loss = gross_loss - result
print("Win rate:", wins / len(trades) * 100, "%")
print("Profit factor:", gross_win / gross_loss)

equity = [100000, 101200, 99800, 100600]
peak = equity[0]
worst = 0
for value in equity:
    peak = max(peak, value)
    worst = max(worst, (peak - value) / peak)
print("Max drawdown:", round(worst * 100, 2), "%")
print("Excess return vs QX-200:", round(0.6 - 0.9, 1), "points")

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Export your trade history after a week of practice. From the CSV, compute the number of closing trades, win rate, profit factor and average win and loss, and compare them with the Performance tab. Then write one paragraph comparing your return with the QX-200.
assignment.solution: The closing trades are the rows with a non-zero realized P&L. Win rate is the share of those rows that are positive; profit factor divides the sum of the positive results by the absolute sum of the negative ones and is undefined if there were no losses. A good comparison with the QX-200 states both returns over the same bars, the excess return, the beta, and the number of sessions, and adds that a week of a generated market is far too short to show skill. The journal entries explain whether the results followed the reasons written beforehand.

realWorld.task: A fictional account returns +3.0% in a week when the QX-200 rises 2.4% and the account's beta is 0.9 (illustrative, ignoring the risk-free rate). Compute the excess return and the part of the return that beta explains.
realWorld.walkthrough: Excess return is 3.0 − 2.4 = +0.6 percentage points. Beta explains 0.9 × 2.4 = 2.16 points, which leaves 0.84 points unexplained. That remainder is an estimate from one week of a generated market, not evidence of skill.

modules.title: Capstone: practice missions and a week inside your trading charter
modules.subtitle: Complete a week of practice inside written limits, judged by process rather than profit, and deliver a review another person could check.
modules.objective: Complete a week of practice inside written limits, judged by process rather than profit, and deliver a review another person could check.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 6 minutes reading the idea and the example, 16 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes recomputing the worksheet and writing your notebook entry; all companies and prices are fictional and the market is simulated.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A practice mission is a lesson's exercise carried into the terminal: a fixed seed, a fixed start, a named company, a short brief and three objectives. Everyone who attempts it meets the same market, and every objective is judged on the server from your orders, fills, positions and clock, never from your profit. That is deliberate. A rule broken profitably is still broken, and a loss taken while following your rules is not proof that the rules were wrong.

The capstone mission, "Trade inside your written limits", asks you to trade a week inside the charter you wrote in the ethics course: every position under 5% of opening equity, a thesis on every order, and every position closed before you finish. A position cap is judged on the largest holding the run ever carried, so closing an oversized position afterwards does not undo the breach. Your review then turns the week into evidence another person could check: settings, sample, costs, benchmark and the limits of what the simulator models.

$$
q_{\max}=\left\lfloor\frac{0.05\,E_0-c}{P_{\text{fill}}}\right\rfloor
$$

## A worked example

The 5% cap on $100,000 of opening equity is $5,000, including fees. If the next bar opens at 52.30, a market buy fills at 52.30 × 1.0003 = 52.31569, which rounds to 52.32. The largest whole number of shares within the cap is the whole-number part of (5,000 − 1) ÷ 52.32 = 95.55, so 95 shares, costing 95 × 52.32 + 1 = $4,971.40.

A buy of 100 shares would cost 100 × 52.32 + 1 = $5,233.00 and breach the cap, even if you sold 5 shares a minute later. The review checklist in the worksheet has twelve items, from the seed and costs to the next experiment you would run; a complete review ticks all twelve.

## Put the idea into practice

**Start the mission.** Open [Trade inside your written limits](/simulator?mission=charter). The link only preselects it: click the **New simulation run** icon, check that **Practice mission (optional)** shows "Trade inside your written limits · MRDN", and click **Create new paper account**. The mission starts on Day 2 at 11:19 ET in a cash account with $100,000.

**Read the brief.** Open the **Practice mission** panel. It shows the title, "N of 3 objectives" and each objective with a note on how far it has come. Copy your written charter into your notebook before the first trade.

**Trade the week.** Size every entry with the formula above before you preview it, write a **Trade thesis** on every order, and add a **Journal** entry on any order you placed without one. Advance through the week with the **1D** jump or the **1W** jump, which moves 1,950 bars.

**Finish flat.** Close every position with **Close** in **Positions**, preview and place each order, and advance until they fill. The panel reads "All objectives met" only when no shares remain after a full week since your first order.

**Deliver the review.** Click **Export simulation** and choose "Run, chart settings & journal (JSON)". Then write the review using the twelve items in the worksheet.

**Check.** Every objective is met, the exported journal contains a thesis for every order, and your review states what the simulator does not model: dividends, queue position, market impact and real borrow availability.

### Practise in the terminal

This lesson is the mission. When it is complete, give your review to someone who did not trade the week and ask them to recompute one number from your export, such as the largest position's peak cost or the profit factor. A review is finished when another person can check it without asking you anything.

Write down what you expect before you advance the clock, and what happened afterwards. Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, so a good result here is practice for a process, not evidence of skill.
modules.code:
from math import floor

def to_cent(x):
    return floor(x * 100 + 0.5) / 100

opening_equity = 100000
cap = 0.05 * opening_equity
commission = 1
fill = to_cent(52.30 * (1 + (2 + 2 / 2) / 10000))
shares = floor((cap - commission) / fill)
print("Cap:", cap, "fill:", fill, "max shares:", shares, "cost:", round(shares * fill + commission, 2))
print("100 shares would cost:", round(100 * fill + commission, 2))

checklist = ["seed", "cost settings", "sessions", "orders", "thesis on every order",
             "largest position vs cap", "QX-200 return", "excess return", "max drawdown",
             "what is not modelled", "lesson learned", "next experiment"]
print("Simulator review checklist:", len(checklist), "of", 12)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Complete the charter mission and write a one-page review covering the twelve checklist items: seed, cost settings, sessions, orders, a thesis on every order, the largest position against the cap, the QX-200 return, the excess return, the maximum drawdown, what the simulator does not model, the lesson you learned and the next experiment you would run.
assignment.solution: A complete review states the mission seed (9006) and the cost settings, the number of sessions and orders, and confirms a thesis on every order. It reports the largest position's peak cost against the $5,000 cap, the account's return beside the QX-200 return with the excess return, and the maximum drawdown. It lists what the simulator leaves out, such as dividends, queue position, market impact and real borrow availability, and it ends with one lesson and one falsifiable next experiment. It does not claim skill from a single generated week.

readingGuide:
The Trading simulator is a practice terminal with $100,000 of paper money and a market made entirely of fictional companies. Nothing in it is real, which is the point: you can make mistakes, repeat a situation and look closely at what you did without risking anything. This course shows you every part of the terminal one small step at a time, so the tools are familiar before you rely on them.

Each lesson explains one idea, works through a short example with real numbers, and then gives you click-by-click steps that use the exact button names you will see on screen. Follow the steps in the terminal while you read, recompute the example in the worksheet, and write down what you expect before you press anything that moves the clock. Several lessons link to a practice mission. A mission judges what you did and wrote, never whether the trade made money, because a good result in a simulation is not evidence of skill.

12 lessons × 30 minutes = 6 hours of planned study across three units: about 8 minutes of reading, 14 minutes following the steps in the terminal and 8 minutes on the worksheet and notebook in each lesson; exam time is additional. Includes 24 practice questions, three four-question checkpoints, a 12-question final and six practice missions linked from the lessons.

Every company, headline and price in the terminal is fictional and the market is simulated, and a profitable simulated trade is not evidence of skill. The simulator does not model dividends, queue position, market impact, real borrow availability or any broker's rules.

exams.title: Unit 1: Set up and read the market
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Why does the course ask you to write the seed and the four cost settings beside every result?
options: The terminal refuses to place orders until the settings have been written down
The settings change the bars you see after each order is placed
The same decisions can score differently under different settings, and the seed lets you rebuild the same market
questions.explanation: A result only means something under stated conditions. The seed and costs are the conditions, so recording them makes a result repeatable and comparable.

questions.question: In the chart header, what does the label SYNTHETIC tell you?
options: The chart is showing a smoothed moving average instead of prices
The bars are generated by the simulator, not recorded from a real market
The prices are delayed by a few minutes
questions.explanation: SYNTHETIC identifies the data source. A price needs its source, symbol, timeframe and time zone before you can interpret it.

questions.question: Why does the course ask you to write your expectation before using a jump button?
options: Once the outcome is on the chart you can rewrite your reasoning to fit it, so the earlier note is the honest record
The terminal rejects orders placed without a written expectation
A jump hides the market data until your note has been saved
questions.explanation: Hindsight does not come from the data, which the terminal limits to the clock, but from reinterpreting your earlier thinking. A dated note prevents that.

questions.question: A learner buys right after a +400 point headline and the stock falls over the next hour. What does this show about the score?
options: That the score is wrong, because the price must follow it on every bar
That the item was chatter, because only chatter fails to move the price
Nothing conclusive, because noise and other items also move prices and one trade is a tiny sample
questions.explanation: A score models one item's contribution. Noise, sector and macro items and drift also act on the price, and a single outcome cannot judge a model or a decision.

Click Reconnect & retry action so the saved request is resent once
Place the order again at once in case the first was lost
questions.explanation: The terminal cannot tell whether the order arrived. Reloading the account and resending the same request keeps the order unique, while placing it again could double it.

questions.question: A learner raises Volume participation from 0.01 to 1 so that every order fills at once. Which comment is most accurate?
options: Fills become easier than a real market is likely to allow, so results will look better for a reason that will not repeat
The change is harmless, because participation only affects the commission
The change makes the whole simulated market more liquid for every other participant
questions.explanation: Participation is a limit on how much of a bar your orders can take. Raising it to the maximum removes a realistic constraint and flatters results.

questions.question: An entry's take-profit and stop-loss are both inside one bar's range. Which does the terminal take?
options: The take-profit, because it is the better outcome for the account
Both, so the position is sold twice
The stop-loss, because it cannot see the order of prices inside the bar and takes the less flattering reading
questions.explanation: Exits are one-cancels-other, and when one bar covers both the conservative rule takes the stop first.

questions.question: What does the simulator charge for holding borrowed shares?
options: The company's dividends, paid to the lender each quarter
A borrow fee of 5% a year, charged once per session as its own ledger line
Nothing, because borrowing is free in paper trading
questions.explanation: The fee appears in Account history once per session. Dividends are not modelled in either direction.

exams.title: Unit 3: Research, review and discipline
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: When in the simulated session do company results arrive?
options: At a session open, so the result arrives with the gap it causes
At the close, after trading has finished
At a random minute inside the session
questions.explanation: Prints land on a session open, which is why the first bar of that session carries most of the reaction.

questions.question: Why does the Screener offer named screens such as Oversold rather than free-form thresholds?
options: Free-form thresholds take too long for the server to compute
Named screens guarantee that the listed stocks will rise
A named screen is a hypothesis fixed in advance, while tuning a threshold after seeing results fits the filter to the answer
questions.explanation: Choosing the threshold after seeing which names rose builds the answer into the screen, which is the screening version of data snooping.

questions.question: Why does an exported CSV cell that begins with '=' gain an apostrophe?
options: To show that the value is negative
To stop a spreadsheet from executing it as a formula when the file is opened
To mark values that changed after the export
questions.explanation: Cells starting with =, +, − or @ can be interpreted as formulas. The apostrophe keeps them as text.

questions.question: What does the objective 'Close every position before finishing' require?
options: No shares held once a full week of bars has passed since your first order
Selling every position at a profit
Closing all positions before the first session ends
questions.explanation: The objective is met when a full week (1,950 bars) has passed since your first order and the account holds no shares.

exams.title: Trading simulator workshop final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: What happens to an earlier run when you click New simulation run and then Create new paper account?
options: It stays in the run history as an archived run that you can review and export but not trade
Its cash is reset to $100,000 in place and its history is erased
It is deleted together with its trade journal
questions.explanation: A new run is a new account. Earlier runs remain under Simulation run history as archived runs, open for review and export only.

questions.question: You type NVRA FA in the Command dialog and press Enter. What happens?
options: A buy ticket for Novara opens in the Trade tab
The dialog stays open because FA is not a valid code
Novara is selected and the Company tab opens in the bottom panel
questions.explanation: A ticker followed by a function code does both in turn. FA is the code for company financials, which live in the Company tab.

questions.question: From Day 2, bar 110 a learner clicks Next replay bar and then 1h. Which counter should the replay bar show?
questions.explanation: The step moves the clock from index 499 to 500 and the 1h jump to 560. Index 560 is Day 2, bar 171, because 560 mod 390 = 170 and the bar number adds 1.

questions.question: Two scored items are released, a high negative one and a low positive one, together with ten routine chatter items. What is the tone?
options: −0.50, because (−3 + 1) ÷ (3 + 1) and chatter has weight zero
−0.14, because each chatter item adds a weight of 1 to the total
−2.00, because the signed weights add to −2
questions.explanation: Tone divides the signed weight by the total weight of scored items. Chatter has weight zero, so (−3 + 1) ÷ (3 + 1) = −0.50.

questions.question: A learner previews a market buy and the ticket shows an Estimated debit. After Place buy order, what is true?
options: Reserved cash stays at zero until the order fills, because it is not final
The shares are owned immediately and the cash is spent
That estimate is reserved as cash, and nothing is owned until a later bar fills the order
questions.explanation: Acceptance reserves the estimated cost and commission so the cash cannot be committed twice. Ownership changes only when a later bar fills the order.

questions.question: Two market buys in the same stock are open: A for 500 shares, placed first, and B for 50 shares. The next bar's capacity is 120. What do they receive?
options: A and B each receive 60 shares, split evenly
A receives 120 shares and B receives none
A receives 70 shares and B receives 50, so the smaller order completes
questions.explanation: Capacity is shared first in, first out. A arrived first and can absorb all 120 shares, so B waits until A has been served or cancelled.

questions.question: A 5% trailing stop is placed when the close is 150.00. The next bar's high is 153.00 and its low 149.00. Which stop does the following bar use?
options: 145.35, because the anchor rises to the 153.00 high after the bar is tested
142.50, because a trailing stop's anchor never moves
141.55, because the stop follows the bar's low
questions.explanation: Each bar is tested against the stop it opened with, then the anchor ratchets to the new high: 153.00 × 0.95 = 145.35.

questions.question: In the simulator, when is a short position bought in?
options: Whenever the stock rises 10% above the short price
At the end of every session, automatically
When equity falls below 30% of gross exposure
questions.explanation: The maintenance rule compares equity with 30% of gross exposure; falling below it triggers a buy-in order that queues like any other.

questions.question: Why does P/E show '—' for some companies in the terminal?
options: Ratios are computed only for the largest companies
Its denominator is zero or negative, so a ratio would be misleading
The company is hiding its earnings from the market
questions.explanation: A ratio with a zero or non-positive denominator is returned as null and shown as '—'. Development-stage companies with losses are an example.

questions.question: How do the prints in the Time & sales window relate to your fills?
options: They are an illustration consistent with the bar's open, high, low, close and volume, and never affect fills
Your orders fill against those prints one by one
They are the recorded tape of a real exchange
questions.explanation: The tape is generated inside each bar's limits for reading practice. Fills come only from the bar's prices under the execution rules.

questions.question: Only 6 sessions have closed and the panel shows a Sharpe ratio of 3.1. What should you conclude?
options: That the approach is excellent and should be scaled up
That the account carried no risk during the period
Very little: annualizing so few returns produces a number, not a measurement
questions.explanation: The panel warns below 20 closed sessions because annualized ratios from a handful of returns are dominated by noise.

questions.question: A position breached the cap and was cut back the next bar at a profit. How does the cap objective treat it?
options: As satisfied, because the trade made money
As a breach, because the cap is judged on the largest holding the run ever carried
As satisfied, because the position was reduced afterwards
questions.explanation: The cap looks at the peak holding, so reducing it later does not undo the breach, and profit does not excuse it.

modules.title: A tour of the lab and the research loop
modules.subtitle: Name the five tools on the Strategy lab page, run the default experiment, and use the four-step research loop to read one result honestly.
modules.objective: Name the five tools on the Strategy lab page, run the default experiment, and use the four-step research loop to read one result honestly.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the tour, 10 minutes working the default run by hand and 12 minutes in the Market sandbox, where the default data is synthetic and every result is a teaching device rather than evidence of a real edge.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The Strategy lab is a research bench: a place to test an idea against assumptions you control, not a trading account. One page holds five tools. The Market sandbox runs a Python rule on a generated market. Valuation turns balance-sheet numbers into per-share values. The Factor studio fits a regression to returns whose true exposures are known. Paper trading sends one order at a time to a mock broker with safety guards. The AMM simulator follows a constant-product liquidity pool. Two companion pages keep your work: Saved experiments stores the code and settings of a run, and My notebook stores your reasoning.

The lab is built around a loop: state a hypothesis you could disprove, change one assumption, read the evidence, and keep a research trail. The default data is synthetic and generated from a seed, so the same settings always give the same bars and every change is a controlled comparison. That is also the lab's limit. A synthetic market has no real news, companies or crowds, so a good result shows that your mechanics work, never that an edge exists. The display below is the comparison we use throughout: a rule's total return against holding the same market.

$$
R=\frac{E_{\text{final}}}{E_{0}}-1,\qquad \Delta R=R_{\text{rule}}-R_{\text{hold}}
$$

## A worked example

Take the hypothesis printed beside the sandbox: a trend rule reduces drawdown in a persistent bear regime. The default market is a three-year geometric Brownian motion path with 8% drift and 20% volatility, seed 42, $100,000 of starting capital, 5 bps commission and 3 bps slippage. That path happens to fall, from about 100 to about 81.70. With the default rule (hold when the close is above its 50-bar average), expect roughly these results: final equity near $76,598, so R = 76,598 ÷ 100,000 − 1 ≈ −23.4%, and a MAX DRAWDOWN near −27.1%.

Now compare with holding. The Buy & hold quick-strategy chip finishes near $81,536, so R ≈ 81,536 ÷ 100,000 − 1 ≈ −18.5%, with a maximum drawdown near −34.2%. The rule's return gap is ΔR ≈ −23.4% − (−18.5%) = −4.9 percentage points, but its worst fall was about 34.2 − 27.1 = 7.1 points shallower. The evidence is mixed and comes from one path: the hypothesis holds on drawdown, fails on return, and says nothing yet about other seeds, costs or scenarios. That is exactly what the next steps of the loop are for.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the lab.** In the sidebar choose **Strategy lab**. The heading reads “Ideas become clearer when you test them.” and five tabs sit beneath it: **Market sandbox**, **Valuation**, **Factor studio**, **Paper trading** and **AMM simulator**. Click each one and watch the address change to `/lab?tool=` followed by market, valuation, factors, broker or amm. Switching tabs discards the tool you leave, including its results, inputs and paper account, so write down any number you need before you click away. Only strategy code is kept, as a draft.

**Start from the default rule.** Click **Market sandbox**, then **strategy.py**. The editor should show `return data["close"] > data["sma_50"]`. If it does not, an earlier visit left a draft: open **Parameters** and click the **Trend following** chip under QUICK STRATEGY, or click the **Restore lesson code** icon above the editor.

**Run the experiment.** Click **Run experiment**, or press Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter with the cursor in the editor. Under EXPERIMENT OUTPUT read the four cards: CAGR, SHARPE, MAX DRAWDOWN and WIN RATE. With the default settings, expect roughly −8.5%, −0.92, −27.1% and 17.2%. Open **All metrics** and find “total return” near −0.2340 and “trades” at 59.0000, then open **Console**: it ends with a line like “756 bars · 59 fills · final equity $76,598.46”.

**Compare with holding.** Click **Parameters**, then the **Buy & hold** chip, then **Run experiment**. MAX DRAWDOWN should read about −34.2% and “total return” in **All metrics** about −0.1846. The chip is a strategy that returns True on every bar, so it enters one bar later than the dashed Buy & hold line on the **Equity curve** and differs from it by a hair. Click the **Trend following** chip to restore the rule.

**Read the loop.** Beside the sandbox, the panel THE RESEARCH LOOP lists four steps: State a hypothesis, Change one assumption, Read the evidence and Keep a research trail. Write the hypothesis you just tested as one sentence that a result could prove wrong.

**Meet the lesson worksheet.** Every lesson also has a worksheet under Try the lesson template. Click **Run in sandbox**, then **Run experiment**: the Console prints the lesson's arithmetic, while the cards show CAGR 0.0%, SHARPE —, MAX DRAWDOWN 0.0% and WIN RATE — because the worksheet's strategy stays in cash. It is an arithmetic aid; real experiments belong in the lab.

**See where work is kept.** Click **Saved experiments** at the top right of the lab page, then **My notebook** in the sidebar. On a new workspace they show “An idea is worth revisiting.” and “Make space for a good question.”

**What you should see.** A losing default run is normal in this market. The chart legend shows SYNTHETIC DATA, and the panel beside the sandbox says “Default data is synthetic.” Our figures were computed with the same code as the lab, so a small difference usually means a changed setting: check the seed and the costs first.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and repeat the default run, write one disprovable hypothesis about the trend rule in your notebook, and record the four card values and the Buy & hold drawdown. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

assignment.prompt: Write a short research note for the default run: one hypothesis about the trend rule that a result could disprove, the single assumption you will change first, the four card values, the Buy & hold maximum drawdown and total return, and one result that would make you drop the hypothesis.
assignment.solution: A good note names a testable claim, for example: the 50-bar trend rule has a shallower maximum drawdown than Buy & hold on synthetic GBM markets. It records the baseline (CAGR about −8.5%, Sharpe about −0.92, maximum drawdown about −27.1%, win rate about 17.2%, and for Buy & hold a drawdown near −34.2% and a total return near −18.5%), says the first change will be the seed, and states a falsifier such as: if the rule's drawdown is not shallower on most of five seeds, drop the claim. It also admits that the evidence so far is one path, that the return is worse than holding, and that synthetic data cannot establish a real edge.

terms.definition: A measured influence used to describe returns or risk across investments, such as a market return or a defined style portfolio. Its meaning depends on how it is constructed.

A model that relates an outcome to one or more inputs. The fitted coefficients describe the relationship under the model; they need separate checks before being used for prediction or causal explanation.
The ability to trade the required quantity within the desired time and price conditions. Displayed prices alone do not establish the cost of trading a larger amount.
The decline in portfolio value from an earlier peak to a later value. Drawdown depth, time spent below the peak, and recovery time describe different parts of the experience.

realWorld.connection: A research loop starts from a question that could come out either way, the same discipline an evaluator needs before crediting a training programme with higher sales.
realWorld.task: A fictional learner opens the lab and writes 'trend following works'. Rewrite it as a claim the sandbox could contradict, naming the rule, the comparison, the metric and the number of seeds (illustrative).
realWorld.walkthrough: A usable version reads like 'close above the 50-day average has a shallower maximum drawdown than buy and hold on at least four of five seeds, with default costs'. It fixes a comparison and a threshold before any run, so a result can reject it. 'Works' can never be wrong, which is why it teaches nothing.

modules.title: Generate a market: processes, scenarios and seeds
modules.subtitle: Choose a stochastic process, scenario, horizon and seed, predict what each will do to the generated bars, and explain why one seed is only one possible path.
modules.objective: Choose a stochastic process, scenario, horizon and seed, predict what each will do to the generated bars, and explain why one seed is only one possible path.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading how the lab generates bars, 10 minutes reproducing the seed-42 arithmetic and 12 minutes changing processes, scenarios and seeds in the Market sandbox, whose default data is synthetic.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The sandbox does not download prices; it generates them. Each bar comes from a stochastic process, which is a rule for drawing random daily returns. The series starts at a price of 100 on 2 January 2020 and uses a weekday calendar with 252 bars a year. Geometric Brownian motion (GBM) draws independent returns with a fixed drift and volatility. Merton jump-diffusion adds occasional jumps, Heston stochastic volatility lets the variance itself wander, and Markov regime switching hops between a calm, a flat and a crash regime. Real markets show fat tails and volatility clustering, which is why the lab offers more than one process.

A seed makes the randomness repeatable: the same settings and the same seed give identical bars, so you can change one setting and see only that setting's effect. It also means a run is one path out of many. A named scenario can override the process settings, so the sliders may keep showing your values while the scenario is in charge, and the scenario names are inspired by history but only illustrate stress mechanisms; they do not recreate historical events. The display below is the daily rule for GBM, where μ is the annual drift, σ the annual volatility and z a standard normal draw fixed by the seed.

$$
r_t=\frac{\mu-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}}{252}+\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{252}}\,z_t,\qquad P_t=P_{t-1}\,e^{r_t}
$$

## A worked example

Run the defaults: GBM, 8% drift, 20% volatility, a three-year horizon and seed 42. The lab creates 3 × 252 = 756 bars from Thursday 2 January 2020 to Thursday 24 November 2022. With the probe in the steps below you should read a first open near 100.09 and a last close near 81.70, a price return of 81.70 ÷ 100 − 1 ≈ −18.3% in a market whose drift is +8% a year.

Is that a bug? Work it out. Expected log growth over three years is (0.08 − 0.20² ÷ 2) × 3 = 0.06 × 3 = 0.18, and one standard deviation of the three-year log return is 0.20 × √3 ≈ 0.346. The seed-42 path has a log return of ln(0.817) ≈ −0.202, which is (−0.202 − 0.18) ÷ 0.346 ≈ −1.1 standard deviations from expectation. Roughly one path in seven ends that low, so seed 42 is an unlucky draw, not an error. Drift describes the average over many paths; it is never a promise about one.

## Put the idea into practice

**Add a probe.** Open the **Market sandbox** and click **strategy.py**. Above the `return` line, add three lines, each indented four spaces: `print("Bars:", len(data["close"]))`, `print("First open:", round(data["open"][0], 2))` and `print("Last close:", round(data["close"][-1], 2))`. They only read the data and do not change the signal.

**Run the baseline.** Click **Run experiment**. The Console opens by itself because the code prints. With the default settings, expect Bars: 756, First open: 100.09 and Last close: 81.7. The Console shows numbers the way Python prints them, so 81.70 appears as 81.7.

**Change the process.** Click **Parameters**. The **Stochastic process** select offers Geometric Brownian motion, Merton jump-diffusion, Heston stochastic volatility and Markov regime switching. Choose Merton jump-diffusion: the **Jumps per year** slider appears at 1, and the last close should come out near 104.93. Drag **Jumps per year** to 0 and run again: with no jumps Merton collapses to the GBM path and the last close returns to 81.7. Choose Heston stochastic volatility to reveal **Mean reversion κ**, **Long-run variance θ**, **Vol of variance ξ** and **Correlation ρ**; expect a last close near 92.78. Choose Markov regime switching and note that **Annual drift** and **Annual volatility** stop mattering; expect about 55.61.

**Change the horizon.** Put the process back to Geometric Brownian motion, then open the **Horizon** select, which offers 1 year, 3 years, 5 years, 10 years, 20 years and 30 years. Choose 1 year: you get 252 bars and a last close near 91.07. With GBM the 1-year run is exactly the first 252 bars of the 3-year run, a fact lesson 14.4 uses to test for look-ahead.

**Try a scenario.** Above the editor, open the **SCENARIO** select: Custom market, Pure random walk, Deflationary crash · 1929-inspired, Stagflation · 1970s-inspired, Liquidity crisis · 2008-inspired and Crypto flash crash · −50%. Choose Crypto flash crash · −50% and run, then open the **Market** tab and look at the middle of the chart, around mid-June 2021: the price roughly halves in a single day, and the last close should be near 40.85. The flash crash keeps your process and sliders and only adds the shock. The 1929-, 1970s- and 2008-inspired scenarios behave differently: they override the process, drift and volatility (the 2008-inspired one runs Heston with −18% drift and 55% volatility) while the sliders keep showing your values.

**Change the seed.** Click the gear icon in the sandbox header (**Execution settings**) and change **Seed** from 42 to 7. The seed is not on the **Parameters** tab. Run again: expect a last close near 45.54. Try 1 and 3 as well (about 68.85 and 195.65), then set the seed back to 42 and the original numbers return exactly.

**What you should see.** The same settings and seed always print the same three lines, and a different seed gives a different path from the same process. That is why a single run proves little. The API also has a synthetic-data endpoint that returns the bars directly; the lab has no screen for it.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and run the probe on seed 42 for each process, then on seeds 1, 2 and 3 for GBM, and write the six last closes next to the one change that produced each. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

modules.title: Write a strategy in the guided Python runtime
modules.subtitle: Write a long-or-cash rule as strategy(data), build signals from whole-series operations instead of loops, and recognize the runtime's limits and look-ahead traps.
modules.objective: Write a long-or-cash rule as strategy(data), build signals from whole-series operations instead of loops, and recognize the runtime's limits and look-ahead traps.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the runtime rules, 10 minutes reproducing the toy loop and cost arithmetic and 12 minutes writing rules in the Market sandbox, whose default data is synthetic and whose wins are never proof of a real edge.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A strategy in the lab is one function, `strategy(data)`. It receives the whole history at once as named series: open, high, low, close, volume, returns, sma_50 and sma_200. It must return a long-or-cash signal: one True or False (or 1 or 0) for every bar, or a single Boolean that applies to every bar. The guided runtime is a small interpreter for a subset of Python, not the full language. It supports assignments, def with positional parameters, if and else, for loops over lists or ranges, comparisons, arithmetic, f-strings, print, a few built-ins and selected math and numpy functions. Anything else fails closed with a plain message instead of doing something surprising. The moving averages use whatever bars exist at the start, so early signals rest on short averages.

Signals are series, so rules are written with whole-series operations: compare series with > and <, combine them with & and |, and wrap each comparison in brackets. Loops are for scalar summaries, because the runtime has no append, no list concatenation and no way to assign to one element of a list. Two limits matter: a two-second budget and 750,000 operations. Finally, the runtime hands your function the entire history, including bars after the one being judged. The engine delays your signal by one bar, but it cannot see what your code looked at, so a threshold built from a whole-sample statistic such as the highest close quietly uses the future.

$$
s_t=\begin{cases}1 & C_t>\overline{C}_{t,n}\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases},\qquad \overline{C}_{t,n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}C_{t-j}
$$

## A worked example

On the default market (seed 42, 5 bps commission, 3 bps slippage), the rule `data["close"] > data["sma_50"]` produces 59 fills and a total return near −23.4%. Write it again with `np.where(close > average, 1, 0)` and the result must be identical, which is the check that two forms of a rule agree. Add a 2% buffer, `data["close"] > data["sma_50"] * 1.02`, and expect 56 fills and about −22.4%. Require the 50-bar average to sit above the 200-bar average and expect 24 fills and about −9.1%.

Why do the fills matter? Each fill pays about 8 bps (5 bps commission plus 3 bps slippage) on roughly $88,600 of value, which is 88,600 × 0.0008 ≈ $71 per fill. Fifty-nine fills cost about 59 × $71 ≈ $4,200, and 24 fills of the same size would cost about $1,700. The last rule loses less partly because it trades less, and partly because one seed is one path, not because it has shown skill.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the editor.** In the **Market sandbox**, click **strategy.py**. The default function has one working line, `return data["close"] > data["sma_50"]`. If the editor shows something else, open **Parameters** and click the **Trend following** chip.

**Count with sum.** Above the return line, add `print("Bars above the average:", sum(data["close"] > data["sma_50"]))`. Run: the Console should print about 309, roughly 41% of the 756 bars, because summing a series of True and False values counts the True ones. The rule is in the market only about two bars in five.

**Write the same rule with numpy.** Add `import numpy as np` as the first line and change the return line to `return np.where(data["close"] > data["sma_50"], 1, 0)`. Run. The cards and the Console summary should match the default run exactly: −8.5%, −0.92, −27.1%, 17.2% and 59 fills. Identical outputs are your evidence that two ways of writing a rule agree.

**Add a condition.** Change the return line to `(data["close"] > data["sma_50"]) & (data["sma_50"] > data["sma_200"])`. Keep the brackets. Expect 24 fills and a total return near −9.1%. Now delete the brackets: `&` binds tighter than `>`, so the line becomes a chained comparison and the run fails with “SandboxError: Use separate comparisons joined with & for series.” Using the word `and` between two series fails too: “Use & and | for series comparisons.”

**Add a buffer.** Try `data["close"] > data["sma_50"] * 1.02`. Expect 56 fills and about −22.4%. Trading less trims costs, but costs are only part of the story.

**Meet the guard rails.** Try each of these and read the red alert under the run bar: `import pandas as pd` (“Imports are limited to math and the guided numpy subset.”), a `while` loop (“While is not supported. Use bounded for loops and documented functions.”) and a return value such as `data["close"] * 0 + 0.5` (“Only long/cash signals (True/False or 1/0) are supported.”). Messages begin with SandboxError. Then restore the default rule with the **Trend following** chip.

**Spot the look-ahead.** Do not run this one for results, only to see why it is wrong: `data["close"] > max(data["close"]) * 0.9`. The runtime accepts it, because the maximum of a series is allowed, but the threshold uses the highest close of the whole history, which nobody knows in real time. Lesson 14.4 gives you a test that catches it.

**What you should see.** Each valid variant runs in a fraction of a second and shows its fill count in the Console summary, so you can compare rules by their fills as well as their returns. The runtime stops anything slower than two seconds or heavier than 750,000 operations, and limits code to 20,000 characters and printed output to 20 KB. Treat that as a design hint: write a rule as a few whole-series expressions. An optional Docker runtime, set up by whoever runs the lab, allows full Python; the default does not.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and rewrite the default rule two more ways, one with np.where and one with an extra condition, and record the fill count and total return of each. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

close = [100, 101, 99, 102, 104, 103, 105, 101]
window = 3
signal_count = 0
fills = 0
holding = 0
for i in range(len(close)):
    start = max(0, i - window + 1)
    total = 0
    for j in range(start, i + 1):
        total += close[j]
    average = total / (i + 1 - start)
    if close[i] > average:
        signal = 1
    else:
        signal = 0
    signal_count += signal
    if signal != holding:
        fills += 1
        holding = signal
print("Bars with a long signal:", signal_count)
print("Signal changes, one fill each:", fills)
bps = 5 + 3
notional = 88616
per_fill = notional * bps / 10000
print("Cost per fill at 8 bps:", round(per_fill, 2))
print("Cost of 59 fills:", round(59 * per_fill))
print("Cost of 24 fills of the same size:", round(24 * per_fill))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.solution: The default rule gives 59 fills and about −23.4%, and the np.where form must give exactly the same numbers because it is the same rule. The extra-condition rule gives 24 fills and about −9.1%; the 2% buffer gives 56 fills and about −22.4%. A fill costs about 8 bps on roughly $88,600, or $71, so 59 fills cost about $4,200 and 24 fills of that size about $1,700. Fewer fills explain part of the improvement and the rest is the luck of one seed, so neither result shows skill; it only shows how a rule's trading frequency feeds into costs.

modules.title: Backtest mechanics: signals, fills, costs and buy-and-hold
modules.subtitle: Trace how a signal becomes a fill at the next open, compute the cost of a round trip, read the buy-and-hold comparison, and run a test that catches look-ahead.
modules.objective: Trace how a signal becomes a fill at the next open, compute the cost of a round trip, read the buy-and-hold comparison, and run a test that catches look-ahead.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 7 minutes reading the execution rules, 9 minutes reproducing the round-trip arithmetic and 14 minutes tracing trades and running the look-ahead test in the Market sandbox; the lab's default data is synthetic, so no result is evidence of a real edge.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The backtest turns your signal into trades with a fixed timing rule: a signal formed on one bar's close trades at the next bar's open. The account is long or in cash, all in, and it may hold fractional shares. A buy pays the open plus slippage and then a commission on top; a sale receives the open minus slippage and pays a commission on its proceeds. Every trade's profit or loss is net of both costs. A position still open at the end is marked to the last close and left out of the win rate and profit factor.

The comparison line, "Buy & hold", buys at the first bar's open, pays the entry costs once and never sells, so it has no exit cost. That is the honest benchmark for a long-or-cash rule on one market: if your rule cannot beat simply owning the asset after costs, its trading is not adding anything. The one-bar delay stops a bar from trading on its own close, but it cannot see inside your code, so the look-ahead from lesson 14.3 needs its own test.

$$
P^{\text{buy}}_t=O_t(1+s),\quad q=\frac{\text{cash}}{P^{\text{buy}}_t(1+c)},\qquad \text{proceeds}=q\,O_{t'}(1-s)(1-c)
$$

## A worked example

Your rule turns long at a close of 100.00 and the next open is 101.00. With $100,000, 3 bps of slippage and a 5 bps commission, the buy price is 101.00 × 1.0003 = 101.0303, and the shares are 100,000 ÷ (101.0303 × 1.0005) ≈ 989.31. Later the rule turns off and the next open is 104.00. The sale price is 104.00 × 0.9997 = 103.9688, the proceeds are about $102,857.10 and the 5 bps commission takes about $51.43, leaving roughly $102,805.67, a net gain of about 2.81% against a 2.97% move in the price.

Here is the look-ahead test promised in lesson 14.3. Run a rule on Horizon "1 year" and again on "3 years" with the same seed, then compare the trades inside the first year. The first 252 bars are identical, so a rule that only looks backwards must make identical first-year trades. On seed 42 the trend rule makes 28 trades both times. The rule that compares the close with 0.9 × the maximum close makes 22 first-year trades on the short run but only 10 on the long one, because its threshold moved when later bars were added. Different trades on identical data are proof that the rule peeked.

## Put the idea into practice

**Run the default rule.** In the **Market sandbox**, click the **Trend following** chip and then **Run experiment** (or Ctrl/Cmd+Enter in the editor). The **Console** ends with a summary such as "756 bars · 59 fills · final equity …".

**Follow one trade.** Open the **Trades** tab. Its columns are Date, Side, Quantity, Price, Fee and P&L. Take the first BUY row's date, open the **Market** tab ("OHLC prices") and find that day's open. The Price column should equal the open × 1.0003.

**Compare with buy and hold.** Open **Equity curve**. The legend shows "Strategy" and "Buy & hold". Then click the **Buy & hold** chip and run it: its total return in **All metrics** should match the end of the Buy & hold line.

**Switch costs off and on.** Click the gear icon (aria "Execution settings"), set **Commission (bps)** and **Slippage (bps)** to 0, restore the **Trend following** chip and run. Note the final equity. Set both to 20 and run again. The fill count stays the same while the final equity falls, because costs never change the signals.

**Run the look-ahead test.** Open **Parameters**, set **Horizon** to "1 year" and run the rule `data["close"] > max(data["close"]) * 0.9`. Note the first-year trades. Set **Horizon** to "3 years", run again and count the trades dated inside the first year. Repeat with the default trend rule.

**What you should see.** Fills dated one bar after each signal, prices equal to the open adjusted by slippage, and identical first-year trades for the trend rule but not for the maximum-based rule.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and rerun the default rule with costs at 0, at the defaults and at 20 bps each, then run the one-year versus three-year look-ahead test on two rules and record what changes. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

slippage = 3 / 10000
commission = 5 / 10000
buy_price = 101.00 * (1 + slippage)
shares = cash / (buy_price * (1 + commission))
sell_price = 104.00 * (1 - slippage)
proceeds = shares * sell_price
net = proceeds * (1 - commission)
print("Buy price:", round(buy_price, 4), "shares:", round(shares, 2))
print("Sale price:", round(sell_price, 4), "net proceeds:", round(net, 2))
print("Net gain:", round((net / cash - 1) * 100, 2), "% against a price move of", round((104 / 101 - 1) * 100, 2), "%")
first_year_short = 22
first_year_long = 10
print("Look-ahead rule trades in year one, 1-year run vs 3-year run:", first_year_short, first_year_long)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

In the look-ahead test the trend rule makes 28 first-year trades on both horizons, while the maximum-based rule makes 22 on the 1-year run and 10 on the 3-year run. A rule whose past trades change when future data is added is using the future, so its backtest cannot be trusted.

modules.title: Read the results: metrics, charts, monthly returns and the trade log
modules.subtitle: Read the four cards and all 14 metrics, connect each chart to the numbers behind it, and explain why no single metric can rank a rule.
modules.objective: Read the four cards and all 14 metrics, connect each chart to the numbers behind it, and explain why no single metric can rank a rule.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the metric definitions, 9 minutes recomputing CAGR and Calmar and 13 minutes reading the cards, charts and trade log in the Market sandbox; the lab's default data is synthetic, so no metric is evidence of a real edge.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

After a run, the four cards show CAGR, SHARPE, MAX DRAWDOWN and WIN RATE, and **All metrics** lists fourteen values with four decimals. CAGR compounds the total return over 252 bars a year. Sharpe and Sortino subtract a 3% annual risk-free rate from the daily returns and divide by their variability (all of it for Sharpe, only the downside for Sortino), scaled by √252. Maximum drawdown is the deepest fall from a running peak, and Calmar divides CAGR by its size. Beta and alpha compare the rule's daily returns with buy and hold, and VaR and CVaR at 95% describe the worst daily losses.

A metric that cannot be computed shows "—" on a card and "Undefined" in All metrics, never a flattering zero. An all-cash rule has no variability, so its Sharpe is undefined; a rule with no closed trades has no win rate. The tabs show the same run from different angles: Equity curve, Drawdown, Market, a Returns heat map by month, Trades, Console and All metrics. If you change a setting after running, the run time gains "· inputs changed" to warn you that the output no longer matches the controls.

$$
\text{Sharpe}=\frac{\bar r-r_f}{s_r}\sqrt{252},\qquad \text{Calmar}=\frac{\text{CAGR}}{\left|\text{MDD}\right|}
$$

## A worked example

With the default settings the Trend following run returns −23.40% over 756 bars. CAGR is (1 − 0.2340)^(252 ÷ 756) − 1 = 0.766^(1/3) − 1 ≈ −8.5%, the card's value. The deepest drawdown is −27.07%, so Calmar is −0.085 ÷ 0.2707 ≈ −0.31. The run made 59 fills, 30 buys and 29 sales, so there are 29 closed round trips; a win rate of 17.2% means 5 of them made money, and a profit factor of 0.32 says the winners earned about a third of what the losers lost.

Now click the Mean reversion chip on the same seed. Its win rate is 76.7%, yet its total return is −2.37%. Many small wins and a few large losses produce exactly that pattern, which is why a win rate is meaningless without the size of wins and losses, the drawdown and the comparison with buy and hold.

## Put the idea into practice

**Run and read the cards.** Run the **Trend following** chip with the defaults. Read CAGR, SHARPE, MAX DRAWDOWN and WIN RATE, then open **All metrics** and find total return, profit factor, trades, final equity, alpha, beta, VaR 95%, CVaR 95% and Calmar.

**Check two numbers by hand.** Recompute CAGR from total return and the bar count, and Calmar from CAGR and maximum drawdown, using the worksheet. They should match the panel to the second decimal.

**Read the charts.** Open **Drawdown** ("Drawdown from peak") and find the date of the deepest point. Open **Returns** and find the worst month in the heat map; empty months show "—". Open **Trades** and count the rows with a positive P&L.

**Compare a second rule.** Click **Mean reversion**, run it, and write both rules' fourteen metrics side by side in your notebook.

**Make the output stale on purpose.** Move the **Annual volatility** slider without running, and look for "· inputs changed" beside the run time.

**What you should see.** Hand-computed CAGR and Calmar that match the panel, a mean-reversion run with a high win rate and a negative total return, and a stale-output warning after any change you have not run.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and run the Trend following and Mean reversion chips on the same seed and compare all fourteen metrics side by side. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

modules.title: The valuation tool: net current assets, haircuts and Graham value
modules.subtitle: Use the Valuation tab to compute unadjusted and adjusted net current asset value, the two-thirds screen and the Graham heuristic, and test how sensitive each is to its assumptions.
modules.objective: Use the Valuation tab to compute unadjusted and adjusted net current asset value, the two-thirds screen and the Graham heuristic, and test how sensitive each is to its assumptions.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading how the tool values a balance sheet, 10 minutes reproducing the NCAV and heuristic arithmetic and 12 minutes stressing the inputs in the Valuation tab; every company in the tool is fictional.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Net current asset value (NCAV) asks what would be left for shareholders if a company collected its current assets and paid every liability. It counts cash, receivables and inventory, subtracts total liabilities and divides by diluted shares, giving fixed assets no value at all. The tool shows that unadjusted figure, a two-thirds screen price that Graham-style investors used as a demanding entry point, and an adjusted NCAV that applies recovery rates: in a forced sale, customers pay late or not at all and inventory sells at a discount.

The tool also computes the Graham heuristic, earnings per share × (8.5 + 2 × growth) × 4.4 ÷ bond yield, with growth and yield entered in percentage points. It is a sensitivity device, not a price: small changes to growth or yield swing it widely. All amounts are in millions except per-share values, the outputs update about a quarter of a second after each edit, and nothing here describes a real company.

$$
\text{NCAV}_{\text{adj}}=\frac{C+\rho_R R+\rho_I I-L}{N},\qquad \text{MoS}=1-\frac{P}{\text{NCAV}_{\text{adj}}}
$$

## A worked example

The defaults describe a company with $40m of cash, $60m of receivables, $80m of inventory, $70m of liabilities and 10m diluted shares at $6. Unadjusted NCAV is (40 + 60 + 80 − 70) ÷ 10 = $11.00 per share, and the two-thirds screen price is $7.33, so the stock passes the screen. Recovering 85% of receivables and 60% of inventory gives (40 + 51 + 48 − 70) ÷ 10 = $6.90, and the margin of safety against that adjusted value is 1 − 6 ÷ 6.90 ≈ 13.0%.

Cut inventory recovery to 40% and adjusted NCAV falls to (40 + 51 + 32 − 70) ÷ 10 = $5.30, so the price now exceeds the adjusted value by about 13%, while the unadjusted screen still passes. The Graham heuristic with EPS $4, growth 5 and yield 4.4 is 4 × 18.5 × 4.4 ÷ 4.4 = $74.00; raising the yield to 6 lowers it to about $54.27.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the tool.** Click the **Valuation** tab. Under "BALANCE SHEET INPUTS" (amounts in millions, except per-share values) you will find **Cash & equivalents**, **Accounts receivable**, **Inventory**, **Total liabilities**, **Diluted shares** and **Market price / share**.

**Read the worksheet.** The panel "VALUATION WORKSHEET" shows "ADJUSTED NCAV / SHARE", a bar comparing "Market price" with "Adjusted asset value", "Unadjusted NCAV", "Two-thirds screen price", "Margin of safety · adjusted NCAV" and "Graham heuristic value", plus a verdict that begins "Passes the unadjusted two-thirds NCAV screen." or "Does not pass".

**Stress the recoveries.** Under **Liquidation assumptions**, drag **Inventory recovered** from 60% down to 40%. Watch "· UPDATING" appear briefly and the adjusted value fall to $5.30 while the screen verdict stays the same.

**Stress the heuristic.** Under **Graham formula inputs**, change **Bond yield (%)** from 4.4 to 6, then **Growth (%)** from 5 to 10, and note how far the value moves.

**What you should see.** An adjusted value that is always at or below the unadjusted one, a margin of safety that turns negative once recoveries fall far enough, and a heuristic that moves sharply with growth and yield.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Valuation](/lab?tool=valuation) and move the two recovery sliders until the margin of safety reaches zero, and record the recovery rates at which the price equals the adjusted asset value. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

print("Unadjusted NCAV:", ncav, "two-thirds screen:", round(ncav * 2 / 3, 2))
for inventory_rate in [0.60, 0.40]:
    adjusted = (cash + 0.85 * receivables + inventory_rate * inventory - liabilities) / shares
    print("Inventory recovery", inventory_rate, "adjusted NCAV:", round(adjusted, 2), "margin of safety:", round((1 - price / adjusted) * 100, 1), "%")
for bond_yield in [4.4, 6.0]:
    print("Graham value at yield", bond_yield, ":", round(4 * (8.5 + 2 * 5) * 4.4 / bond_yield, 2))

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

assignment.prompt: Find the inventory recovery rate at which the adjusted NCAV equals the $6 price, using the default inputs. Then record the Graham heuristic at growth 0, 5 and 10 with a 4.4 yield, and explain which output you would trust least and why.
assignment.solution: Adjusted NCAV is (40 + 0.85 × 60 + r × 80 − 70) ÷ 10; setting it to 6 gives 21 + 80r = 60, so r = 48.75%. Below that recovery rate the price exceeds the adjusted asset value. The Graham heuristic gives $34.00 at zero growth, $74.00 at 5 and $114.00 at 10, so a five-point change in assumed growth moves it by $40. It deserves the least trust because its result depends almost entirely on a growth guess, while the asset-based values rest on balance-sheet items you can check.

modules.title: The factor studio: models, coefficients and robust errors
modules.subtitle: Fit CAPM and Fama–French models to known synthetic data, read each coefficient with its HAC standard error, and judge an alpha estimate by its uncertainty rather than its size.
modules.objective: Fit CAPM and Fama–French models to known synthetic data, read each coefficient with its HAC standard error, and judge an alpha estimate by its uncertainty rather than its size.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading what a factor model estimates, 10 minutes computing distances in standard errors and 12 minutes fitting models in the Factor studio; its observations are generated, not historical factor returns.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A factor model explains an asset's excess return with a few common exposures: the market, small versus large companies (SMB), value versus growth (HML), and, in larger models, momentum or profitability and investment factors. The studio fits these by ordinary least squares. Because the data are generated with known exposures, shown in the box "KNOWN DATA-GENERATING PROCESS", you can check every estimate against the truth, which no real dataset allows.

Each coefficient comes with a standard error labelled "SE · HAC": a Newey–West estimate that stays valid when errors change size over time or are correlated from day to day. The p-value asks how surprising the estimate would be if the true value were zero. "TEST R² · RIDGE" fits a ridge regression on the earlier 75% of observations and scores the later 25%, an out-of-sample check that ordinary R² cannot give. The data are generated observations, not historical factor returns.

$$
r_t-r_{f,t}=\alpha+\sum_{k}\beta_k f_{k,t}+\varepsilon_t,\qquad t_{\beta}=\frac{\hat\beta-\beta_0}{\operatorname{SE}_{\text{HAC}}(\hat\beta)}
$$

## A worked example

With the defaults ("Fama–French · three factors", 756 observations, seed 42 and 1.0% idiosyncratic volatility), the planted exposures are 1.10 to the market, 0.25 to SMB and 0.40 to HML, with a daily alpha of 0.0001. The fit returns 1.0907 for the market with a standard error of 0.0393, about a quarter of a standard error from the truth. HML comes out at 0.3662 with a standard error of 0.0371, about 0.9 standard errors low. R² is 0.564 and the ridge test R² is 0.496.

The alpha estimate is 0.000586 a day, which annualizes to roughly 0.000586 × 252 ≈ 14.8%, an impressive-looking number. Its t-statistic is only 1.54 and its p-value 0.124, so the data cannot separate it from zero, and indeed the planted value is much smaller. Precise exposures and an imprecise alpha are the usual outcome, with real data as well as generated data.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the studio.** Click the **Factor studio** tab. Leave **Factor specification** on "Fama–French · three factors", **Observations** on 756, **Random seed** on 42 and **Idiosyncratic daily volatility** on 1.0%, and click **Fit factor model**.

**Read the diagnostics.** Under "MODEL DIAGNOSTICS", note "R² · OLS", "ADJUSTED R²" and "TEST R² · RIDGE", then the table with Factor, β, SE · HAC and p-value for "Alpha (daily)", "Market", "SMB" and "HML". The footnote reads "756 observations · 6 HAC lags · ridge training/test split 567/189."

**Compare with the truth.** For each factor, subtract the planted exposure from the estimate and divide by its standard error. Values within about two standard errors are ordinary sampling noise.

**Change the model.** Switch to "CAPM · market only" and fit again. The market beta moves because the omitted factors now load onto it. Switch to "Carhart · four factors" and "Fama–French · five factors" and note how R² changes.

**Add noise.** Raise **Idiosyncratic daily volatility** to 3% and fit. Standard errors widen and R² falls, while the planted exposures stay the same.

**What you should see.** Estimates within a couple of standard errors of the planted values, an alpha that is rarely significant, and a "OLS residuals" chart without obvious structure.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Factor studio](/lab?tool=factors) and fit the three-factor model at seeds 42, 43 and 44 and record how far each estimated exposure lands from its planted value, measured in standard errors. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

for i in range(3):
    distance = (estimates[i] - truth[i]) / errors[i]

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.

assignment.prompt: Fit the three-factor model at seeds 42, 43 and 44 with the other defaults. For each seed record every estimate, its HAC standard error and its distance from the planted value in standard errors, and the alpha's p-value. Summarize what changes across seeds and what does not.
assignment.solution: Across seeds the estimates move by a few hundredths around the planted exposures of 1.10, 0.25 and 0.40, and nearly all distances stay within about two standard errors, which is what sampling noise looks like. The alpha estimate changes sign or size from seed to seed with p-values usually far above 0.05, because a tiny planted alpha is hard to detect in 756 noisy observations. The lesson for real data is to report exposures with their errors and treat an unstable, insignificant alpha as unproven rather than as skill.

An estimate of how much a fitted quantity, such as a sample mean or regression coefficient, would vary across samples. It differs from the spread of the individual observations.
