modules.title: Robustness in the sandbox: costs, seeds and scenarios
modules.subtitle: Test one rule across seeds, cost settings and named stress scenarios, summarize the spread of results honestly, and count every trial you ran.
modules.objective: Test one rule across seeds, cost settings and named stress scenarios, summarize the spread of results honestly, and count every trial you ran.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 6 minutes reading why one path is not evidence, 8 minutes summarizing results across seeds and 16 minutes running the sweeps in the Market sandbox; the lab's data is synthetic and its scenarios do not recreate historical events.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

One seed is one path through a random market. A rule that looks good on seed 42 may look poor on seed 43, and the only way to know is to run it on several seeds with every other setting fixed, then report the average, the spread and the comparison with buy and hold on each path. Costs are the second dimension: a rule whose edge disappears when costs are raised slightly has no edge worth trusting.

Named scenarios are the third. "Pure random walk" uses geometric Brownian motion with no drift; "Deflationary crash · 1929-inspired" uses jumps, a 15% annual decline and 38% volatility; "Stagflation · 1970s-inspired" a 1.5% drift with 32% volatility; "Liquidity crisis · 2008-inspired" stochastic volatility with an 18% decline and 55% volatility; and "Crypto flash crash · −50%" adds a one-day −50% shock at the middle bar. They illustrate stress mechanisms and do not recreate historical events. Every run you try is a trial, and the best of many trials looks better than it is.

$$
\bar{R}=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}R_s,\qquad \hat\sigma_R=\sqrt{\frac{1}{S-1}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\left(R_s-\bar{R}\right)^{2}}
$$

## A worked example

With default costs and a three-year horizon, the trend rule returns −23.4%, +4.9%, +19.6%, +2.3% and −5.8% on seeds 42 to 46, an average of about −0.5% with a standard deviation near 15.8 points. Buy and hold returns −18.5%, +5.1%, +88.4%, +30.7% and +0.4% on the same seeds, so the rule trails it every time, though its maximum drawdown is shallower on four of the five seeds. At zero cost seed 42 still loses 19.7%, so costs are not the whole story.

The scenarios tell a different part of the story. On seed 42 the rule loses 26.6% against 35.8% for buy and hold in the pure random walk, 75.4% against 92.0% in the 1929 crash, 36.8% against 51.4% in stagflation, 37.3% against 64.1% in the liquidity crisis and 57.5% against 59.2% in the flash crash. Stepping aside in falling markets limits damage, but the flash crash's one-day shock arrives before any signal can act.

## Put the idea into practice

**Fix everything but one setting.** Click **Trend following**, keep the defaults and open the gear icon (aria "Execution settings"), where **Seed** lives.

**Sweep five seeds.** Run seeds 42, 43, 44, 45 and 46 in turn. For each, write the total return and maximum drawdown from **All metrics**, and the buy-and-hold return from the end of the Buy & hold line or a run of the **Buy & hold** chip.

**Sweep costs.** On seed 42, run with **Commission (bps)** and **Slippage (bps)** at 0, at the defaults (5 and 3) and at 20 each, and record final equity.

**Sweep scenarios.** On seed 42 with default costs, open **Parameters** and choose each **SCENARIO** in turn, from "Pure random walk" to "Crypto flash crash · −50%". Read the fine print "Named stress scenarios override selected process defaults."

**Count your trials.** Add up every run you made in this lesson and write the number at the top of your notes, before any conclusion.

**What you should see.** Results that vary widely across seeds, a final equity that falls as costs rise, and scenario results that differ in a pattern you can explain.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and run the default rule on five seeds and on the five named scenarios with every other setting fixed, and tabulate total return against buy and hold for all ten runs. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

from math import sqrt

rule = [-23.4, 4.9, 19.6, 2.3, -5.8]
hold = [-18.5, 5.1, 88.4, 30.7, 0.4]
mean = sum(rule) / len(rule)
total = 0
for value in rule:
    total += (value - mean) ** 2
spread = sqrt(total / (len(rule) - 1))
beats = 0
for i in range(len(rule)):
    if rule[i] > hold[i]:
        beats += 1
print("Rule mean:", round(mean, 2), "% standard deviation:", round(spread, 2), "points")
print("Seeds where the rule beat buy and hold:", beats, "of", len(rule))
print("Trials in this lesson so far:", 5 + 3 + 5)

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Run the default trend rule on five seeds, three cost settings and the five named scenarios. Report the average and standard deviation of total return across seeds, how often the rule beat buy and hold, the cost sensitivity, the scenario results and the total number of runs.
assignment.solution: With default settings the rule averages about −0.5% across seeds 42–46 with a standard deviation near 15.8 points and trails buy and hold on all five, though it has a shallower drawdown on four. On seed 42 it loses 19.7% at zero cost and 23.4% with default costs, so costs matter but do not explain everything. Across the named scenarios it loses less than buy and hold in every falling market, because stepping aside limits damage. A complete report lists all thirteen runs and states that synthetic paths cannot establish a real-market edge.

modules.title: Paper trading: liquidity, stale-data, spread and drawdown guards
modules.subtitle: Place paper orders through the mock broker, compute a fill with spread, slippage, commission and a participation cap, and trigger each pre-trade guard deliberately.
modules.objective: Place paper orders through the mock broker, compute a fill with spread, slippage, commission and a participation cap, and trigger each pre-trade guard deliberately.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 7 minutes reading how the mock broker fills and refuses orders, 9 minutes reproducing the fill and drawdown arithmetic and 14 minutes tripping each guard in the Paper trading tab; the broker never touches real money.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The **Paper trading** tab is a single-session mock broker that shows the checks a real trading system should run before an order reaches a market. A fill takes at most 10% of the available bar volume, so a large order fills partly and the remainder is not retried. The fill price moves away from the reference price by slippage plus half the spread, and a commission is charged on the filled value. The account is long-only and holds $100,000 of paper cash.

Before filling, the broker runs guards in a fixed order: a halted account is refused; equity below 97.5% of the starting amount trips a drawdown circuit breaker and halts the account; a price older than 60 seconds is stale; a spread wider than 100 bps is refused; no volume means no liquidity; and the order must be affordable, or the shares must be owned. Each rejection is written to the audit log with its reason. The account has no live brokerage connection and its state lives in your browser.

$$
P_{\text{fill}}=P_{\text{ref}}\left(1\pm\frac{s+\sigma/2}{10^{4}}\right),\qquad q_{\text{fill}}=\min(q,\ 0.1\,V)
$$

## A worked example

With the defaults (10 shares, a $100 reference price, 1,000 shares of bar volume, a 5 bps spread, 3 bps slippage and a 5 bps commission) a buy fills all 10 shares at 100 × (1 + (3 + 5 ÷ 2) ÷ 10,000) = $100.055, and the commission is 10 × 100.055 × 0.0005 ≈ $0.50. An order for 150 shares against the same volume fills only 100, the 10% cap, and is marked partially filled.

To see the drawdown breaker, set the volume to 100,000 and buy 990 shares: that costs 990 × 100.055 = $99,054.45 plus a $49.53 commission, leaving about $896.02 of cash. Now set the reference price to 97 and submit any order. Marked equity is 896.02 + 990 × 97 ≈ $96,926, which is 96.9% of the starting amount, below the 97.5% limit, so the order is rejected and the account halts.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the broker.** Click the **Paper trading** tab. The header reads "QUANTA MOCK BROKER" and the stats show "CASH AVAILABLE", "SHARES HELD", "MARKED EQUITY" and "RISK STATE".

**Place a default order.** Keep **Buy**, **Order quantity** 10, **Reference price ($)** 100, **Available bar volume** 1000, **Bid-ask spread (bps)** 5, **Slippage (bps)** 3, **Commission (bps)** 5 and **Price age (seconds)** 0, and click **Submit buy order**. The "ORDER AUDIT LOG" shows the fill at $100.06 a share and the commission.

**Hit the participation cap.** Set **Order quantity** to 150 and submit. Only 100 shares fill and the status reads partially filled.

**Trip each guard.** Set **Price age (seconds)** to 90 and submit ("Price data is stale."); restore it and set the spread to 150 ("Spread exceeds the 100 bps guard."); set the volume to 0 ("No available liquidity."); then follow the drawdown recipe above ("Drawdown circuit breaker triggered.").

**Reset.** Click the icon with aria "Reset paper account", read "Reset the paper account?" and choose **Reset simulation**.

**What you should see.** A rejection message for every guard you trip, a "Halted" risk state after the drawdown breaker, and the message "Circuit breaker is halted. Reset the paper account after reviewing the event." for any order placed before you reset.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Paper trading](/lab?tool=broker) and trigger every guard on purpose, one at a time (stale price, wide spread, no volume, insufficient cash and the drawdown breaker), and copy each rejection from the ORDER AUDIT LOG. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

spread = 5
slippage = 3
commission_bps = 5
price = reference * (1 + (slippage + spread / 2) / 10000)
print("Fill price:", price, "commission on 10 shares:", round(10 * price * commission_bps / 10000, 4))
print("Shares filled for 150 ordered against 1,000 volume:", min(150, 1000 * 0.10))
cost = 990 * price
fee = cost * commission_bps / 10000
cash = 100000 - cost - fee
equity = cash + 990 * 97
print("Cash after 990 shares:", round(cash, 2), "marked equity at 97:", round(equity, 2))
print("Equity as a share of the start:", round(equity / 100000 * 100, 2), "% against a 97.5% limit")

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Trigger every guard in the Paper trading tab, one at a time: participation cap, stale price, wide spread, no volume, insufficient cash and the drawdown breaker. Copy each message from the audit log and explain the risk each guard prevents.
assignment.solution: The participation cap fills at most 10% of the bar's volume, preventing the fantasy of trading any size at one price. The stale-price guard rejects prices older than 60 seconds, so decisions are not based on old information. The spread guard refuses spreads above 100 bps, where a quote is unreliable. Zero volume gives 'No available liquidity.', and an unaffordable order gives 'Insufficient cash for the simulated fill and fees.' The drawdown breaker halts the account once marked equity falls below 97.5% of the start, forcing a review before more trading, which is the control Knight Capital's systems lacked.

modules.title: The AMM simulator: pool prices, fees and impermanent loss
modules.subtitle: Quote swaps in a constant-product pool, separate spot price from execution price and impact, and compare full-range and concentrated liquidity against simply holding.
modules.objective: Quote swaps in a constant-product pool, separate spot price from execution price and impact, and compare full-range and concentrated liquidity against simply holding.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading how a constant-product pool prices trades, 10 minutes reproducing the swap and impermanent-loss arithmetic and 12 minutes in the AMM simulator; the pool is a model and never touches real tokens.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An automated market maker holds two assets and prices trades with a rule rather than an order book. In a constant-product pool the product of the reserves, x · y = k, stays the same after each trade, apart from fees. The spot price is the ratio of the reserves, but a trade moves along the curve, so the price you actually get is worse than spot, and the gap grows with the size of the trade. The fee is taken from the input and kept by the pool.

Liquidity providers face a different risk. When the external price moves, the pool's arbitrage-driven rebalancing leaves them with more of the asset that fell, and the value of their share trails simply holding the original tokens. That gap is called impermanent loss. Concentrating liquidity in a price range uses capital more efficiently inside the range but amplifies the loss, and a position outside its range stops earning. The simulator's comparisons exclude fees earned and gas costs.

$$
\Delta y=\frac{y\,\Delta x\,(1-\varphi)}{x+\Delta x\,(1-\varphi)},\qquad \text{IL}(r)=\frac{2\sqrt{r}}{1+r}-1
$$

## A worked example

The default pool holds 10 ETH and 20,000 USDC, so spot is 2,000 USDC per ETH. Swapping 1 ETH with a 0.3% fee returns 20,000 × 0.997 ÷ (10 + 0.997) ≈ 1,813.22 USDC, an execution price of $1,813.22 and a price impact of 1 − 1,813.22 ÷ 2,000 ≈ 9.34%. A 0.1 ETH swap returns about 197.43 USDC, an execution price near 1,974.32 and an impact of about 1.28%.

If the ETH price doubles, the full-range impermanent loss is 2√2 ÷ (1 + 2) − 1 ≈ −5.72% against holding. A position concentrated between 0.5× and 2× of the starting price loses about 19.53% against holding at the same move, more than three times as much, and it sits at the edge of its range. These are the simulator's default outputs.

## Put the idea into practice

**Open the pool.** Click the **AMM simulator** tab: "CONSTANT-PRODUCT POOL", "Explore an ETH / USDC pool with x · y = k." Inputs are **ETH reserves** 10, **USDC reserves** 20000, **ETH to swap** 1 and **Swap fee (decimal)** 0.003.

**Read a quote.** Note "Estimated swap output", "Execution price", "Price impact including fee" and "Fee retained by pool". Change **ETH to swap** to 0.1 and then 5, and watch the impact grow faster than the size.

**Move the price.** Drag **Future price / initial price** from 2.00× down to 0.5× and up to 4×. Read "Full-range impermanent loss", "Concentrated position vs. holding" and "Position status".

**Change the range.** Under **Concentrated liquidity range**, set **Lower price ratio** and **Upper price ratio** wider and narrower. A range must contain the starting price, or the tool refuses it with "The starting price must lie within the liquidity range."

**Read the curve.** The chart under "LIQUIDITY PROVIDER ANALYSIS" draws full-range impermanent loss from 0.1× to about 4.9×. Find the price ratio where the loss is zero.

**What you should see.** Execution prices below spot for every sale of ETH, losses against holding for any price move away from 1×, and larger losses for narrower ranges.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [AMM simulator](/lab?tool=amm) and quote swaps of 0.1, 1 and 5 ETH, record each execution price and impact, then move the price slider from 0.5× to 4× and note where the concentrated position leaves its range. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).
modules.code:
from math import sqrt

eth = 10
usdc = 20000
fee = 0.003
spot = usdc / eth
for size in [0.1, 1, 5]:
    output = usdc * size * (1 - fee) / (eth + size * (1 - fee))
    execution = output / size
    print("Swap", size, "ETH: output", round(output, 2), "execution", round(execution, 2), "impact", round((1 - execution / spot) * 100, 2), "%")
for ratio in [0.5, 2, 4]:
    loss = 2 * sqrt(ratio) / (1 + ratio) - 1
    print("Price ratio", ratio, "full-range impermanent loss:", round(loss * 100, 2), "%")

# This worksheet computes the case above. The price sandbox stays in cash.
# Its equity curve is not evidence for the model or strategy's performance.
def strategy(data):
    return data["close"] < 0

assignment.prompt: Quote swaps of 0.1, 1 and 5 ETH in the default pool and record output, execution price and impact for each. Then record full-range and concentrated losses at price ratios of 0.5, 2 and 4, and explain why the concentrated position loses more.
assignment.solution: The swaps return about 197.43, 1,813.22 and 6,653.32 USDC, with impacts near 1.3%, 9.3% and 33.5%, because each unit sold moves the pool's price further. Full-range impermanent loss is about −5.72% at both 0.5× and 2× and about −20% at 4×. A concentrated position provides the liquidity of a much larger full-range position inside its range, so the same price move rebalances it harder and its loss against holding is larger; outside the range it holds only one asset and stops earning fees, which this simulator excludes.

modules.title: Saved experiments, the notebook and historical imports
modules.subtitle: Save and reopen experiments that reproduce their results, export your research, keep notes tied to lessons, and know what an imported dataset changes.
modules.objective: Save and reopen experiments that reproduce their results, export your research, keep notes tied to lessons, and know what an imported dataset changes.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 7 minutes reading what experiments and notes keep, 8 minutes checking the horizon arithmetic and 15 minutes saving, reopening and exporting in the lab and notebook; the lab's default data is synthetic.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A saved experiment stores the code and the exact market settings behind the result on screen, plus its metrics when the output is fresh. It does not store bars, curves or trades: reopening it regenerates them from the seed, which is why the seed matters so much. Saving from the free lab or a lesson creates a new record each time; only a session opened from **Saved experiments** overwrites its own record. Your work is kept in your browser and synced to your account when you are signed in.

Two behaviours catch people out. Clicking another lab tab drops the experiment from the address, so returning to the Market sandbox shows the free lab rather than your experiment. And unsaved code is kept as a draft that wins over the saved code when the experiment reopens. The notebook holds your reasoning: notes you write, notes created from lesson assignments and case prompts, all exportable as Markdown. A historical dataset can replace the synthetic market, but none ships with Quanta, and an import's prices are used exactly as supplied.

$$
n_{\text{rows}}=252\,H,\qquad \text{rows used}=\{1,\dots,252H\}
$$

## A worked example

Suppose you import a file of 2,520 daily rows, ten years of prices, and leave **Horizon** at "3 years". The run reads the first 3 × 252 = 756 rows, which are the oldest three years of the file, not the latest. To test the most recent period you would have to import a file that starts where you want the test to begin.

A saved experiment is small because it stores settings rather than bars. Reopening it and running again must give the same metrics as the card in **Saved experiments**, so a mismatch is a signal that a draft or a changed setting is in play. These rules are what make an experiment reproducible by someone else, given the same code and settings.

## Put the idea into practice

**Save an experiment.** Run any rule in the **Market sandbox**, then click **Save** in the footer. The dialog "Keep this experiment" asks for an **Experiment name** (up to 120 characters, placeholder "My first market hypothesis"); click **Save experiment**. The icon "Export experiment" downloads quanta-experiment.json with the code, settings and result.

**Find and reopen it.** Open **Saved experiments** in the sidebar. Use **Search experiments** to filter by title, read the card's tags (data type, model, "Seed …" and date) and its CAGR and MAX DRAWDOWN, then click the title. The lab heading now shows the experiment's name. Run it and compare the metrics with the card.

**See the traps.** Click the **Valuation** tab and then **Market sandbox** again: the free lab appears. Reopen the experiment, edit the code without saving, and reload the page: your draft appears. Click the icon "Restore lesson code" to return to the saved code.

**Use the notebook.** Open **My notebook**, click **New note**, fill in **Title** and **Your note** and click **Save note**. On a lesson page, **Write in notebook** on the assignment creates a prefilled note. **Export notebook** saves quanta-notebook.md.

**Check the data source.** In **Parameters**, set **DATA SOURCE** to "Historical data". Without an import you will see a notice explaining that no historical dataset is installed; imports are added from the command line, as described in How Quanta works.

**What you should see.** Reopened experiments that reproduce their card metrics, a free lab after a tab click, and a notebook export that contains your notes in order.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and save two experiments that differ only by seed, export both JSON files, and confirm that reopening each from Saved experiments reproduces its own metrics. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

modules.title: Capstone: a complete research loop from hypothesis to saved evidence
modules.subtitle: Run the lab's research loop end to end: state a falsifiable hypothesis, fix the criteria, develop on some seeds, test on reserved seeds, and leave a trail another person can rerun.
modules.objective: Run the lab's research loop end to end: state a falsifiable hypothesis, fix the criteria, develop on some seeds, test on reserved seeds, and leave a trail another person can rerun.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 5 minutes reading the loop, 5 minutes planning trials and 20 minutes running, saving and exporting the capstone in the lab; the lab's data is synthetic, so the capstone tests a process, not a market edge.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The lab's sidebar names the research loop in four steps: state a hypothesis, change one assumption, read the evidence, keep a research trail. The capstone adds the two habits that make the loop honest. First, write the claim and the criteria that would reject it before you run anything. Second, split your seeds: develop and tune on one set, and keep another set untouched until the end, because results on the seeds that shaped your choices are optimistic by construction.

Every variant you try is a trial, and the trail records all of them, including the failures. A rule that holds up on reserved seeds under stated settings has passed a fair test on synthetic paths; it has not shown an edge in any real market. That modest claim is the correct output of the lab, and a reviewer can trust it precisely because it does not claim more.

$$
N_{\text{trials}}=V\times S_{\text{dev}}+S_{\text{test}}
$$

## A worked example

A worked plan: the hypothesis is that adding the condition "the 50-day average is above the 200-day average" to the trend rule gives a shallower maximum drawdown than buy and hold in the "Liquidity crisis · 2008-inspired" scenario. The rejection criterion is a shallower drawdown on fewer than four of five reserved seeds. You develop on seeds 42–46 with two variants of the window, which is 2 × 5 = 10 development runs, then run the chosen variant once on seeds 47–51, five more, for 15 trials in total.

The report states the hypothesis, criterion, seeds, settings, all 15 results and the decision, and it names what the lab does not model. The worksheet counts the twelve steps of the loop, from writing the hypothesis to exporting the notebook; a complete capstone ticks all twelve.

## Put the idea into practice

**Write before you run.** In **My notebook**, create a note with your hypothesis, the metric, the comparison, the rejection criterion, the development seeds and the reserved seeds.

**Develop.** In the **Market sandbox**, choose the scenario and settings, write the rule, and run each variant on each development seed. Save each run with a name that includes the variant and seed, using **Save** and **Save experiment**.

**Test once.** Run the chosen variant on each reserved seed without changing anything else. Save these runs too.

**Decide.** Apply your written criterion to the reserved-seed results only, and record the decision whether or not it is the one you hoped for.

**Leave the trail.** In **Saved experiments**, check that every run is listed with its seed tag, export the ones your report cites, and click **Export notebook** to save your notes.

**What you should see.** A note written before the first run, one saved experiment per trial, a decision taken from the reserved seeds, and exports that let someone else rerun every number.

### Practise in the lab

Open the [Market sandbox](/lab?tool=market) and run your capstone loop: write the hypothesis and criterion first, develop on five seeds, test on five reserved seeds, save every run and export your notebook. The worksheet on this page is only an arithmetic aid: it stays in cash and does not run your experiment, so take every result that matters from the lab itself. The lab's default data is synthetic, so a good result there is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Finish by writing what you changed, what you saw and what you would test next in [My notebook](/notebook).

readingGuide:
The Strategy lab is a bench for testing ideas, not a place to make money. This workshop takes each tool one control at a time: how the lab generates a market, how a one-line Python rule becomes trades, what the metrics and charts say, how a balance sheet becomes a value per share, what a factor regression can and cannot show, why a broker refuses some orders, and how a liquidity pool moves its price. The lab's default data is synthetic, so every result is a teaching device and a strong backtest is a reason to test harder, never evidence of a real edge. Each lesson takes thirty minutes: read, reproduce the arithmetic by hand, then repeat it in the lab and write down what you saw.

The workshop has 12 lessons × 30 minutes = 6 hours of planned study across three units: about 8 minutes of reading, 10 minutes of arithmetic and 12 minutes in the lab per lesson; exam time is additional. It includes 24 practice questions, three four-question checkpoints and a 12-question final.

The lab's default data is synthetic, so every price, company and result is a teaching device; a good simulated result is never evidence of a real edge, and the paper broker and AMM never touch real money.

exams.title: Unit 1: The market sandbox
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: On the default run the trend rule returns about −23% with a drawdown near −27%, while the Buy & hold chip returns about −18% with a drawdown near −34%. What is the fairest reading?
options: The rule is proven to work because its drawdown is smaller
The rule is proven useless because its return is lower
Mixed evidence from one synthetic path, so more tests are needed
questions.explanation: One seed is one path. The drawdown claim holds on this path and the return claim does not; neither is a verdict until seeds, costs and scenarios are varied.

questions.question: What does the Crypto flash crash · −50% scenario do to the generated market?
options: It cuts every daily return in half
It keeps the selected process and settings and adds a one-day −50% shock at the middle bar
It replaces the bars with real crypto prices from a past crash
questions.explanation: The scenario adds a single shock to the path. It is a synthetic stress mechanism, not a reconstruction of a historical event.

questions.question: A rule sets its threshold at 0.9 × max(data["close"]). Why is that a look-ahead problem even though the engine delays signals by one bar?
options: The maximum is computed over the whole history, including bars after the one being judged
The engine fills at the previous close instead of the next open
The runtime does not support max()
questions.explanation: A live trader cannot know the full-period maximum. The one-bar delay stops a bar from trading on its own close; it cannot detect whole-sample statistics inside your code.

questions.question: Run on 1 year and on 3 years with the same seed, a rule makes different trades inside the first year. What does that show?
options: The seed was ignored by the second run
Longer horizons always change early trades
The rule uses information from later bars, because the first year's data is identical in both runs
questions.explanation: The first 252 bars match exactly, so a rule that looks only backwards must trade identically on them. Different trades reveal look-ahead.

exams.title: Unit 2: Read evidence and value businesses
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: What does '· inputs changed' beside the run time tell you?
options: The market data was refreshed from a live feed
A setting changed after the last run, so the output no longer matches the controls
The lab rewrote your strategy code
questions.explanation: The output belongs to the previous settings. Run again before reading or saving the numbers.

questions.question: In the Graham heuristic, what does raising the bond yield from 4.4% to 6% do to a value of $74?
options: Leaves it unchanged, because the yield is not in the formula
questions.explanation: The yield divides the heuristic: 74 × 4.4 ÷ 6 ≈ $54.27.

questions.question: Why does the studio also report 'TEST R² · RIDGE'?
options: It is the same R² computed with a different formula
It counts how many factors are in the model
It fits on the earlier 75% of observations and scores the later 25%, an out-of-sample check
questions.explanation: In-sample R² rewards fitting the sample. The ridge test R² measures how well a model fitted on earlier data explains later data.

questions.question: Setting commission and slippage to zero turns a losing rule into a winner. What does that show?
options: Any edge the rule has is smaller than its trading costs
Costs should always be set to zero
questions.explanation: If costs decide whether the rule wins, the rule cannot be expected to survive real trading frictions.

exams.title: Unit 3: Execution, DeFi and your research trail
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: After the drawdown breaker halts the account, how does trading resume?
options: Only after resetting the paper account, once the event has been reviewed
questions.explanation: A halted account rejects every order until it is reset, which forces a deliberate review.

questions.question: What do the simulator's comparisons with holding leave out?
options: Fees earned by the pool and gas costs
questions.explanation: The tool notes that fees and gas are excluded, so a real liquidity provider's result could be better or worse.

questions.question: How do you save a lesson's assignment answer to your notebook?
options: It is saved automatically when you pass a practice question
Click Write in notebook on the assignment, complete the prefilled note and save it
questions.explanation: Write in notebook opens a note prefilled with the assignment, which you complete and save.

questions.question: What belongs in the research trail besides the winning experiment?
options: Every variant tried, with its seed, settings and result, including failures
questions.explanation: Reporting every trial lets a reader judge selection bias and rerun any result.

exams.title: Strategy lab workshop final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: Which sequence matches the lab's research loop?
options: State a hypothesis, change one assumption, read the evidence, keep a research trail
Run many variations, keep the best curve, save it, then write the hypothesis
Pick a seed that shows a profit, change every setting at once, discard weaker runs
questions.explanation: The hypothesis comes first so the result can disprove it, one change at a time keeps comparisons clean, and keeping every run and note keeps the trail honest.

questions.question: A learner selects Markov regime switching and then drags the Annual drift slider from 8% to 20%. What happens to the generated bars?
options: Every regime's drift rises by 12 percentage points
The market switches back to geometric Brownian motion
Nothing changes: regime switching uses its own three regimes and ignores the drift and volatility sliders
questions.explanation: The regime process takes drift and volatility from three built-in regimes. The sliders only matter for GBM, Merton and Heston.

questions.question: Why can a signal list not be built bar by bar inside a loop in the guided runtime?
options: Loops are allowed only after the first 200 bars
There is no append, list concatenation or element assignment, so signals come from whole-series expressions
questions.explanation: For loops over lists and ranges work, but a list cannot be extended or edited. Series comparisons, &, |, ~ and np.where produce the signal instead.

questions.question: How does the lab treat a position that is still open when the backtest ends?
options: It is marked to the last close and left out of win rate and profit factor
It is sold at the last close and counted as a closed trade
It is removed from the results entirely
questions.explanation: Open positions count in equity at the last close, but only closed round trips enter the win rate and profit factor.

questions.question: Why does an all-cash rule show '—' for Sharpe?
options: Sharpe is hidden whenever the data is synthetic
Sharpe needs at least one losing trade to be computed
Its daily returns have no variability, so the ratio's denominator is zero
questions.explanation: Sharpe divides by the standard deviation of daily returns. With no variability the ratio is undefined, and the lab shows '—' rather than a misleading number.

questions.question: Why can a stock pass the two-thirds NCAV screen yet trade above its adjusted asset value?
options: The Graham heuristic overrides the screen
The screen uses unadjusted NCAV, while the adjusted value applies recovery haircuts
The screen already includes the haircuts
questions.explanation: The screen is computed from book values. Realistic recoveries can push the adjusted value below the price even when the screen passes.

questions.question: The daily alpha estimate is 0.000586 with a p-value of 0.124. What can you conclude?
options: The data cannot distinguish it from zero, even though it annualizes to about 15%
The strategy earns about 15% a year of skill
questions.explanation: A p-value of 0.124 means an estimate this large is not unusual when the true alpha is zero. Annualizing does not make it more certain.

questions.question: You tried 40 variants and want to report the best Sharpe ratio. What must accompany it?
options: Nothing, because the best result is the true one
The number of trials, because the best of many is inflated by chance
questions.explanation: Selecting the maximum of many noisy results biases it upward. Reporting the number of trials lets a reader judge that bias.

questions.question: Price age is set to 90 seconds. What does the broker do?
options: Rejects the order with 'Price data is stale.'
Fills at the old reference price
questions.explanation: Prices older than 60 seconds fail the stale-data guard, regardless of the other inputs.

questions.question: Why does the concentrated position lose about 19.53% while the full-range position loses 5.72% at the same move?
options: Concentrated liquidity acts like a larger position inside its range, so the same move rebalances it harder
Concentrated liquidity pays higher swap fees
The concentrated calculation includes gas costs
questions.explanation: A narrow range provides more liquidity per unit of capital, which amplifies both fee income and impermanent loss.

questions.question: An imported dataset has 2,520 daily rows and Horizon is 3 years. Which rows does a run use?
options: The last 756 rows, the most recent three years
The first 756 rows, the oldest three years in the file
questions.explanation: The run reads the first Horizon × 252 rows of an import, which are the earliest dates in the file.

questions.question: Your final rule beats buy and hold on the reserved seeds. What can you claim?
options: It held up on fresh synthetic paths under the stated settings, which is not evidence of a real-market edge
It will beat the real market
questions.explanation: The lab's evidence is about its generated markets. A fair test there is a reason for further work, not proof about real prices.

title: The intelligent & careful investor
description: Build patient investing habits, understand the risks you can afford, and write a practical investment plan inspired by The Intelligent Investor.
source: Benjamin Graham · The Intelligent Investor · Original Quanta companion with modern Investor.gov references

modules.title: Intelligent investing starts with temperament
modules.subtitle: Define careful investing as a repeatable decision process rather than an IQ contest.
modules.objective: Define careful investing as a repeatable decision process rather than an IQ contest.
modules.reading: Book companion theme: Investor temperament and a disciplined process. 30-minute session: 10 minutes of reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of investor-plan work. Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Being an intelligent investor does not mean predicting every price movement. It means making decisions you can explain and managing the emotions that might pull you away from your plan. Begin with a familiar situation: two people make money decisions and receive different outcomes. We need to examine their reasons and circumstances before deciding which process was better.

## Understand the idea

In this course, an intelligent investor is someone who can work within limits, examine evidence and maintain a deliberate process when prices provoke emotion. Fast calculation and a confident forecast cannot replace those habits. The Indonesian phrase investor yang hati-hati captures the intended attitude: think through consequences, acknowledge uncertainty and avoid commitments whose downside you cannot carry.

A good decision can have a disappointing outcome, while an impulsive decision can be lucky. Evaluate what was knowable at the time: the investment's claim, price, costs, alternatives and possible failure. Write your reasons before buying and revisit them on a schedule. This creates evidence about the quality of the process instead of rewriting a story to fit each price movement.

$$
\mathrm{decision\ review}=f(\mathrm{available\ evidence},\mathrm{alternatives},\mathrm{downside},\mathrm{process})
$$

## A worked example

Rani buys a diversified allocation after documenting a ten-year goal and a loss scenario; the market falls 15%. Dito buys a promoted stock without reading disclosures and gains 20%. Those two outcomes alone cannot establish which process deserves repetition. Starting wealth of 100 falls to 85 in Rani's case, but whether she can continue depends on her plan and circumstances.

### Separate the decision from the outcome

Start with Rani's arithmetic. A 15% fall from wealth of 100 removes 15, leaving 85. That is a real loss in the example, even if her original process was careful. To assess whether she can continue, you need to know her goal, cash needs, and the loss scenario she planned for.

Dito's 20% gain is also an observed outcome. It does not supply the business analysis he skipped before buying. One favorable result cannot tell us whether the same approach would be dependable across other decisions.

The comparison is not a claim that a careful process prevents losses. It shows why a review should ask two questions: what happened, and whether the original choice used the available evidence responsibly. A decision journal preserves the second question by recording the reasons before the outcome is known.

## Put the idea into practice

Start the investor plan with goals, limits and a decision journal. Write one behavior you will follow after a large gain and one after a large loss. Keep the quality of the original decision separate from its realized result.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to investor-plan.md. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's warning against grading a decision by its result has a name in psychology: outcome bias. Baron and Hershey gave undergraduates decisions made by others, in medical matters and monetary gambles; the students understood they held all the relevant information available to the decision maker. Favorable outcomes still earned better ratings of the thinking, more credit for competence or more willingness to yield the decision, though those asked said outcomes should not count. Shown only Rani's 15% fall and Dito's 20% gain, a reader may drift the same way; that is our inference, not a finding about investors.

Temperament shows up in real accounts. Odean studied trading records for 10,000 brokerage accounts and found a strong preference for realizing winners rather than losers, not justified by later performance and costly after tax in taxable accounts. Schatzmann and Haslhofer found a disposition effect in Bitcoin too, varying in intensity and not present throughout. Dichev found that investors' dollar-weighted returns fall systematically below buy-and-hold returns in nearly all major international stock markets, because of the timing and size of flows in and out. That is an aggregate result, so tying it to Rani or Dito is our inference.

Treat the lesson's +20% and −15% as consecutive years of one fund. Holding 100 throughout ends at 102, about 1.0% a year. Adding 100 after the good year ends at 187 on 200 contributed, roughly −4.4% a year: same fund, same two years (our arithmetic).

Exercise: date your deposits and withdrawals (fictional figures work), compute your money-weighted return (IRR) and compare it with the fund's published return. Then note what you did after each large move and whether your journal predicted it.

### Sources for this section

- [Baron & Hershey (1988) · Outcome bias in decision evaluation](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.54.4.569) — *Research paper.* Five studies in which judges who held all the decision maker's information still rated decisions better when outcomes were favorable, while saying outcomes should not matter.
- [Odean (1998) · Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00072) — *Research paper.* Trading records of 10,000 brokerage accounts show a strong preference for selling winners over losers that later performance and, for taxable accounts, after-tax returns do not justify.
- [Dichev (2007) · What Are Stock Investors' Actual Historical Returns? Evidence from Dollar-Weighted Returns](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.1.386) — *Research paper.* Shows that aggregate investor returns fall below buy-and-hold returns in nearly all major markets because of the timing and size of capital flows.
- [Schatzmann & Haslhofer (2020) · Exploring investor behavior in Bitcoin: a study of the disposition effect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12415) — *arXiv 2010.12415.* Finds a disposition effect of varying intensity in Bitcoin transactions, not present throughout the sample, so the habit is not confined to stocks.

modules.subtitle: Distinguish analysis of a security's claim from a bet on another buyer's enthusiasm.
modules.objective: Distinguish analysis of a security's claim from a bet on another buyer's enthusiasm.
modules.reading: Book companion theme: Investment versus speculation. 30-minute session: 10 minutes of reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of investor-plan work. Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A share represents an economic claim on a business, while its quoted price is the amount another participant currently offers to transact. An investment argument examines the business, financing, expected distributions and price paid. A speculative argument may rely mainly on a near-term price move or someone else's willingness to pay more. The label depends on the reasoning and risk assumed, not merely on holding period or the word 'stock'.

Neither a popular company nor a low nominal share price makes an investment suitable. A strong business can be overpriced; a weak business can still rise temporarily. If a learner chooses to study speculation, keep its assumptions and potential full loss explicit rather than allowing it to masquerade as required long-term capital. This course does not prescribe a personal speculative allocation.

$$
\mathrm{ownership\ fraction}=n/N,\qquad \mathrm{equity\ market\ value}=PN
$$

## A worked example

Cedar has 1,000 shares and a quoted price of 12, giving equity market value of 12,000. Buying ten shares creates a 1% equity ownership interest, not ownership of 1% of gross assets free of creditors. An argument based only on a rumor of tomorrow's price target has not analyzed that residual claim.

## Put the idea into practice

Write two purchase rationales for the same fictional share: one based on business evidence and valuation uncertainty, one based on anticipated price action. Identify the missing evidence in each without assuming either return in advance.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to investor-plan.md. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Scheinkman and Xiong give the lesson's "bet on another buyer" a precise form. In their equilibrium model, overconfidence makes traders disagree about fundamentals and, with short sales restricted, a buyer also acquires an option to resell to someone more optimistic. Echoing earlier work, traders then pay prices above their own valuation of future dividends because they expect to find a buyer who will pay even more, and bubbles come with heavy trading volume and high price volatility. It is a model, not a measurement. Our inference is a test for any purchase: would you still pay this price if resale were impossible and only the business's distributions counted?

Evidence on who makes such bets concerns retail investors. Kumar found that individual investors prefer stocks with lottery features and, because those stocks underperform, the damage is larger for low-income investors who overweight them. Barber and co-authors found that intense buying by Robinhood users forecasts negative returns: average 20-day abnormal returns of −4.7% for the top stocks bought each day. Costola and co-authors found that meme stocks share common patterns in price, trading volume and social-media activity that differ from other heavily discussed stocks. These are averages and associations; none proves any single purchase wrong.

Exercise: for Cedar, write the distributions per share you would need to expect, now or later, to justify paying 12 if no buyer ever appeared. If you cannot, the rumor of a price target is carrying the argument.

### Sources for this section

- [Scheinkman & Xiong (2003) · Overconfidence and Speculative Bubbles](https://doi.org/10.1086/378531) — *Research paper.* Equilibrium model in which traders pay more than their own valuation of future dividends because they expect to resell to someone more optimistic; a precise form of the lesson's bet on another buyer.
- [Kumar (2009) · Who Gambles in the Stock Market?](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2009.01483.x) — *Research paper.* Individual investors prefer lottery-type stocks, which underperform, and the loss is greater among low-income investors who overweight them.
- [Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz (2022) · Attention-Induced Trading and Returns: Evidence from Robinhood Users](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13183) — *Research paper.* Intense buying by Robinhood users forecasts negative returns; the top stocks bought each day show average 20-day abnormal returns of -4.7%.
- [Costola, Iacopini & Santagiustina (2021) · On the "mementum" of Meme Stocks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03691) — *arXiv 2106.03691.* Shows that meme stocks share common patterns in price, trading volume and social-media activity, and that their mementum regime differs from other stocks with heavy social-media activity.

modules.subtitle: Choose a research commitment that matches time, skill and willingness to maintain it.
modules.objective: Choose a research commitment that matches time, skill and willingness to maintain it.

Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

The defensive approach seeks a sound process with limited ongoing security-selection demands. An enterprising approach accepts substantial additional work to investigate opportunities and monitor them. The distinction concerns commitment and method; it is not a promise that taking more action or buying riskier securities earns a higher return. Research effort has an opportunity cost and still may fail to add value.

Inventory the time you can sustain, the statements you can interpret and the decisions you can explain. A complex portfolio that is neglected after purchase is not improved by having an elaborate starting spreadsheet. A simpler diversified policy can provide a meaningful baseline for judging active research. Historical selection criteria in the book need context; do not apply old numerical thresholds as timeless commands without examining today's business and market structure.

$$
\mathrm{annual\ research\ hours}=N_{\mathrm{companies}}\times h_{\mathrm{quarter}}\times4
$$

## A worked example

A learner can reliably spend two hours a month maintaining an investment plan, while a proposed individual-company process needs three hours per company each quarter for twelve companies. That proposal requires 144 hours yearly before event-driven updates; the stated capacity is only 24. The mismatch is operational even before any return comparison.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a workload budget and define what will trigger simplification. Compare a broad allocation plan with an individual-company research plan under the same goal, costs and review horizon. State what added evidence would justify the extra work.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to investor-plan.md. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Sharpe showed why the lesson's simple baseline is hard to beat, using only arithmetic. If active and passive management are defined sensibly, then before costs the average actively managed dollar earns the same return as the average passively managed dollar, and after costs it earns less, in any period. This describes the average dollar, not each investor: our reading is that an individual can still beat the market, but only at the expense of other active investors.

French priced the search. He compared the fees, expenses and trading costs of investing in the U.S. stock market with what everyone investing passively would pay; averaged over 1980–2006, investors spent 0.67% of the market's aggregate value each year searching for superior returns. Under reasonable assumptions, he estimated, the typical investor would have gained 67 basis points a year by switching to a passive market portfolio.

Heaton, Polson and Witte add a model-based reason beyond fees. Because the best performers in a broad index often do much better than the rest, randomly choosing a subset of stocks can dramatically raise the chance of trailing the index, a risk they argue likely matters more than the extra fees. Their subset is random, not researched, so this is a warning rather than a verdict; our inference is that a twelve-company portfolio is also a small subset.

Exercise: the lesson's plan needs 144 hours against 24 available, a 120-hour gap. Put a rupiah value on those hours, add the extra trading costs, and divide by the portfolio's value. The result is the annual outperformance the research must earn just to match the simple baseline.

### Sources for this section

- [Sharpe (1991) · The Arithmetic of Active Management](https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v47.n1.7) — *Research paper.* Short proof that, before costs, the average active dollar matches the average passive dollar and, after costs, falls behind it, for any period; it concerns the average dollar, not each investor.
- [French (2008) · Presidential Address: The Cost of Active Investing](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01368.x) — *Research paper.* Estimates that investors spent 0.67% of the U.S. market's value a year in 1980-2006 searching for superior returns, about 67 basis points a year for the typical investor.
- [Heaton, Polson & Witte (2015) · Why Indexing Works](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.03550) — *arXiv 1510.03550.* Model, published in 2017, in which a random subset of an index often trails it because a few top performers drive index returns; underperformance risk may matter more than higher fees.

modules.subtitle: Use market prices as information and opportunities without letting them dictate every judgment.
modules.objective: Use market prices as information and opportunities without letting them dictate every judgment.

Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Graham's discussion of market fluctuations invites the investor to distinguish the quoted price from a considered estimate of value. A price is real and actionable, but it need not be an authoritative judgment of long-term worth. Repeatedly checking a quote can amplify fear, imitation and overconfidence without adding business evidence. A prewritten review policy helps distinguish a changed price from a changed thesis.

Ignoring every price change is also careless: a falling price can accompany new information or make a previously tolerable position too risky for its owner. Revisit business facts, valuation assumptions and personal liquidity before deciding whether to hold, add or reduce. Never infer that a price must return to its previous high simply because that number is psychologically salient.

$$
\mathrm{discount\ to\ estimate}=1-P/V
$$

## A worked example

A fictional company is quoted at 70 and later at 50 while the analyst's conservative value range remains 60–80. The fall increases the apparent discount, but an unreviewed lawsuit could invalidate that range. Against the lower estimate of 60, the discount at 50 is 16.67%; against 80 it is 37.5%. Different assumptions produce different cushions.

## Put the idea into practice

Write a price-change response sheet: what evidence to inspect, what assumptions to update, and what actions require a cooling-off period. Record an opposing interpretation before acting on either excitement or fear.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to investor-plan.md. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Shiller made the lesson's gap between quote and value testable. He formed an ex-post rational price from the dividends paid afterward and found it very stable and smooth next to the actual detrended real price. A market whose price is the optimal forecast of that series is inconsistent with the data if the long-run dividend trend is taken as given; reconciling the two requires market expectations of dividends to have strayed from trend much more than they historically did. That conditional is the caveat: the result tests one model under an assumed trend and says nothing about whether any single quote is wrong.

Joulin and co-authors matched high-frequency stock returns against news feeds and found that neither company-specific nor market-wide news explains the frequency and amplitude of price jumps; they conjecture that most jumps come from order-flow fluctuations near vanishing liquidity. Their data are intraday and the lesson's horizon is months, so our inference is that a fall alone is weak evidence of a changed thesis, and finding no news does not prove it unchanged.

In an experiment, Gneezy and Potters found that the more often returns are evaluated, the more risk averse investors are, in line with myopic loss aversion. Our inference: how often you look is a design choice for your review policy.

Exercise: add a third case in which the lawsuit cuts the value range to 40–55. At a price of 50 the discount against 55 is 9.09%, and against 40 the price sits 25% above the estimate. Then list what a move to 50 should make you re-examine (the lawsuit, the value range, your liquidity) and what evidence you would wait for before acting.

### Sources for this section

- [Shiller (1980) · Do Stock Prices Move Too Much to be Justified by Subsequent Changes in Dividends?](https://doi.org/10.3386/w0456) — *Research paper.* NBER working paper (1980); the American Economic Review version followed in 1981. A price built from later dividends is far smoother than actual prices, so an efficient-market price needs unusual dividend expectations, given the assumed trend.
- [Joulin, Lefevre, Grunberg & Bouchaud (2008) · Stock price jumps: news and volume play a minor role](https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.1769) — *arXiv 0803.1769.* Intraday study finding that neither company-specific nor market-wide news explains the frequency and amplitude of price jumps; a price move alone is weak evidence of new information.
- [Gneezy & Potters (1997) · An Experiment on Risk Taking and Evaluation Periods](https://doi.org/10.1162/003355397555217) — *Research paper.* Experiment showing that the more frequently returns are evaluated, the more risk averse investors are, in line with myopic loss aversion.

modules.title: Goals, liquidity and the capacity to bear losses
modules.subtitle: Separate willingness to accept risk from the financial ability to absorb it.
modules.objective: Separate willingness to accept risk from the financial ability to absorb it.
modules.reading: Book companion theme: Defensive planning; modern course extension. 30-minute session: 10 minutes of reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of investor-plan work. Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A portfolio should serve a person's needs. Start this unit by separating upcoming spending from longer-term goals and considering how a loss would affect each one. Willingness to take risk describes how you feel; capacity to take risk depends on what your finances can withstand. These questions give diversification and a margin of safety a practical purpose.

## Understand the idea

Risk tolerance describes willingness to experience uncertainty and losses; risk capacity concerns what those losses would do to required spending and commitments. A person may feel comfortable with volatility while having a near-term obligation that cannot tolerate a large drawdown. Build the plan around dates and cash needs before choosing an attractive security.

Separate emergency liquidity, known near-term commitments and genuinely long-horizon capital. The size and instruments of those pools depend on circumstances and local protections; this fictional worksheet does not prescribe a universal reserve. Borrowing to invest adds obligations whose timing may not match the investment's recovery. The ability to wait is a balance-sheet condition as well as a personality trait.

$$
C_{\mathrm{long\ horizon}}=A-C_{\mathrm{near\ term}}-C_{\mathrm{reserve}}
$$

## A worked example

A fictional household has 120 million rupiah of available financial assets, 30 million of identified near-term spending and a chosen 24 million reserve. The residual long-horizon pool is 66 million. A 30% decline in that pool would lose 19.8 million. Whether the household can tolerate it requires a full view of income and obligations, not only confidence about stocks.

## Put the idea into practice

Complete the goals and liquidity page using fictional numbers or broad categories; do not put account credentials or sensitive balances into a shared notebook. Stress the long-horizon pool and record which obligation would force a sale.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to investor-plan.md. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Willingness, the lesson's risk tolerance, is a shaky foundation for two reasons. It moves: Guiso, Sapienza and Zingales repeatedly surveyed an Italian bank's clients and found that qualitative and quantitative measures of risk aversion both rose substantially after the 2008 crisis, and in a lab experiment people who watched a horror movie had certainty equivalents 27% lower, pointing to fear. And a recorded tolerance may not predict behavior: in an investment dealer's data on over 23,000 clients, Thompson and co-authors found that the know-your-client information Canadian rules require, such as age or risk tolerance, did not explain what clients did; trading frequency and volume did.

Capacity lives on the balance sheet. Lusardi, Schneider and Tufano used a 2009 survey to ask whether Americans could come up with $2,000 in 30 days: about a quarter would certainly not, and another 19% would manage by relying at least partly on pawning, selling possessions or payday loans. Kaplan, Violante and Weidner found "wealthy hand-to-mouth" households across eight countries: little liquid wealth despite sizable housing or retirement assets. These are not Indonesian samples, so carrying the mechanism over is our inference.

Now stress the lesson's household. Its 66 million long-horizon pool is a residual, not a promise. Suppose a 48 million bill, twice the reserve, arrives right after the 30% fall: the reserve covers 24 million, and the other 24 million must come from a pool then worth 46.2 million, so about 52% of it is sold at the low (our arithmetic, assuming no borrowing and untouched near-term spending).

Exercise: using fictional or broad-category figures, not real balances, find the shock that would exhaust the reserve and note which holdings would be sold first.

### Sources for this section

- [Guiso, Sapienza & Zingales (2013) · Time Varying Risk Aversion](https://doi.org/10.3386/w19284) — *Research paper.* NBER working paper version of the 2018 article: an Italian bank's clients became markedly more risk averse after the 2008 crisis, and a horror-movie experiment points to fear.
- [Thompson, Feng, Reesor & Grace (2020) · Know Your Clients' behaviours: a cluster analysis of financial transactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.03625) — *arXiv 2005.03625.* In a dealer's data on over 23,000 clients, collected know-your-client information such as risk tolerance did not explain client behavior; trading frequency and volume did.
- [Lusardi, Schneider & Tufano (2011) · Financially Fragile Households: Evidence and Implications](https://doi.org/10.3386/w17072) — *Research paper.* 2009 survey data on whether Americans could come up with $2,000 in 30 days, and the coping methods people use, from savings to pawning, selling possessions or payday loans.
- [Kaplan, Violante & Weidner (2014) · The Wealthy Hand-to-Mouth](https://doi.org/10.1353/eca.2014.0002) — *Research paper.* Household portfolio surveys from eight countries show households with sizable illiquid assets but little liquid wealth, so net worth alone does not measure the ability to wait.

modules.reading: Book companion theme: Inflation and the investor. 30-minute session: 10 minutes of reading, 8 minutes of calculations, and 12 minutes of investor-plan work. Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An account can grow in currency units while losing purchasing power. Compare the net nominal return with the change in the prices relevant to the goal. The exact real-return relationship compounds the two factors; simple subtraction is an approximation. A household's actual spending basket can differ from a published inflation index, and future inflation is uncertain.

Cash, bonds and equities each carry different risks to purchasing power and nominal capital. Equities are claims on businesses whose pricing power, costs and valuations vary; they are not an automatic inflation hedge over every horizon. A fixed nominal payment can become less useful when prices rise, while inflation-linked products have their own terms, availability and market-price risks. Study the mechanism rather than replacing uncertainty with a single protective label.

$$
1+r_{\mathrm{real}}=\frac{1+r_{\mathrm{nominal,net}}}{1+\pi}
$$

## A worked example

Savings rise by 6% over a year while the illustrative cost of the goal rises 4%. The exact real return is 1.06/1.04 − 1, about 1.923%, rather than exactly 2%. If nominal return were 3% under the same inflation assumption, purchasing power would decline about 0.962%.

## Put the idea into practice

Add a nominal and real column to the plan, state whether fees are already included, and compare two inflation scenarios. Keep local inflation, tax and product rules as items for current source verification before making a personal decision.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to investor-plan.md. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Bekaert and Wang put evidence behind the lesson's caution about equities. They estimated inflation betas, the sensitivity of returns to inflation, for standard bond and well-diversified equity indices in over 45 countries and concluded that such securities are poor inflation hedges. Adding Treasury bills, foreign bonds, real estate and gold helped, but inflation risk stayed hard to hedge.

Horizon changes the answer. Boudoukh and Richardson note that earlier work, using horizons of a year or less, found stocks a poor hedge; with two centuries of U.S. and U.K. data they found a positive relation between stock returns and inflation at long horizons. Albulescu and co-authors, testing U.S. sector indexes over 2002–2015 by cointegration, found inflation and its uncertainty negatively related to stock prices in the long run, contrary to the Fisher effect, though for several sectors the relation vanished after the crisis. The studies differ in method and sample (price levels in a recent period against returns over two centuries), so they do not refute each other; "long run" is not one number.

In the lesson's example, 6% against 4% inflation leaves a real return of about 1.923%, but that is one year's outcome, and these studies suggest it says little about how the same holding would fare if inflation changed (our inference). Exercise: for each holding, write the channel through which it should keep pace with your goal's own prices (indexation, resetting rates, pricing power) and the horizon at which the evidence above supports it. Mark any channel you cannot name as a hope, not a hedge.

### Sources for this section

- [Bekaert & Wang (2010) · Inflation risk and the inflation risk premium](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-0327.2010.00253.x) — *Research paper.* Estimates inflation betas for bond and equity indices in over 45 countries and finds standard securities poor inflation hedges; broader asset menus help but inflation risk stays hard to hedge.
- [Boudoukh & Richardson · Stocks are a Good Hedge for Inflation (In the Long Run)](https://ideas.repec.org/p/fth/pennfi/14-92.html) — *Research paper.* Working-paper version of the authors' 1993 American Economic Review article: stocks hedge inflation poorly at short horizons, but two centuries of data show a positive relation at long horizons.
- [Albulescu, Aubin & Goyeau (2016) · Stock prices, inflation and inflation uncertainty in the U.S.: Testing the long-run relationship considering Dow Jones sector indexes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.01231) — *arXiv 1603.01231.* Cointegration study of U.S. sector indexes over 2002-2015: in the long run inflation and its uncertainty were negatively related to stock prices, with the effect vanishing for several sectors after the crisis.

modules.subtitle: Look through labels to identify the actual sources of portfolio risk.
modules.objective: Look through labels to identify the actual sources of portfolio risk.

Modern product, fraud and planning examples are course extensions, not claims about Graham's historical recommendations.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Diversification spreads exposure across different claims and economic drivers. Counting tickers or fund names is insufficient when their holdings overlap or they depend on the same industry, employer, country or currency. A portfolio can contain many lines while remaining one concentrated bet. Examine look-through holdings and relate them to the investor's income and obligations.

Diversification can reduce company-specific risk but does not eliminate broad market losses. Correlations can change, and assets that appeared different may fall together under stress. Choose a maintainable allocation whose exposures you can explain rather than continually adding products for the appearance of sophistication. The course's weights are calculation examples, not recommended allocations for every learner.

$$
w_{\mathrm{company}}=\sum_jw_{\mathrm{fund},j}w_{\mathrm{company\ within\ fund},j}
$$

## A worked example

Fund A is 60% of a portfolio and holds 30% in one company; Fund B is 40% and holds 20% in the same company. Combined look-through exposure is 0.6×0.3 + 0.4×0.2 = 26%. Owning two funds has not capped that company at either fund's portfolio weight.

## Put the idea into practice

Draw a holdings overlap table and stress a common exposure. Include employer stock alongside labor income conceptually, since both can deteriorate together. State the information needed to maintain the look-through audit over time.

### Build your careful-investor plan

Write the calculation, decision rule and one reason the conclusion might be wrong in your notebook. Add the evidence to investor-plan.md. Read the named theme in your own copy of The Intelligent Investor; these explanations and fictional cases are original Quanta material, not reproduced chapters or publisher exercises. The worksheet calculates the case and keeps the price sandbox in cash. Its chart is not an investment recommendation or a test of Graham's approach.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's 26% company shows what overlapping funds can hide. Three studies point to other places where one risk can sit behind many labels.

Country. French and Poterba estimated that Japanese investors held more than 98% of their equity portfolios at home, against 94% for U.S. and 82% for British investors. Their model implied that investors expected domestic returns to beat foreign ones by several hundred basis points, and they read the pattern as investor choice rather than institutional constraint. A portfolio of funds that are each labelled diversified can still be mostly one country, so the look-through table needs a country column (our inference).

Employer. Meulbroek priced the lost diversification of company stock held in pension plans. In her estimates, an employee who puts one-quarter of assets into the employer's shares gives up 42 percent of their market value relative to a well-diversified equity portfolio. Counting wages, which depend on the same firm, total exposure is larger than the portfolio weight alone suggests.

Shared drivers. Plerou and co-authors applied random-matrix methods to correlations among up to 1,000 U.S. stocks. Most of the structure looked like noise; what stood out was one influence common to all stocks and groups of stocks matching business sectors. Our inference: hundreds of tickers can reduce to one market factor plus sector bets.

Exercise: add country, sector and employer columns to the lesson's look-through table. Then halve the 26% company's price: the portfolio loses 13% (26% × 50%) before any effect on your wages. If that loss would break your plan, the exposure is larger than the plan can bear.

### Sources for this section

- [French & Poterba (1991) · Investor Diversification and International Equity Markets](https://doi.org/10.3386/w3609) — *Research paper.* Estimates the home share of Japanese, U.S. and British equity portfolios (98%, 94%, 82%) and argues the gap reflects investor choice, so a country column belongs in a look-through audit.
- [Meulbroek (2005) · Company Stock in Pension Plans: How Costly Is It?](https://doi.org/10.1086/430807) — *Research paper.* Values the lost diversification of employer stock held in pension plans; one-quarter of assets in it sacrifices 42 percent of the stock's market value, relative to a diversified equity portfolio.
- [Plerou et al. (2001) · A Random Matrix Approach to Cross-Correlations in Financial Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0108023) — *arXiv cond-mat/0108023.* Random-matrix study of U.S. stock correlations: one influence common to all stocks, groups that match business sectors, and a bulk that is close to random.
