modules.title: Net current assets and liquidation haircuts
modules.subtitle: Calculate NCAV and a separate stressed realization estimate after every senior claim.
modules.objective: Calculate NCAV and a separate stressed realization estimate after every senior claim.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VI. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Assets listed in accounts are not necessarily worth their recorded amounts in a sale. Some cash may be needed to keep operating, some customers may not pay, and some inventory may sell at a discount. This unit asks what could remain for shareholders after those realities and all obligations are considered. Follow the order of deductions carefully.

## The balance sheet is a starting inventory of claims

Net-current-asset value deducts all liabilities and applicable preferred claims from current assets. It is not ordinary working capital, which deducts only current liabilities. Long-term debt still stands ahead of common owners even when the analyst focuses only on cash, receivables, and inventory.

Recorded current assets need not realize their carrying amounts. Collection quality, obsolescence, restricted cash, and sale conditions affect recovery. Haircuts should be tied to evidence about specific assets. Fixed percentage assumptions are useful for sensitivity exercises, not universal recovery laws.

A discount to NCAV is a research screen. Check whether losses will consume the surplus, whether owners can access it, and whether unrecognized obligations or closure costs remain. A low quoted price does not force liquidation or guarantee realization.

$$
NCAV/share=(CA-TL-Pref)/N
$$

## A worked example

Alder has cash of $40 million, receivables of $60 million, inventory of $80 million, total liabilities of $70 million, no preferred claim, and 10 million common shares. NCAV is $110 million, or $11 per share. A two-thirds screening price would be approximately $7.33, using this stipulated rule.

Apply a 15% haircut to receivables and 40% to inventory. Adjusted resources become 40 + 51 + 48 = $139 million. After liabilities, $69 million remains, or $6.90 per share. Additional closure costs would reduce it further. The original $11 is not a conservative liquidation promise.

## Separate scenarios and deductions

Prepare a reported NCAV column, an orderly-realization case, and a more adverse case. Show every liability and preferred claim exactly once. Include a timeline and expected cash consumption if the thesis requires waiting.

A business can be cheap on a current-asset screen and still destroy owner value. The next analytical step is understanding whether the surplus can survive and eventually reach common shareholders.
modules.code:

modules.title: Hidden obligations and the realization clock
modules.subtitle: Stress an asset surplus for cash burn, closure costs, and claims omitted from a first-pass screen.
modules.objective: Stress an asset surplus for cash burn, closure costs, and claims omitted from a first-pass screen.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VI. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Time can consume the apparent bargain

An asset-based thesis requires more than a balance-sheet surplus. The business may continue losing cash while owners wait for a sale, restructuring, or change in policy. Management may invest the surplus in an unattractive project. A static calculation should therefore be accompanied by a timeline.

List restrictions on cash, commitments, guarantees, customer deposits, disputed obligations, and likely realization expenses. In contemporary accounts, some lease obligations and other items may already be recognized. Reconcile the claims schedule to recorded liabilities before adding any incremental estimate, so that you do not deduct the same obligation twice.

Distinguish a known liability, an estimated additional cost, and a downside contingency. Show the probability or scenario premise if relevant rather than presenting all possibilities as certain cash payments. The objective is a transparent range.

$$
V_0=(A-\text{burn}-\text{incremental costs})/(1+r)^T
$$

## A worked example

An initial asset screen leaves $40 million for common shareholders. The proposed realization takes two years. Expected net operating cash burn is $6 million each year, incremental closure costs are $5 million, and an additional obligation not included in the original claims schedule is estimated at $3 million. The residual before discounting is 40 − 12 − 5 − 3 = $20 million.

At a stipulated 10% annual discount rate, a single $20 million receipt at the end of year two has present value of about $16.53 million. This timing simplification differs from a detailed schedule in which individual costs occur earlier; state which model you use.

## Demand a path to realization

Identify who can initiate a sale or distribution, what approvals and financing are required, and what prevents delay. A catalyst is an event with a plausible mechanism, not just the hope that investors notice a low multiple.

Track the thesis through time. Compare actual cash burn with the estimate and update value when evidence changes. A lower share price cannot offset a vanishing asset surplus indefinitely.

modules.title: Book value, intangibles, and asset productivity
modules.subtitle: Explain why book value is neither a universal floor nor a complete account of business worth.
modules.objective: Explain why book value is neither a universal floor nor a complete account of business worth.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VI. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Interpret what the carrying amount measures

Book equity is the residual of recognized assets and liabilities under accounting conventions. It can reflect historical costs, estimates, acquisitions, and past losses. It is useful evidence about capital supplied and resources recorded, but it does not automatically measure sale proceeds or sustainable earning power.

Tangible assets may be specialized, obsolete, or costly to remove. Intangible assets can be economically valuable even when little appears on the balance sheet. Conversely, an acquisition premium recorded as goodwill does not itself establish value that a new buyer would pay.

Separate an asset's independent realization value from its contribution to an operating system. Customer relationships, trained staff, and distribution arrangements can support earnings without being readily saleable in isolation. The analytical premise determines how to treat them.

$$
\text{Tangible equity}=\text{assets}-\text{liabilities}-\text{goodwill}
$$

## A worked example

Alder reports assets of $200 million, including $50 million of goodwill, and liabilities of $120 million. Book equity is $80 million. A simple tangible-equity calculation removes goodwill, leaving $30 million. With 10 million shares, the two figures are $8 and $3 per share.

Neither figure settles value. If tangible assets can realize only $130 million in total after removing goodwill and considering recoveries, the residual before further costs is $10 million. Alternatively, a durable profitable business could have going-concern value exceeding book equity. Those are separate hypotheses requiring different evidence.

## Connect assets to earning power

Compare the resources required to generate normalized profit with the profit actually earned. A large asset base earning very little may signal poor economics, excess capacity, or understated future improvement. A small recorded asset base earning a great deal requires an explanation of durability and competition.

Avoid declaring every intangible worthless or every high return permanent. Write what a buyer would need to recreate, what could be sold independently, and what might disappear if the organization stopped operating.

modules.title: Compare businesses on consistent terms
modules.subtitle: Construct a peer comparison with matching claims, normalized earnings, and accounting assumptions.
modules.objective: Construct a peer comparison with matching claims, normalized earnings, and accounting assumptions.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VII. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A comparison is useful when the numbers describe similar things. Before comparing two companies, check their accounting choices, debts, share counts, and business conditions. A low ratio may reflect an attractive price, a weaker business, or a mismatched calculation. This unit turns separate valuation observations into a decision with explicit reasons and a plan for review.

## A multiple compresses assumptions

A price-to-earnings ratio combines the market value of common equity with earnings attributable to common owners. An enterprise multiple pairs the value of operating claims with an operating measure. Mixing enterprise value with common EPS produces an incoherent comparison.

Cheapness is relative to an economic denominator. Two identical reported multiples can conceal different leverage, cyclicality, accounting policies, reinvestment needs, and customer concentration. Begin with a small comparable set and explain the reasons for inclusion. A large automated ranking does not establish comparability.

Normalize earnings before comparing multiples. Record how taxes, unusual items, minority interests, and diluted shares are treated. A low multiple at peak profit can be more expensive than a higher multiple on depressed but recoverable earnings.

$$
EV=\text{equity market value}+\text{debt}-\text{excess cash}
$$

## A worked example

Alder has equity market value of $120 million, debt of $60 million, and excess cash of $20 million. Enterprise value is $160 million. Normalized EBIT is $20 million, giving EV/EBIT of 8 times. A peer has equity value of $150 million, debt of $10 million, no excess cash, and normalized EBIT of $20 million: also 8 times.

The companies have the same enterprise multiple but different financing risk. Alder's common holders stand behind more net debt. If operating values fall by the same amount, the percentage impact on their smaller residual equity can be larger.

## Explain the residual difference

Build a bridge from reported to comparable figures for each company. Then identify the facts a multiple does not capture: asset quality, business durability, governance, and required reinvestment. A peer's market price is another market observation, not independent proof of intrinsic value.

Use comparables to challenge an estimate. If your conclusion requires a much higher multiple than similarly exposed businesses, explain the difference in economics. Do not import the peer average solely because it creates an attractive upside.

modules.title: Special situations and contingent outcomes
modules.subtitle: Analyze a price discrepancy using completion, failure, timing, and funding scenarios.
modules.objective: Analyze a price discrepancy using completion, failure, timing, and funding scenarios.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VII. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## A spread describes a contingent claim

A announced cash transaction, liquidation, or exchange can create a difference between today's price and a possible future receipt. The spread is not free profit. Completion can fail, timing can stretch, and interim financing or liquidity can become expensive.

Start with the actual mechanism that turns the security into cash or another claim. List conditions, required approvals, financing dependencies, and what the holder owns if the event fails. Treat probability estimates as assumptions to be tested, not objective frequencies merely because a spreadsheet accepts them.

A positive expected payoff can coexist with a large loss in an adverse outcome. Position size, correlation among events, and the ability to hold through delays matter separately from the expected value calculation.

$$
p_{break-even}=(P-V_{failure})/(V_{success}-V_{failure})
$$

## A worked example

A fictional target costs $45. A stipulated cash deal pays $50 if completed; estimated standalone value after failure is $32. If the analyst assumes an 80% completion probability, expected terminal proceeds are 0.8 × 50 + 0.2 × 32 = $46.40, before discounting and costs. Expected gain is $1.40, while failure loses $13.

Ignoring timing and costs, the break-even completion probability solves 45 = p × 50 + (1 − p) × 32. It is 13 / 18 = 72.22%. A lower assumed probability produces a negative expected payoff. Longer waiting periods can reduce attractiveness even if the event ultimately completes.

## Write both stories

Describe why completion should occur and what evidence would support failure. Avoid treating management's target date as a certainty. Test the failure value independently; it may have changed since the announcement.

Keep the arithmetic, probability judgment, and risk budget separate. An attractive spread may compensate for a risk the portfolio cannot tolerate. The decision should survive a plausible adverse scenario rather than relying entirely on the most likely outcome.

modules.title: From an estimate to a monitored decision
modules.subtitle: Write an investment memo with an opposing case, price discipline, and explicit review triggers.
modules.objective: Write an investment memo with an opposing case, price discipline, and explicit review triggers.
modules.reading: Graham & Dodd, Security Analysis, 1940 edition · Part VII. Read the relevant discussion in your own copy, then apply it to this original case.
modules.content:
## Analysis must lead to a revisable decision

A useful memo connects evidence to action. State the security, claim priority, value premise, conservative range, required discount, and source of realization. Then present the strongest opposing case. If the adverse argument is trivial, the research may not yet have confronted the real uncertainty.

Separate business review triggers from price review triggers. A lost customer, covenant change, or unexpected cash drain can alter value. A quotation reaching a target can alter the prospective return without changing the business. Both matter, but they should not be confused.

Position sizing introduces portfolio considerations beyond the security estimate. Several apparently unrelated bargains may depend on the same refinancing market or economic cycle. A discount to value does not eliminate the consequences of concentrated exposure.

$$
\text{Scenario portfolio loss}=\text{position weight}\times\text{position loss}
$$

## A worked example

A researcher estimates weak-case value at $40 per share and requires a 30% discount, producing a maximum purchase price of $28. The stock trades at $26. The memo identifies a customer representing 35% of revenue and a debt maturity in eighteen months as its two major risks.

A stress loss of 40% on the position would cost 2% of portfolio value if the initial position were 5%, assuming other holdings were unchanged. This is a scenario budget, not a bound on possible loss. A larger impairment or correlated losses could be worse.

## Use a repeatable review

Record the dated evidence supporting each assumption, the next expected information release, and the condition requiring reassessment. Compare actual results with the thesis rather than only with the share price. Preserve the original memo so later success does not erase the uncertainties present at purchase.

A sound conclusion can be buy, watch, avoid, or insufficient evidence. No numerical valuation obliges a trade. What matters is whether the claim, price, and evidence together satisfy the stated process.

modules.title: The Graham growth heuristic: a separate extension
modules.subtitle: Audit the units and sensitivity of a later growth heuristic without treating it as the 1940 book's valuation method.
modules.objective: Audit the units and sensitivity of a later growth heuristic without treating it as the 1940 book's valuation method.
modules.reading: Course extension · modern valuation and synthesis. These tools and the growth heuristic are not presented as methods from the 1940 text.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

The final unit connects the earlier business analysis to additional valuation tools and a complete case. A formula can help you explore an assumption, but it cannot choose that assumption for you. Keep the historical method, later extensions, and your own estimates clearly identified. Use more than one view of the business to investigate disagreement between results.

## Keep historical layers separate

This optional bridge retains the earlier course's growth worksheet. The expression below is a later heuristic commonly associated with Graham; it is not the organizing valuation method of the 1940 Security Analysis course. The course does not use it to replace analysis of earning power, assets, and creditor protection.

The worksheet combines EPS, an assumed growth input, and a reference-yield scaling factor. Its constants are fixed assumptions rather than a complete economic model. It has no explicit cash-flow forecast, reinvestment schedule, fade of competitive advantage, or probability of failure.

In this expression, growth and yield are entered in percentage points: 5 for 5%, and 4.4 for 4.4%. Mixing decimals with percentage points can create an apparently precise but meaningless answer. The mathematical requirement of a positive yield denominator does not establish that the resulting value is appropriate.

$$
V=EPS(8.5+2g)\frac{4.4}{Y}
$$

## A worked example

With EPS of $4, growth input of 5, and yield input of 4.4, the worksheet gives $74. Raising the yield input to 6 reduces the result to about $54.27. Keeping the original yield but raising growth to 10 produces $114.

These large changes come from a few assumptions, without any explicit modeling of the investment needed to achieve growth. If normalized EPS is actually $3 rather than $4, every result falls by 25%. Sensitivity can overwhelm the supposed discount to the market price.

## Use the worksheet as a critique

Reproduce the calculation, label every input, and explain what the formula leaves out. Compare its conclusion with a separate asset and earning-power analysis. A disagreement is a reason to investigate assumptions, not to average three outputs until the desired answer emerges.

For book study, keep this exercise in the extension unit. Its role is to demonstrate the danger of compressing a complex business into a popular rule of thumb.

modules.title: Modern bridge: earning-power and cash-flow valuation
modules.subtitle: Convert operating value into common equity and test discount-rate assumptions in a transparent modern model.
modules.objective: Convert operating value into common equity and test discount-rate assumptions in a transparent modern model.
modules.reading: Course extension · modern valuation and synthesis. These tools and the growth heuristic are not presented as methods from the 1940 text.
modules.content:
## A modern model should preserve analytical discipline

This extension uses contemporary cash-flow notation to apply the course's emphasis on normalized operations and conservative assumptions. It is not attributed to the 1940 text. Begin by defining the cash flow: to the business before debt financing, or to common owners after financing. Use a discount rate consistent with that claim.

A no-growth operating model can capitalize sustainable cash available before financing at an assumed required return. A growing perpetuity additionally assumes stable growth, a consistent reinvestment policy embedded in cash flow, and a discount rate above growth. Those are strong assumptions.

After estimating operating value, add only excess nonoperating assets and deduct debt and other senior claims not already reflected. Do not deduct debt twice if the modeled cash flow and discount rate already value common equity directly.

$$
EV=FCF_1/(r-g);\quad V_{common}=(EV+Cash-Debt)/N
$$

## A worked example

Alder's sustainable annual cash flow to operating capital is estimated at $15 million. A no-growth perpetuity discounted at 10% gives operating value of $150 million. Add $10 million of excess cash and deduct $40 million of debt: common value is $120 million, or $12 with 10 million shares.

At a 12% required return, operating value falls to $125 million and common value to $9.50 per share. If next year's cash flow is still $15 million but a perpetual 2% growth assumption is introduced at a 10% rate, operating value becomes $187.5 million. The increase is an assumption effect, not a newly discovered asset.

## Test the model's dependencies

Show a grid of sustainable cash flow and required return. If growth is included, explain how investment requirements are funded and why the growth-rate assumption is sustainable. Compare with asset evidence without adding mutually exclusive values.

A model is useful when it makes the decision's dependencies inspectable. Its formula does not reduce uncertainty unless the underlying evidence improves.

modules.reading: Course extension · modern valuation and synthesis. These tools and the growth heuristic are not presented as methods from the 1940 text.
modules.content:
## Your case file

All amounts below are fictional millions except per-share figures. The date is the case decision date; assume all listed information was available then. Alder has 10 million common shares at $6.20. Cash is 30, of which 10 is required for operations. Receivables are 50, inventory 70, and recorded fixed assets 90. Total liabilities are 100, including interest-bearing debt of 60. There is no preferred claim.

Reported EBIT is 24, including a nonrecurring pretax asset-sale gain of 4. Annual interest is 5. Weak-case recurring EBIT is 12. For a separate modern no-growth model, use a stipulated sustainable unlevered cash-flow range of 9–12 and a required return of 10%. These cash flows already reflect operating investment needs and taxes.

For an asset realization scenario, recover cash in full, 80% of receivables, 50% of inventory, and 20% of fixed assets. Deduct all recorded liabilities and incremental closure costs of 8. Assume no additional burn in this immediate-realization scenario; then challenge that assumption.

$$
P_{max}=V_{conservative}(1-M_{required})
$$

## A worked example

Normalized EBIT is 20 and normal interest coverage is 4 times; weak coverage is 2.4 times. NCAV is (30 + 50 + 70 − 100) / 10 = $5 per share. Adjusted realization is (30 + 40 + 35 + 18 − 100 − 8) / 10 = $1.50.

No-growth operating value is 90–120. Add only 20 of excess cash, deduct debt of 60, and divide by 10: common value is $5–8 per share. The other operating liabilities are reflected in this case's stipulated operating cash flows; the asset realization separately deducts all liabilities. Explain that difference in your claims bridge.

At $6.20 the discount to the upper endpoint is 22.5%, but the quote exceeds the lower endpoint. A required 30% discount to the $5 conservative operating estimate implies a maximum price of $3.50. The current quote fails that rule.

## Committee deliverable

Write 600–900 words with a claims map, normalized earnings bridge, three valuation premises, downside case, price decision, and monitoring plan. Cite case facts and clearly label your assumptions. Explain why the three values should not be added or mechanically averaged.

Self-assess five criteria, each from 0 to 4: traceable evidence, correct reconciliations, consistent valuation premises, serious downside analysis, and a revisable decision. A score of 3 means correct with explicit limitations; 4 also explains a plausible alternative. Aim for 15/20 with no zero. The notebook stores your memo; the app grades the numerical final exam separately and does not certify the written work.

for cash_flow in [9, 12]:

print("Maximum conservative price:", 5 * .70)

readingGuide:
A share price tells you what someone is asking. It does not tell you what the business can earn or what would remain for investors if it ran into trouble. This course teaches you to build that picture from evidence, following Graham and Dodd's approach to security analysis.

Start by identifying the investment you are examining: a lender's claim, a preferred share, or common ownership. Then look at the cash, earnings, assets, and obligations that support it. The worked examples show how changing an assumption changes an estimate. Keep a separate note of facts, assumptions, and unanswered questions. By the end, you will bring those notes together in an investment committee case and explain why the evidence supports your conclusion.

Use your own copy of the 1940 edition alongside the seven book-aligned units. The publisher's sixth-edition contents also preserves the seven-part organization around the historical text.

Unit VIII is a clearly separated course extension. These are original teaching cases and exercises, not reproduced chapters or publisher exam questions.

Allow additional time for the book readings and written assignments beyond the displayed lesson estimates.

modules.title: From a headline to an investment question
modules.subtitle: Separate a reported fact, a management claim, an inference, and a stock-price prediction.
modules.objective: Separate a reported fact, a management claim, an inference, and a stock-price prediction.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Before deciding whether news is good or bad for a stock, turn the headline into a question you can investigate. What was actually announced, how large is it relative to the business, and what must happen before it affects cash? The worked example separates a contract's headline value from the revenue it might contribute in one year.

## Understand the idea

Security Analysis gives you a framework for business value. News analysis asks which assumptions need updating when new information arrives. A headline is an entry point: read the underlying announcement, identify its date and scope, and translate it into a question about revenue, costs, assets, financing, or uncertainty.

Keep four columns. A fact is directly supported by a dated source; a claim is attributed to its speaker; an inference explains a mechanism under stated assumptions; a price forecast adds assumptions about expectations and valuation. Even a verified contract does not reveal its margin, collection timing, or whether investors already expected it. Your first output can be a research question rather than a trading decision.

$$
\text{Annual exposure ceiling}=\frac{\text{Contract ceiling}/\text{Years}}{\text{Existing annual sales}}
$$

## A worked example

Fictional Cedar Components announces a three-year contract with a maximum value of $90 million. Its existing annual revenue is $600 million. The headline calls this a 'transformational win'. Dividing the ceiling evenly implies at most $30 million a year, or 5% of current revenue, before delivery conditions, cancellations, and displacement of other work. The filing verifies the announcement; it does not verify the word transformational or a future share-price increase.

### Slow down the headline's arithmetic

The $90 million figure is a maximum across three years. It is not stated as $90 million of revenue in the next year. If you spread the ceiling evenly for this illustration, divide $90 million by 3 to get $30 million per year.

To judge the size, compare annual amounts with annual amounts. Divide that $30 million by the company's existing $600 million annual revenue. The ratio is 0.05, or 5%. This gives you a scale for the question. It does not establish the actual delivery schedule or guarantee that the maximum amount will be earned.

Revenue is also different from profit and cash. The company may incur costs to perform the contract, receive payment later, or use capacity that would otherwise serve another customer. After checking the headline amount, investigate those terms before estimating the effect on earnings or value. The source supports an announced contract; your interpretation requires additional steps.

## Put the idea into practice

Record the original source and exact period. Ask whether $90 million is committed revenue, an optional ceiling, or backlog. Then ask about capacity, incremental costs, capital spending, customer concentration, and cash collection. Build a chain: contract terms → recognized sales → operating cash flow → value per share. Stop at each missing link and write what evidence would resolve it. Do not convert a maximum into a probability-weighted forecast without an explicit assumption.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's $90 million is a ceiling, and contract design shows why a ceiling and committed revenue can differ. Take a U.S. federal indefinite-quantity contract as a model. The Federal Acquisition Regulation says such a contract must require the government to order at least a stated minimum, and the contractor must furnish any further quantities that are ordered only up to a stated maximum. The minimum must be more than nominal but should not exceed what the government is fairly certain to order, so the guaranteed amount can sit far below the headline maximum. Other contract types work differently, which is why the filing's own terms matter more than a press-release summary.

Order backlog is a related disclosure. Rajgopal, Shevlin and Venkatachalam studied backlog as a leading indicator and found that the stock market overweights its contribution to predicting future earnings. A strategy that exploited the overweighting earned significant abnormal returns, and the authors say the mispricing was not due to analysts being unable to use backlog in their forecasts. Backlog is an input with an uncertain conversion into profit, not sales already earned.

The headline itself is a presentation choice. Huang, Nekrasov and Teoh counted the quantitative items in earnings press-release headlines. More items were associated with stronger announcement reactions and later reversals, and managers were more likely to choose them before selling shares after the announcement. That evidence concerns earnings releases, not contract announcements, so read it as a reason to test a big number, not as a rule (an inference, not a finding).

Verification is also hard to automate. Zhao and co-authors built FinDVer, 2,400 expert-annotated examples for checking claims against long financial documents, and reported that even the best system they tested, GPT-4o, lagged human experts.

Check: find the minimum, maximum and term in a real contract announcement. For Cedar, suppose the minimum were $9 million (hypothetical). The annual floor would be $3 million, or 0.5% of $600 million, against the 5% ceiling. Report the range, not one number.

### Sources for this section

- [Federal Acquisition Regulation · eCFR · Indefinite-quantity contracts (48 CFR 16.504)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-48/chapter-1/subchapter-C/part-16/subpart-16.5/section-16.504) — *Official source.* The U.S. federal rule defining a stated minimum and maximum in indefinite-quantity contracts; it separates the guaranteed amount from the ceiling.
- [Rajgopal, Shevlin & Venkatachalam (2003) · Does the Stock Market Fully Appreciate the Implications of Leading Indicators for Future Earnings? Evidence from Order Backlog](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1027364031775) — *Research paper.* Tests whether order backlog predicts earnings and whether prices reflect it correctly; the market overweights backlog.
- [Huang, Nekrasov & Teoh (2018) · Headline Salience, Managerial Opportunism, and Over- and Underreactions to Earnings](https://doi.org/10.2308/accr-52010) — *Research paper.* Shows how the number of quantitative items in an earnings headline relates to market reactions and to managers' share sales.
- [Zhao et al. (2024) · FinDVer: Explainable Claim Verification over Long and Hybrid-Content Financial Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05764) — *arXiv 2411.05764.* A claim-verification benchmark on long financial documents in which the best model tested still trails human experts.

modules.title: Source quality, timestamps, and corrections
modules.subtitle: Build a traceable source chain and distinguish fresh information from repeated reporting.
modules.objective: Build a traceable source chain and distinguish fresh information from repeated reporting.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Ten posts repeating one anonymous message provide one underlying claim, not ten independent confirmations. Follow links backward to the original disclosure, dataset, transcript, or named observer. Record publication time, event time, access time, time zone, and later corrections separately. An article updated after the close cannot be treated as fully available at the open.

Primary material is closer to the event but still requires interpretation. A company release reflects management's incentives; an auditor's report has a defined scope; a social post can impersonate an official source. Confirm the issuing entity and distinguish independent corroboration from syndication. Keep rejected evidence in the research log with its rejection reason.

$$
\text{Eligible evidence}_i=\mathbf{1}(t_{\mathrm{available},i}\leq t_{\mathrm{decision}})
$$

## A worked example

A rumor appears at 09:00. Four blogs repeat it at 09:15. Cedar publishes a clarification at 11:00: a proposed deal is still under negotiation. An aggregator updates the article at 12:00 without preserving its old headline. For a decision at 10:00, the clarification was unavailable. For a decision at 12:30, continuing to classify the rumor as confirmed ignores a known correction.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a timeline with an 'available by decision time' flag. Prefer links and your own short factual notes over copying articles. Preserve permitted versions or document hashes where lawful and useful, with source-use terms. Do not invent an earlier consensus or a historical headline from today's revised page. An unresolved original source should lower confidence and can justify waiting.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson counts four blog posts as one claim. Research shows why that discipline matters, because repeated or old information can still move prices. Huberman and Regev studied EntreMed after a Sunday New York Times article on potential cancer-curing drugs. The stock closed at 12.063 on Friday, opened at 85 on Monday, closed near 52, and stayed above 30 for the following three weeks. The same breakthrough had been reported in Nature and in popular newspapers more than five months earlier, and the authors conclude that no genuinely new information had been presented.

Tetlock made staleness measurable: a story's textual similarity to the previous ten stories about the same firm. Returns responded less to stale news, but the return on a stale-news day negatively predicted the following week's return, and individual investors traded more aggressively when news was stale. So log repetition rather than assume the market ignores it.

Corrections have a long tail too. In September 2008 a six-year-old article about United Airlines' 2002 bankruptcy resurfaced and was mistaken for a new filing. Carvalho, Klagge and Moench report that the stock fell by as much as 76% within minutes before NASDAQ halted trading, and still ended the day 11.2% below the previous close even after the news was identified as false. After three trading sessions it remained below their model's two-standard-deviation band, and it was back at the predicted level on the seventh day. Our inference: an 'available by' flag says what was knowable at a time, not that prices or other readers had already absorbed it.

The same rule applies to AI helpers. Glasserman and Lin warn that a language model trained on many years of text biases a backtest when the training and backtesting periods overlap. Inside the training window, anonymized headlines outperformed the originals, which they read as a distraction effect, and out of sample look-ahead bias was not a concern.

Check: in Cedar's timeline, mark each item eligible or not at 10:00 and at 12:30. Write 'one claim' beside the 09:00 rumor and the four 09:15 reposts unless a repost adds a fact the original lacked.

### Sources for this section

- [Huberman & Regev (2001) · Contagious Speculation and a Cure for Cancer: A Nonevent That Made Stock Prices Soar](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00330) — *Research paper.* A case in which re-reported, already public news produced a lasting price jump in EntreMed.
- [Tetlock (2011) · All the News That's Fit to Reprint: Do Investors React to Stale Information?](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhq141) — *Research paper.* Defines news staleness by textual similarity to earlier stories and tests how prices and investor types respond.
- [Carvalho, Klagge & Moench (2011) · The persistent effects of a false news shock](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jempfin.2011.03.003) — *Research paper.* Event study of the 2008 United Airlines false-bankruptcy episode and the days it took the price to recover.
- [Glasserman & Lin (2023) · Assessing Look-Ahead Bias in Stock Return Predictions Generated By GPT Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17322) — *arXiv 2309.17322.* Shows how overlapping model-training and backtest periods can contaminate headline-sentiment strategies.

modules.title: Materiality, denominators, and units
modules.subtitle: Translate big-looking numbers into exposure relative to the specific company.
modules.objective: Translate big-looking numbers into exposure relative to the specific company.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Economic importance depends on scale, persistence, and the affected claim. A $10 million cost can be negligible to one firm and absorb a small firm's annual profit. Compare a flow with a flow for the same period; compare a debt balance with liquidity, asset value, and maturities. Use consistent currencies, units, and consolidated versus segment scope.

Percent changes, percentage points, and basis points answer different questions. Moving a margin from 10% to 11% is one percentage point, 100 basis points, and a 10% relative improvement in the margin. None automatically describes the change in net profit or equity value. Qualitative events such as a lost license can also matter before a precise cost is known; a simple size screen is an analyst's triage tool, not a legal definition of materiality.

$$
\text{EBIT impact ratio}=\frac{\Delta\text{Recurring cost}}{\text{Base EBIT}}
$$

## A worked example

Fictional Nusa Retail sells Rp2,000 billion a year with EBIT of Rp100 billion. A recurring Rp15 billion logistics cost equals 0.75% of sales but 15% of EBIT if nothing else changes. A quoted margin improvement of '50 points' is ambiguous: 50 basis points would be Rp10 billion on unchanged sales, while 50 percentage points would be Rp1,000 billion. Request the exact unit before modeling.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a units box: currency, millions or billions, annual or quarterly, stock or flow, gross or net, total or per share. Then compute exposure against both revenue and profit. Check persistence and management responses instead of treating the static calculation as a forecast. In your memo use 'Rp15 billion annually, 15% of base EBIT before offsets' rather than simply 'small cost'.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson calls its size screen a triage tool, and official guidance agrees. In Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99 the SEC staff accepted a percentage threshold such as 5% as a basis for a preliminary assumption that a smaller deviation is unlikely to be material. It added that expressing a misstatement as a percentage is only the start of the analysis and cannot replace weighing every relevant consideration. Its qualitative factors include whether an item masks a change in earnings or other trends, hides a miss against analysts' consensus, turns a loss into income, or affects loan covenants or regulatory compliance. The bulletin is aimed at preparers and auditors, so using those factors as an analyst's checklist for looking past a ratio is our inference.

Size can also understate consequences. Karpoff, Lee and Martin examined 585 firms targeted by SEC enforcement for financial misrepresentation from 1978 to 2002. Legal penalties averaged $23.5 million per firm, but their estimated reputational penalty was over 7.5 times all legal and regulatory penalties combined. For each dollar of inflated market value, firms lost that dollar plus $3.08, of which $0.36 was expected legal penalty and $2.71 lost reputation. These are misconduct cases, so they illustrate the principle rather than set a rate.

Units are a practical hazard. The builders of the TAT-QA dataset note that magnitudes such as thousand, million and billion are often omitted or shown only in headers or nearby paragraphs, and they call this a number's scale. Their proposed model reached 58.0% F1 against 90.8% for human experts, so an automated extraction still needs your units box.

Check: Nusa's Rp15 billion is 0.75% of sales and 15% of EBIT. Pick one factor from the bulletin's list that would make it matter more. For example, if a covenant required EBIT of at least Rp90 billion (hypothetical), headroom would fall from Rp10 billion to negative Rp5 billion.

### Sources for this section

- [U.S. SEC · Federal Register (1999) · Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1999-08-19/html/99-21484.htm) — *Official source.* The SEC staff's guidance that a percentage rule of thumb is only a starting point for materiality, with a list of qualitative factors.
- [Karpoff, Lee & Martin (2008) · The Cost to Firms of Cooking the Books](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109000004221) — *Research paper.* Compares legal penalties with the much larger reputational loss for 585 firms that faced SEC misrepresentation actions.
- [Zhu et al. (2021) · TAT-QA: A Question Answering Benchmark on a Hybrid of Tabular and Textual Content in Finance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.07624) — *arXiv 2105.07624.* A financial-report question-answering dataset that treats a number's unit scale as something a model must infer from headers.

modules.title: Expectations, surprises, and 'priced in'
modules.subtitle: Explain why favorable business news can coexist with a falling stock.
modules.objective: Explain why favorable business news can coexist with a falling stock.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A change in business conditions and a surprise relative to expectations are different measurements. Markets price a distribution of future outcomes, not just last year's reported result. Compare actuals with a dated, definition-matched expectation and with what the price appears to assume. A consensus estimate is an imperfect proxy for expectations; record its provider, sample, timestamp, currency, and accounting basis.

A statement that news was 'priced in' should specify what was expected before release and how that inference was obtained. A subsequent price move alone cannot prove it. Guidance, margins, risk premia, positioning, and other announcements can dominate the headline number. A miss can also be less bad than investors feared.

$$
\text{Surprise}=\frac{\text{Actual}-\text{Expected}}{|\text{Expected}|},\quad \text{Expected}\ne0
$$

## A worked example

Cedar reports EPS of $1.20 versus $1.00 a year earlier, but the dated estimate was $1.30. EPS grew 20% year over year and missed the estimate by about 7.69%. Management also reduces next-year volume guidance. The stock falls 6%. The growth headline is true; it does not establish that the release improved the outlook relative to the pre-release price.

## Put the idea into practice

Write three separate comparisons: actual versus prior period, actual versus dated consensus, and your revised valuation versus the current price. Match GAAP or adjusted definitions and share counts. If expectations are unavailable, write 'surprise cannot be measured reliably' instead of using the prior year as a substitute. Keep price response as an observation to explain, not as evidence that every assumption in your story is correct.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's Cedar example, a 20% EPS gain that still misses the estimate, fits a pattern that Skinner and Sloan documented. Growth stocks, they found, are at least as likely to report negative earnings surprises as positive ones, but they react with an asymmetrically large price drop to the negative ones. After controlling for that asymmetric response, they found no remaining return gap between growth and value stocks, and they read the gap as optimistic expectations corrected by later disappointments. Whether Cedar fits depends on what its pre-release price assumed, which the 6% fall alone cannot tell you.

The word 'expected' also hides a choice. Livnat and Mendenhall measured surprises two ways: from analysts' forecasts and from a time-series model built on Compustat earnings. The post-announcement drift was significantly larger with the analyst-based surprise, and they suggest the two measures may capture somewhat different forms of mispricing. A dated consensus and a naive 'last year plus trend' benchmark are therefore different tests, not interchangeable ones.

Is the news fully priced at the announcement? Studies disagree by period and firm size. Martineau argues that stock prices now fully reflect earnings surprises on the announcement date: drift has been non-existent for large stocks since 2006 and has disappeared only recently for microcaps. Christensen, Timmermann and Veliyev, in a recent preprint, find that earnings announcements almost always trigger price jumps and that a post-announcement trading strategy is consistent with efficient price formation after 2016. Our inference: for a large listed company, a continued slide after a miss is more likely new information or noise than a slow reaction, while a microcap or an older sample deserves a different prior.

Check: scale Cedar's 10-cent miss two ways. Against $1.30 expected EPS it is 7.69%; against a hypothetical $26 share price it is 0.38%. Write down which scaling you chose, because it changes how large the surprise looks.

### Sources for this section

- [Skinner & Sloan (2002) · Earnings Surprises, Growth Expectations, and Stock Returns or Don't Let an Earnings Torpedo Sink Your Portfolio](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1020294523516) — *Research paper.* Shows that growth stocks react asymmetrically to negative surprises, which explains why a miss can hurt when expectations are high.
- [Livnat & Mendenhall (2006) · Comparing the Post-Earnings Announcement Drift for Surprises Calculated from Analyst and Time Series Forecasts](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-679X.2006.00196.x) — *Research paper.* Compares surprises built from analyst forecasts with those from time-series models and finds different drift.
- [Martineau (2022) · Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift](https://doi.org/10.1561/104.00000122) — *Research paper.* Argues that prices now reflect earnings surprises on the announcement date, so drift has vanished for large stocks.
- [Christensen, Timmermann & Veliyev (2026) · Warp speed price moves: Jumps after earnings announcements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08962) — *arXiv 2601.08962.* High-frequency evidence that announcements trigger price jumps and that later returns look consistent with efficient pricing.

modules.title: Read an earnings release through the income statement
modules.subtitle: Bridge sales growth into operating profit and identify mix, price, and volume effects.
modules.objective: Bridge sales growth into operating profit and identify mix, price, and volume effects.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Company news becomes easier to interpret when you can place it in the accounts. More sales may bring more profit, but they may also require additional inventory or leave customers owing more money. Follow the path from revenue to expenses, profit, and cash. Each step gives you a different question to ask of an earnings release.

## Understand the idea

Read an earnings release in layers: headline measures, segment results, accounting statements, reconciliations, and outlook. Build a consistent bridge from revenue to gross profit to operating profit before interpreting EPS. Revenue may rise through price increases, unit sales, acquisitions, or currency translation, each with different persistence and costs.

Do not compare an adjusted metric with an unadjusted expectation. Note exclusions, repeated restructuring, stock compensation, and changes in reporting definitions. Management's preferred metric can be informative when reconciled and consistently used, but it does not replace cash flow or the claims senior to shareholders. Keep recurring operating developments separate from disposal gains and financing effects.

$$
\text{EBIT}=\text{Revenue}\times\text{Gross margin}-\text{Operating expense}
$$

## A worked example

Cedar's quarterly revenue increases from 200 to 220, but gross margin falls from 40% to 35%. Gross profit falls from 80 to 77. Operating expense rises from 50 to 52, taking EBIT from 30 to 25, a 16.67% decline despite 10% sales growth. A $12 property gain could lift reported net profit without improving this operating bridge.

## Put the idea into practice

Create old and new columns using one accounting basis and the same period. Reconcile price, volume, mix, acquisitions, and FX where the release permits it; mark unavailable components instead of forcing them to sum through invented estimates. Compare each segment with its prior trajectory. Ask whether weaker margin reflects a temporary launch, permanent competition, or a mix shift, then attach a measurable follow-up indicator.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Where you stop on the income statement matters. Novy-Marx argued that gross profit is the cleanest accounting measure of true economic profitability, because measures grow more polluted the farther down the income statement you go. He found that gross profits-to-assets has roughly the same power as book-to-market in predicting the cross-section of average returns. Cedar's gross profit fell from 80 to 77 while revenue rose 10%, so the headline growth hides the line he emphasizes. His result concerns portfolios of many firms, not one quarter, so it tells you where to look rather than what Cedar's stock will do.

The next question is which earnings number the release leads with. Bradshaw and Sloan found that over the past 20 years the frequency and magnitude of gaps between GAAP and 'Street' earnings rose dramatically, with a very strong bias toward a Street figure above the GAAP figure. They also found that the market response to the Street number had displaced GAAP earnings as a primary determinant of prices, and that management actively defines and emphasizes the Street number in earnings releases.

Exclusions are not necessarily harmless. Doyle, Lundholm and Soliman found that higher levels of expenses excluded from pro forma earnings led to predictably lower future cash flows, that investors did not fully appreciate this at the announcement, and that a strategy based on the exclusions earned large positive abnormal returns in later years. For measures in SEC filings, Item 10(e) of Regulation S-K requires the GAAP measure with equal or greater prominence plus a quantitative reconciliation. It also bars adjusting a performance measure to eliminate an item labelled non-recurring, infrequent or unusual when a similar charge is reasonably likely to recur within two years or occurred within the prior two years.

Check: for Cedar, write the gross-margin change in percentage points, the gross-profit change and the EBIT change. Then, for each item the release excludes, search the previous two years of releases for a similar charge or gain. A repeat is a reason to treat it as part of ongoing operations in your own bridge.

### Sources for this section

- [Novy-Marx (2013) · The other side of value: The gross profitability premium](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.01.003) — *Research paper.* Argues that gross profit is the cleanest profitability measure and that it predicts returns about as strongly as book-to-market.
- [Bradshaw & Sloan (2002) · GAAP versus The Street: An Empirical Assessment of Two Alternative Definitions of Earnings](https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-679X.00038) — *Research paper.* Documents the widening gap between GAAP and Street earnings and the market's greater reliance on the Street figure.
- [Doyle, Lundholm & Soliman (2003) · The Predictive Value of Expenses Excluded from Pro Forma Earnings](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1024472210359) — *Research paper.* Shows that expenses excluded from pro forma earnings predict lower future cash flows that investors underweight.
- [Regulation S-K · eCFR · Item 10 (17 CFR 229.10): Use of non-GAAP financial measures in Commission filings](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-229/subpart-229.1/section-229.10) — *Official source.* The SEC rule requiring a GAAP comparison and reconciliation, and barring certain non-recurring labels on items likely to recur.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Revenue recognition and cash collection can occur in different periods. Growing receivables or inventory may absorb cash even when reported profit rises. Start with earnings and reconcile noncash charges, working-capital changes, and capital spending. Specify the sign convention: an increase in operating working capital uses cash; depreciation is a noncash expense added back in a simplified reconciliation.

A single weak quarter does not prove aggressive accounting. Seasonality, product launches, contract terms, or strategic inventory can explain timing. Conversely, repeated collection delays may contradict management's growth narrative. Compare the change with sales, prior seasonal patterns, receivable aging, and customer concentration. Free cash flow definitions vary; state yours explicitly.

$$
\text{Illustrative cash after capex}=NI+D\&A-\Delta NWC-\text{Capex}
$$

## A worked example

Nusa reports net income of 40 and depreciation of 10. Operating working capital rises by 25 and capex is 20. Under the simplified assumptions, operating cash flow is 25 and cash after capex is 5. Last year the comparable amount was 20. Profit alone misses the financing required to support the new inventory and receivables. These numbers omit other possible cash-flow adjustments and are not a complete statement reconstruction.

## Put the idea into practice

Read the cash-flow statement alongside balance-sheet notes. Break working capital into receivables, inventory, and payables; distinguish cash held by the group from cash available to the parent. Ask what reverses next quarter and what is structural. Model a collection-delay sensitivity instead of automatically adding all working-capital investment back to value. Keep dividends, buybacks, and debt repayments separate from operating cash generation.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Guidance is conditional management communication, not a contractual promise. Record the metric, period, range, assumptions, and exclusions. Compare with prior guidance and dated market estimates on the same basis. A range midpoint is a convenient summary, not necessarily management's expected value or a probability distribution.

Conference-call answers can clarify mix, pricing, or capacity, but tone is weaker evidence than an attributable numeric commitment. Changes in KPI definitions can break comparability: active users, backlog, recurring revenue, and same-store sales depend on inclusion rules. Look for reconciliation, discontinued measures, changing cohorts, and a widening range. Treat a missing answer as unresolved rather than filling the gap with optimism.

$$
\text{Midpoint revision}=\frac{(L_1+U_1)/2}{(L_0+U_0)/2}-1
$$

## A worked example

Cedar previously guided annual revenue to 900–1,000 and now guides 920–960. Both midpoints are 950 and 940 respectively, a 1.05% decline in the midpoint. The lower bound improves while the upper bound falls. Management calls this 'greater confidence', which may describe a narrower range but does not erase the lower central estimate. A new backlog definition includes cancellable orders absent from the old definition.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a guidance-change table and write a question for each major movement. Separate changes in demand from changes in the reporting metric. Tie management's narrative to a future release: conversion of backlog to recognized sales, churn by cohort, or capacity utilization. Preserve the old definition in your history and do not splice incompatible series into one growth chart.

assignment.solution: Ask which demand assumptions reduced the upper bound, whether the narrower range reflects visibility or conservatism, and how backlog reconciles under the old definition. Review order conversion and cancellations next quarter. The midpoint falls from 950 to 940; the narrower range is not by itself a stronger earnings forecast.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A financing headline changes both resources and claims on those resources. Issuing shares brings cash into the firm and expands the share count. A buyback reduces cash and shares; whether it creates value per remaining share depends on the price paid, financing, alternative uses, and future economics. EPS accretion alone is not proof of value creation.

For acquisitions, separate stand-alone value, payment, financing costs, integration spending, and uncertain synergies. For dividends and buybacks, distinguish authorization from completed cash distributions. A split changes units of ownership rather than the underlying business value. Read the actual terms before comparing per-share metrics, including convertible instruments and employee dilution.

$$
V_{\mathrm{share,new}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{equity,old}}+\mathrm{Net\ proceeds}+\mathrm{Project\ NPV}}{\mathrm{Shares}_{old}+\mathrm{Shares}_{new}}
$$

## A worked example

Nusa has equity value of 500 and 50 shares, or 10 per share. It raises 80 by issuing 10 shares at 8. With no fees or new project value, total equity becomes 580 across 60 shares, or about 9.67 per share. Cash increased while estimated value per old share fell. A new investment could offset that transfer only if its net value is supported, not simply because gross spending is large.

## Put the idea into practice

Use a before-and-after table for cash, debt, equity value, and diluted shares. Model the transaction separately from operating assumptions so the same cash or synergy is not counted twice. For a rights offering, examine the rights terms and participation assumptions rather than transplanting this simple placement example. Evaluate deals under downside integration and financing cases before relying on management's headline accretion figure.

modules.title: Inflation releases: levels, rates, and base effects
modules.subtitle: Read inflation data without confusing slower price growth with falling prices.

modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Economic releases describe a particular quantity over a particular period. A price level, a monthly change, and an annual inflation rate answer different questions. Before interpreting the headline number, identify its units, comparison period, and revision status. Then consider how that change could reach a company through customers, costs, financing, or currency exposure.

## Understand the idea

A price index measures a level; an inflation rate measures how that level changes over a specified interval. Slower inflation can coexist with rising prices. Read the release's population, basket, period, units, adjustment method, and revision policy before interpreting the headline. Monthly seasonally adjusted changes and annual unadjusted changes should not be treated as interchangeable observations.

For companies, map the release to actual exposures. Wages, energy, rents, and selling prices affect different businesses on different schedules. A broad index does not equal a particular firm's input-cost inflation. A favorable inflation surprise can lower financing pressure while also signaling weaker demand, so the earnings and discount-rate channels may oppose each other.

$$
\pi_{m}=\frac{I_t}{I_{t-1}}-1,\qquad \pi_{y}=\frac{I_t}{I_{t-12}}-1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional index rises from 120.0 last month to 120.6 today and was 115.0 a year ago. Monthly inflation is 0.5%, while the twelve-month change is about 4.87%. If last year's comparison base had been 118.0 instead, the same current index would produce only 2.20% annual inflation. Nothing about that denominator change means today's price level fell.

## Put the idea into practice

Calculate both rates from consistent index series, label any seasonal adjustment, and compare the surprise with a dated forecast on the same basis. Then identify the company's cost basket, pricing power, and contract-reset lags. Build a two-channel note: input margin effect and demand/financing effect. Do not extrapolate a single month's change into a reliable annual forecast; annualization is a conditional arithmetic exercise.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Macroeconomic releases summarize an economy through measurement systems with sampling error, revisions, and different publication lags. GDP growth, payroll changes, unemployment, and business surveys are different objects. A diffusion index is not a direct revenue growth rate. A seasonally adjusted annualized quarterly growth rate is not the quarter's raw percentage change.

Separate the new observation from revisions to earlier periods. A strong headline can coexist with weaker earlier estimates. For company analysis, narrow the aggregate to relevant customers, geographies, and products; a domestic construction supplier may respond differently from a global subscription business. A causal mechanism needs an exposure link and time horizon, not just two lines on the same chart.

$$
g_{\mathrm{quarter}}=(1+g_{\mathrm{annualized}})^{1/4}-1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional jobs release adds 180 thousand jobs for the latest month, while the prior two months are revised down by 40 and 30 thousand. The sum of those reported changes relative to the previous vintage is 110 thousand, but that arithmetic is not itself an official measure of current monthly growth. A fictional annualized quarterly GDP growth figure of 4% corresponds to about 0.985% growth during the quarter: 1.04 to the one-quarter power minus one.

## Put the idea into practice

Record vintage, units, revision size, and consensus timestamp. Keep first-release data for historical decisions and revised data for a clearly labeled retrospective analysis. Map demand to company orders and revenue recognition lags. Ask whether the release changes the distribution of future demand or merely confirms a trend already reflected in orders. Avoid declaring a recession or recovery from a single noisy indicator.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A policy announcement can affect short rates, longer yields, credit spreads, currencies, and expected activity. Separate the decision from prior expectations and the accompanying guidance. Long-term yields need not move by the same amount as the policy rate. A firm's borrowing cost also reflects maturity, credit risk, contract terms, and whether existing debt is fixed or floating.

For equities, distinguish cash-flow news from discount-rate news. Lower rates can increase the present value of unchanged future cash flows, yet lower expected sales or a wider risk premium can offset that benefit. Banks require both asset and funding repricing analysis: lower rates may reduce borrower stress while also compressing margins. Avoid a universal 'rate cuts mean stocks rise' rule.

$$
PV=\frac{CF_1}{1+r},\qquad \Delta\mathrm{Interest}\approx\mathrm{Repricing\ debt}\times\Delta r
$$

## A worked example

An unchanged cash flow of 110 due in one year has value 100 at a 10% discount rate and about 101.85 at 8%. If the same news reduces the expected cash flow to 100, its value at 8% is only 92.59. For a separate company with 200 of floating-rate debt, a full-year 100-basis-point borrowing-cost increase adds 2 of interest before tax, assuming immediate repricing and unchanged principal.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a four-column rate map: debt maturity and repricing, customer demand, discount rate, and credit conditions. For banks, add deposit pricing and credit losses. Show sensitivities rather than multiplying all debt by the policy change indiscriminately. Record whether your cash flows and rates are nominal or real and use the same currency. Verify the actual statement and rate definition before analyzing any live policy event.

The worksheet's values are 101.85 and 92.59, not forecasts of market prices.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

When USD/IDR rises, more rupiah are required to buy one dollar. The business effect depends on the net cash exposure, not merely the company's listing location. Identify the currencies of sales, inputs, debt service, and cash balances, then separate transaction cash flows from accounting translation. Natural offsets and financial hedges may reduce exposure, but their amounts, maturities, and costs matter.

Read Bank Indonesia communication in its own policy context rather than copying a Federal Reserve narrative. Distinguish the policy announcement, rupiah movement, domestic credit conditions, and global dollar effects. An exporter can face dollar-denominated costs or weak external demand; an importer can have pricing power or hedges. 'Rupiah weakens' is not a complete company thesis.

$$
\Delta\mathrm{IDR\ cost}=\mathrm{Unhedged\ USD\ payments}\times\Delta(\mathrm{USD/IDR})
$$

## A worked example

Fictional Nusa imports $10 million of goods and earns rupiah revenue. USD/IDR moves from 15,000 to 16,000. With unchanged volume, no pass-through, and no hedge, rupiah cost rises from Rp150 billion to Rp160 billion. Hedging half at 15,000 leaves a simplified blended cost of Rp155 billion, before hedge fees. A fictional exporter with $12 million receipts and $8 million dollar operating payments has a $4 million operating surplus; debt service may reduce that surplus further.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a currency ladder by settlement month. Match hedge notional and maturity to the actual underlying cash flows, and distinguish operating flows from debt principal. Test pass-through and volume responses in rupiah. In the notebook write the connection explicitly: berita kurs → biaya atau pendapatan → arus kas → nilai perusahaan. Use the issuer's disclosures for exposure and the central bank's own release for policy facts.

modules.title: Commodity shocks: producers, users, and realized margins
modules.subtitle: Map oil, coal, and input-price news through contracts, costs, and operating leverage.

modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

The same event can help one business and hurt another. A rise in an input price may support a producer's sales while increasing a manufacturer's costs. Follow the chain of suppliers, customers, contracts, and timing before describing the effect. This unit develops that chain into a map you can use when comparing companies in an industry.

## Understand the idea

A commodity price is not a company's realized selling price or profit margin. Benchmark movements pass through contracts, product grades, transportation, taxes, hedges, and production costs. A supply disruption and a demand boom can both raise prices but have different consequences for volumes and customers. Identify which mechanism the evidence supports.

Compare producers with users. A coal producer may benefit from higher realized prices while a power-intensive manufacturer faces higher costs. An airline can face fuel pressure at the same time as strong travel demand raises fares. Contract resets, inventory accounting, and hedges create lags. Keep a static sensitivity separate from a complete forecast, and distinguish a temporary shock from a durable change in earning power.

$$
\mathrm{EBIT}=Q(P-C_v)-C_f
$$

## A worked example

A fictional commodity producer sells one million units at $80 with a variable cost of $50 and fixed cost of $20 million. EBIT is $10 million. At $90 with the same volume and costs, EBIT doubles to $20 million. If variable cost also rises to $56, EBIT is only $14 million. Separately, a manufacturer buying two million units pays $20 million more after the same $10 input increase before pass-through or hedges.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a value-chain map from input extraction through processing, distribution, and the final buyer. For each firm, document realized-price formulas, unit costs, spare capacity, and balance-sheet resilience. Stress lower volumes as well as higher prices. Avoid applying a windfall multiple to a peak margin without testing a normalized commodity case and required reinvestment.

The user can be protected by hedges, regulated or contractual pass-through, or offsetting output-price gains. Falling producer volumes, higher royalties, or expensive expansion can reduce its benefit. The static producer EBIT cases are 10, 20, and 14 million.

modules.subtitle: Trace a policy or logistics shock through unit economics and customer behavior.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A supply-chain shock changes more than a purchase price. Lead times, alternative suppliers, certification, inventory, working capital, and customer delivery commitments can all matter. Identify the exact product, jurisdiction, timing, and scope in the original announcement. A proposal, enacted measure, exemption, and implemented charge are distinct states; do not model them as interchangeable.

Pass-through is a behavioral and contractual assumption. A firm may raise prices but lose volume, absorb costs but preserve share, or redesign its supply chain at an upfront cost. A supplier's country of headquarters does not by itself determine the treatment of every shipment. For a live case, verify applicable terms through official material; the worksheet below is a fictional cost shock, not a statement of tariff law.

$$
\mathrm{Contribution}=Q\left(P-C_{\mathrm{import}}(1+\tau)-C_{\mathrm{other}}\right)
$$

## A worked example

Nusa sells 100 units at 100 each. Its per-unit imported cost is 60 and other variable cost is 20, leaving contribution of 2,000. A fictional 10% charge on the imported-cost base raises unit cost by 6. With no response, contribution falls to 1,400. Raising price by 3 while volume falls to 95 gives contribution of (103 - 66 - 20) × 95 = 1,615. Partial pass-through does not restore the original economics.

## Put the idea into practice

Build a cost bridge with the explicitly assumed charge base. Model at least no pass-through, partial pass-through with lost volume, and a supplier-switch scenario with upfront costs. Add inventory and financing needs where lead times increase. Separate the policy's announced effective date from the date the firm's income statement first reflects it. Keep uncertain scope as an open question, not a silently chosen input.

modules.title: Regulation, litigation, and event-stage uncertainty
modules.subtitle: Separate allegations, proposals, decisions, appeals, and economic consequences.
modules.objective: Separate allegations, proposals, decisions, appeals, and economic consequences.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Read the status of an event before assigning a cash-flow impact. An allegation is not a judgment; an investigation is not a quantified liability; an announced rule may have implementation conditions. Identify the issuing authority, affected entity, procedural stage, stated effective date, and the source's actual claims. Do not turn legal vocabulary into a probability without a documented basis.

The economic impact can exceed an explicit fine through remediation, restricted operations, lost customers, or capital requirements. It can also be smaller if a remedy is limited or reversible. Keep a decision tree with mutually exclusive outcomes and show ranges when probabilities are uncertain. This is an analysis framework; live legal interpretation requires the current primary documents and appropriate expertise.

$$
E[C]=\sum_s p_s C_s,\qquad \sum_s p_s=1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional licensing dispute has analyst-assigned teaching scenarios: 50% no operating restriction with cost 2, 35% remediation with cost 10, and 15% closure with cost 50, all in millions and discounted to the same date. Expected cost is 12. A separate 8 of remediation spending already included in a chosen scenario must not be deducted again. The 12 is a scenario-weighted input, not a prediction that a court will order that amount.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a status timeline and a matrix of direct payments, operational restrictions, and timing. Label which facts are documented and which estimates belong to the analyst. Stress the probability of the adverse branch and the liquidity available to survive it. A small expected cost can hide an unacceptable tail outcome. Update the scenario tree when the event's stage changes, keeping the previous version for review.

print("Expected cost:", probabilities[0] * costs[0] + probabilities[1] * costs[1] + probabilities[2] * costs[2])

assignment.solution: The provided probabilities are invented analysis assumptions. They sum to one and imply expected cost 12, while the adverse branch costs 50. Compare that branch with accessible liquidity and continuing cash burn. Record the actual event stage and identify the next source update needed; do not call the expected cost a legal outcome.

modules.title: Build a sector and company transmission map
modules.subtitle: Translate the same news into different business-model sensitivities instead of trading sector labels.
modules.objective: Translate the same news into different business-model sensitivities instead of trading sector labels.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes reading the lesson and linked primary material, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes writing and challenging your interpretation. Every company, release, forecast, and price in this course is a fictional teaching case.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Sector membership is a starting point, not an exposure measurement. Two banks can have different deposit mixes and loan repricing schedules; two retailers can sell necessities or discretionary goods; two software companies can differ in renewals, usage pricing, and customer concentration. Read segment economics and funding structure before generalizing from an industry headline.

Build a causal map with measurable links: news → relevant demand or cost driver → company KPI → revenue or margin → cash flow → valuation. Identify the time lag at every step and a counteracting channel. Correlated share-price moves can result from shared ownership or index flows even when near-term operating exposures differ. Distinguish that market linkage from a business linkage.

$$
\mathrm{Net\ interest\ income}=A y_A-F c_F
$$

## A worked example

A fictional bank has 1,000 of earning assets yielding 8% and 900 of funding costing 4%, for net interest income of 44 before credit losses and operating costs. In a rate-cut scenario, asset yield falls 100 basis points while funding cost falls only 50 basis points; income becomes 70 - 31.5 = 38.5. Lower borrower defaults could offset part of that decline. A retailer could instead benefit through consumer financing, while a software vendor may respond mainly through enterprise budgets and valuation rates.

## Put the idea into practice

For three firms, create an exposure table with one primary metric, one lag, one offset, and one disconfirming observation. Score evidence completeness rather than inventing a universal stock signal. Separate effects on this quarter's earnings from effects on long-run competitive position. Rank research priorities by exposure and uncertainty, then open the relevant filings to refine them.
