options: Freedom from every possible implementation error
Only that this diagnostic did not reveal the tested failure
questions.explanation: A diagnostic has a defined scope and cannot certify all assumptions.

exams.title: Unit 7: Portfolio and implementation
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Realized portfolio volatility above its target is:
options: Possible because the estimate and future conditions differ
Proof that transaction costs are zero
questions.explanation: A target uses past estimates and cannot control all future shocks.

questions.question: Why stress correlations upward?
options: To prove every strategy always loses together
To remove the need for a benchmark
Diversification can weaken during common shocks
questions.explanation: A stressed joint-risk case challenges reliance on quiet-period diversification.

questions.question: A fixed commission rate alone models strategy capacity adequately:
options: Only if gross returns are high
No; liquidity and market impact also matter
questions.explanation: Trading more capital can change fill prices and available size beyond fixed fees.

questions.question: Open positions at the final mark should be described as:
options: Marked holdings with liquidation costs omitted unless explicitly modeled
Realized cash profits regardless of sales
questions.explanation: A closing mark and an executed liquidation are different economic events.

exams.title: Unit 8: Validate and defend a strategy
exams.description: Four original transfer questions. Use your notes, show calculations, and review the explanations after submitting. This checkpoint samples the preceding unit; the final covers every module.

questions.question: Indicator warm-up before a test boundary may use:
options: Historical observations available before each decision
questions.explanation: Past data can initialize indicators without allowing future evaluation information into decisions.

questions.question: Citing a PBO paper allows a report to claim it computed PBO:
options: Whenever there are at least two trials
Only if the stated procedure was actually implemented and validated
questions.explanation: Method attribution does not substitute for performing and checking the claimed analysis.

questions.question: Successful deterministic replay establishes:
options: Reproducibility under the tested inputs and implementation
questions.explanation: Replay checks engineering consistency rather than the economic value of the strategy.

questions.question: What should be handed to the final reporting course?
options: Invented holdings for an unimplemented pairs engine
Aligned net valuations, benchmark, manifest and supporting research evidence
questions.explanation: The report needs traceable data and assumptions rather than an isolated or fabricated performance claim.

exams.title: The strategy lab final exam
exams.description: Open-book, untimed assessment with new cases from every module. Budget about three minutes per question. Answers and explanations appear after submission. Pass at 80%; retries remain available. The written capstone is self-assessed separately.

questions.question: A researcher changes the rule after inspecting the final result. The changed rule is:
options: Proof that the original hypothesis passed
A new exploratory specification requiring new evidence
questions.explanation: Outcome-driven revisions must be logged and evaluated as new research choices.

questions.question: A net strategy is compared with a costless index. What belongs in the report?
options: The benchmark cost convention and a matched-cost sensitivity
A claim that the cost basis is identical
questions.explanation: A costless index can be useful, but it does not isolate selection under identical costs.

questions.question: What happens to a new signal on the dataset's final close?
options: It fills at an invented next open
It is moved backward one day
It has no modeled fill without a later bar
questions.explanation: Missing future execution data cannot be replaced by a favorable assumption.

questions.question: A viewed test segment is reused to choose a parameter. It is now:
options: Equivalent to a new future sample
Part of the research selection process
questions.explanation: Once outcomes influence decisions, the segment has participated in selection.

questions.question: A date-only feed lacks publication time. A defensible lab convention is:
options: Delay use until a later session and document it
Assume every release preceded the open
questions.explanation: A conservative explicit delay avoids claiming intraday knowledge the data cannot establish.

questions.question: Dropping a −80% delisted stock from a +20%/−80% equal-weight pair changes the record through:
questions.explanation: Removing failed securities conditions the universe on future survival.

questions.question: A contemporaneous cross-sectional rank uses:
options: Only the universe and values available at that decision
questions.explanation: Ranking is causal only when its membership and inputs are available at the decision time.

questions.question: Why keep stocks from the same date together in a chronological split?
options: They share time information and market shocks
questions.explanation: Random stock-row splitting can expose evaluation-period structure to training.

questions.question: A stock passes raw NCAV but fails after conservative inventory haircuts. The analyst should:
options: Delete the haircut to preserve the purchase
Claim the raw screen guarantees liquidation proceeds
Retain the sensitivity and investigate realizable asset values
questions.explanation: The discrepancy exposes dependence on asset-recovery assumptions.

questions.question: A candidate fails a mandatory coverage floor but has exceptional earnings yield. It should:
options: Have its debt removed from the data
Remain excluded under the predeclared rule
Automatically pass because the composite is high
questions.explanation: Hard eligibility constraints are applied before compensating composite scores.

questions.question: A known earnings date provides advance knowledge of:
options: The scheduled event, not the eventual earnings surprise
questions.explanation: Event timing and event content are different information sets.

questions.question: Only one name qualifies under a fixed 40% cap. The allocation should:
questions.explanation: A shortage of candidates does not justify changing the predeclared concentration rule.

questions.question: A close-based trend rule signals at 105 before an open of 110. Its modeled entry uses:
questions.explanation: The next-open convention cannot choose an earlier or retrospectively favorable price.

questions.question: A top-two long-only daily rule and the French momentum factor are:
options: Different constructions whose calendars and exposures must be disclosed
Identical because both use past returns
questions.explanation: A common broad idea does not make the universe, horizon or long-short construction identical.

questions.question: A permanent earnings impairment should prompt a reversal researcher to:
options: Remove the bad announcement from the sample
Reassess whether the previous reference level remains valid
questions.explanation: A permanent information change differs from temporary price pressure.

questions.question: A single excellent parameter surrounded by poor validation results suggests:
options: No need to count attempted settings
questions.explanation: An isolated optimum may depend on noise or fragile implementation assumptions.

questions.question: A log-price hedge coefficient can be used directly as a fixed share ratio:
options: Only after a justified conversion; not automatically
Only when the test return is positive
questions.explanation: Log-price exposure and share quantities have different units and need an explicit sizing conversion.

questions.question: Choosing the smallest p-value among hundreds of pairs requires disclosure of:
options: The full search and independent stability evidence
questions.explanation: Multiple searched hypotheses change the interpretation of the selected result.

questions.question: A long-short profit divided by nearly zero net notional is:
options: Equivalent to return on gross exposure
An unsuitable return measure without an economic capital basis
questions.explanation: Offsetting notionals do not eliminate the capital, collateral or risk supporting the trade.

questions.question: Re-estimating the hedge after a break should be treated as:
options: A revised model needing later validation
Proof the old model never failed
A reason to remove the loss
questions.explanation: New parameters change the hypothesis and cannot retroactively repair its historical trade.

questions.question: Which record allows a fill to be linked to the model that requested it?
options: Versioned predictions with decision and model timestamps
questions.explanation: Prediction provenance connects trained artifacts to the resulting orders.

questions.question: A later refit learns from an earlier completed evaluation block. What must stay unchanged?
options: The predictions originally issued for that earlier block
questions.explanation: Live-like refitting can use newly historical data while preserving past prediction provenance.

questions.question: A long-short bucket spread can be labeled as a long-only strategy return:
options: Only after constructing and evaluating the actual long-only allocation
questions.explanation: Diagnostic portfolios and implemented holdings have different exposures and costs.

questions.question: Excellent independent-looking performance on random labels should first trigger:
options: An audit of leakage, selection and evaluation code
questions.explanation: An uninformative target performing exceptionally can reveal a broken research process.

questions.question: A 40% target on 10000 equity at price 103 requests how many whole shares?
questions.explanation: Flooring 4000/103 gives 38 shares before next-open execution constraints.

questions.question: A covariance optimizer assigns extreme weights after a tiny data change. This suggests:
options: Estimation sensitivity requiring constraints and diagnostics
questions.explanation: Unstable weights can amplify noisy covariance estimates.

questions.question: Using today's total volume to size an opening fill introduces:
options: Information unavailable at that opening event
questions.explanation: The session's eventual total volume is future information at its open.

questions.question: Which invariant should hold on every valuation row?
options: Fees are added back to cash
Equity equals cash plus marked holdings
questions.explanation: Portfolio wealth reconciles the cash account and current value of all holdings.

questions.question: A reset test account differs from a continuous simulation because:
options: It starts in cash instead of carrying prior holdings
It can use future prices freely
questions.explanation: Boundary state affects trades and returns and must be part of the evaluation contract.

questions.question: A block interval computed on a selected winner automatically corrects all strategy search:
options: Only if the chart has confidence bands
No; selection must be addressed explicitly
questions.explanation: Resampling one selected path does not reproduce the process that selected it.

questions.question: Editing only future prices changes earlier fills. This indicates:
questions.explanation: Decisions and fills in the past must not depend on later observations.

questions.question: A high concept-exam score with unreconciled cash means the project:
options: Still requires revision before its results are credible
questions.explanation: Concept knowledge does not repair a broken accounting result.

modules.title: Specify a bot before writing a loop
modules.subtitle: Turn an investment idea into a testable decision contract with explicit data, execution, and failure assumptions.
modules.objective: Turn an investment idea into a testable decision contract with explicit data, execution, and failure assumptions.
modules.reading: Start here. Deliverable: a bot decision contract. Read the project guide, then complete the data and event units before designing a trading rule.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Before writing the bot's loop, describe one complete decision in words. Which data arrives, what rule uses it, what checks can reject a trade, and what record proves what happened? Those details are the specification. This first unit connects the research idea to an event-driven system, where each new event can update state or trigger a carefully defined action.

## Define the operation

A bot is a process that turns observations into state changes. Start with a decision contract: eligible instruments, information cutoff, signal rule, target holdings, rebalance frequency, execution convention, risk budget, and conditions for doing nothing. A slogan such as buy strong companies leaves almost every engineering choice unresolved.

Distinguish an alpha model from an execution algorithm. The first proposes which exposure might be useful. The second tries to obtain an already chosen exposure under trading constraints. A good execution algorithm does not establish predictive edge; a useful signal does not guarantee affordable fills.

The course follows a fictional Harbor research team building a long-only paper system. Dollar amounts, thresholds, and model outputs are stipulated teaching inputs. Each lesson produces one artifact for the final design dossier. Small calculations run in the in-app sandbox; the downloadable Python project runs an offline event and ledger simulation.

$$
\text{Net edge}_{bps}=\text{gross edge}-\text{spread}-\text{fees}-\text{slippage}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor proposes a daily strategy in a $100,000 paper portfolio. It may allocate at most 10% to one eligible stock, observes completed daily bars, and places a target order at the next eligible open. An estimate of 12 basis points of gross benefit faces 4 basis points of spread cost, 2 of fees, and 3 of slippage. The rough expected net benefit is only 3 basis points.

A second analyst assumes 6 basis points of slippage. That consumes the entire gross estimate. Before building a faster bot, the team must decide whether the underlying idea survives a plausible cost range. An estimate is not a realized return, and these cost components must not overlap.

### Connect the specification to the cost estimate

A 10% single-stock limit in a $100,000 paper portfolio allows at most $10,000 for that stock under the stated rule. It does not require the bot to use that entire amount. The timing rule is another separate condition: the signal uses completed daily bars and the target order is placed at the next eligible open.

Now examine the claimed benefit. One basis point is 0.01 percentage points. The estimated costs total 4 + 2 + 3 = 9 basis points. Subtracting them from 12 basis points of gross benefit leaves only 3 basis points, or 0.03 percentage points, under those assumptions.

If slippage rises to 6 basis points, the costs become 4 + 2 + 6 = 12 basis points. That uses up the entire estimated gross benefit. Writing this down before building the bot helps the team see which assumption matters and what needs stronger evidence. Faster execution code alone does not settle whether the research idea survives its costs.

## Acceptance evidence

Write observable requirements: duplicate delivery does not duplicate exposure; missing features produce no new order; a fill changes cash exactly once; a restart recovers a halted state. Pair each requirement with a normal and adverse example. Define success in terms of reconciliation and sound evaluation before looking at a profit chart.

Keep research permission, paper execution, and any later live release as separate stages. Completing this course produces a tested educational prototype and a review packet. It does not silently connect credentials or authorize a brokerage trade.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A decision contract should state how many alternatives will be tried, because that count changes what a good result means. Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu make the point with a random walk. They generated 1,000 daily prices, about four years, searched a mesh of 8,800 combinations of entry day, holding period, stop loss and side, and the best combination showed an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.27 even though the series contains no pattern. Their rule of thumb is that five years of data supports no more than 45 independent configurations before a skill-less winner with a Sharpe ratio near 1 becomes almost guaranteed, and they describe that length as necessary but not sufficient.

Edges also fade once they are known. McLean and Pontiff studied 97 predictors taken from published papers and found portfolio returns 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication. As an illustration of our own, not a forecast, a 58% haircut on Harbor's 12 basis points of gross benefit leaves about 5, already below the 9 basis points of assumed costs.

The cost line is an assumption about a particular trader. Frazzini, Israel and Moskowitz used nearly a trillion dollars of one large manager's live trades across 19 developed equity markets from 1998 to 2011 and found actual costs under a tenth of earlier estimates. They attribute the gap to two things: earlier studies priced the average investor, and the portfolios they tested were not designed with costs in mind. That manager is far larger and more sophisticated than a paper bot, so its numbers are not a template for Harbor. They do show that 9 basis points needs a named trader, size and portfolio design behind it.

Exercise: add three lines to Harbor's contract before any code exists. State the maximum number of variants you will compare, the history length that supports that number, and a pessimistic case that combines a decay haircut with 6 basis points of slippage. If the idea fails the pessimistic case, do not write the loop.

### Sources for this section

- [Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2014) · Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism: The Effects of Backtest Overfitting on Out-of-Sample Performance](https://doi.org/10.1090/noti1105) — *Research paper.* Shows with a random-walk experiment and a minimum-backtest-length rule how the number of configurations tried inflates in-sample Sharpe ratios.
- [McLean & Pontiff (2016) · Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12365) — *Research paper.* Measures how much the returns of 97 published predictors fall out of sample and after publication.
- [Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz (2012) · Trading Costs of Asset Pricing Anomalies](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.2294498) — *Research paper.* Live institutional trade data showing actual costs far below earlier estimates, and why estimates depend on who trades and how portfolios are built.

modules.subtitle: Separate market events, targets, orders, and fills so repeated or delayed messages cannot silently change the strategy.
modules.objective: Separate market events, targets, orders, and fills so repeated or delayed messages cannot silently change the strategy.
modules.reading: Deliverable: event schema and architecture diagram. Broker reference: stable client identifiers and order lookup; implementation semantics must be verified per adapter.
modules.content:
## Design a pipeline with explicit boundaries

Market ingestion records an observation. Feature computation produces a dated input set. Strategy logic proposes a target. Risk logic permits, resizes, or rejects that target. An order manager tracks instructions, and a fill handler updates the ledger. These steps can live in one process initially while retaining separate interfaces.

A vectorized research calculation is useful for rapid experiments; an event-driven replay is useful for modeling chronology and operational state. Neither architecture automatically prevents look-ahead. Both require correct timestamps and information boundaries.

Give each event a stable identity, source, event time, receipt time, and schema version. Event time describes the underlying observation; receipt time describes when the bot learned about it. A late event should follow a documented policy rather than revise a decision as if the data had arrived earlier.

$$
\text{Observation}\rightarrow\text{Features}\rightarrow\text{Target}\rightarrow\text{Risk}\rightarrow\text{Order}\rightarrow\text{Fill}
$$

## A worked example

The feed delivers event E101 twice, followed by E102. The strategy intends one rebalance per completed event, so the expected count is two distinct intents. If each delivery creates a fresh random order ID, the bot can accidentally produce three orders. A deterministic intent key such as strategy-version plus symbol plus decision timestamp ties retries to the same decision.

Now crash after a broker accepts E101's order but before acknowledgement is stored. Local absence of confirmation means unknown external state, not rejection. Reconcile using the stable client identifier and broker records before deciding whether another submission is permissible. Identifier support and retry semantics are adapter-specific; verify the actual broker contract.

## Make replay a first-class tool

Keep an immutable input log and enough state to reconstruct what each component believed. Test duplicate events, a missing sequence number, late data, an out-of-order acknowledgement, and a fill arriving during cancellation. Record the transition and the reason for every rejected action.

A single owner of account mutations makes reasoning easier. If multiple workers are introduced, use a durable transactional boundary and uniqueness constraints. An in-memory set alone does not survive a crash or coordinate two processes.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Two clocks sit behind every event a bot receives. Akidau and co-authors, describing a model for processing unbounded and out-of-order data, define event time as when an event actually occurred and processing time as when the pipeline observes it. They stress that the skew between the two is inherent and keeps changing, and that a system usually lacks the knowledge to build a fully correct watermark, its running estimate of how complete the data is. A bot faces the same problem with a sharper edge, because a dashboard can quietly revise a late number but an order cannot be retracted. My inference is that the late-event rule belongs in the specification: say in advance what happens to an event that arrives after the decision it should have informed.

Identity needs the same discipline. The FIX standard for electronic order messages requires a client order ID to be unique within a single trading day and advises firms that trade across days to embed a date in it. A separate PossResend field marks a message that may carry information already sent under another sequence number. Harbor's key of strategy version, symbol and decision timestamp fits that pattern, but each broker's guarantee has its own scope, so read the adapter's contract.

Replay and live trading also differ more than the pipeline diagram suggests. QuantConnect's LEAN documentation says algorithm events fire synchronously in backtests, while in live trading order events fire immediately from the brokerage thread, asynchronously. Its own example is a limit order on hourly data that fills between bars. The ABIDES simulator of Byrd and co-authors makes such timing visible instead: every agent talks to the exchange through messages with configurable network latencies, in a design modelled on Nasdaq's ITCH and OUCH protocols.

Exercise: replay the feed E101, E101, E102 three ways. Run it in order, with the duplicate delayed until after E102, and with a simulated crash between broker acceptance and the stored acknowledgement. Each run should end with exactly two intents and the same ledger. Any difference exposes a hidden dependence on arrival order or on in-memory state.

### Sources for this section

- [Akidau et al. (2015) · The Dataflow Model](https://doi.org/10.14778/2824032.2824076) — *Research paper.* Defines event time versus processing time for out-of-order streams and explains why completeness estimates (watermarks) are heuristic.
- [FIX Trading Community · ClOrdID field definition, FIX Latest](https://fiximate.fixtrading.org/en/FIX.Latest/tag11.html) — *Technical documentation.* Standard definition of the client order ID, including the day-level uniqueness requirement and the advice to embed a date.
- [QuantConnect · Algorithm Engine](https://www.quantconnect.com/docs/v2/writing-algorithms/key-concepts/algorithm-engine) — *Technical documentation.* Documents how one engine triggers events synchronously in backtests but fires order events asynchronously in live trading.
- [Byrd, Hybinette & Balch (2019) · ABIDES: Towards High-Fidelity Market Simulation for AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12066) — *arXiv 1904.12066.* A discrete-event market simulator in which agents interact only through messages with configurable latencies, modelled on Nasdaq protocols.

modules.title: Market data contracts and trading clocks
modules.subtitle: Reject stale or historically unavailable inputs and make sessions, adjustments, and missing data explicit.
modules.objective: Reject stale or historically unavailable inputs and make sessions, adjustments, and missing data explicit.
modules.reading: Deliverable: point-in-time data contract and six bad-data fixtures. Reuse the data-provenance methods from Quantitative Investment Analysis.
modules.content:
## A timestamp is part of the value

A price needs an instrument, venue or source, currency, event timestamp, receipt timestamp, and adjustment convention. A financial statement also needs its publication timestamp and revision identity. Calendar dates alone are insufficient when a decision depends on intraday availability.

Store a consistent clock representation and convert to the exchange's session schedule at the boundary. Daylight-saving changes, holidays, half-days, and trading halts should come from a maintained calendar or broker session interface. Never equate a weekday with an open market. The offline project uses a supplied session-open flag rather than pretending to implement an exchange calendar.

Distinguish a missing bar from a genuine zero return. Mixing adjusted historical closes with raw order prices can fabricate a signal around splits. Keep corporate actions and total-return assumptions separate from executable quotes.

$$
\text{Age}=t_{decision}-t_{event};\quad 0\leq\text{Age}\leq\text{limit}
$$

## A worked example

A quote event is timestamped 10:00:00.000 and arrives at 10:00:00.400. At a decision time of 10:00:00.900, its age from the event clock is 900 ms. Under a stipulated 750 ms freshness limit, the bot rejects a new entry even though network transport took only 400 ms.

A second quote carries a timestamp after the decision time because of clock skew. It must not pass merely because the computed age is negative. Validate both clock ordering and a maximum age. These thresholds are policy examples, not universal trading standards.

## Reconstruct the information set

For each decision, retain the exact quote or bar ID and the latest eligible filing version. A March release describing December cannot enter a February historical decision. Reject unsupported instruments and nonfinite or nonpositive prices before computing exposure.

The assignment should include fixtures for stale data, future timestamps, duplicate bars, missing volume, a split, and a closed session. Explain whether each causes an abstention, a delayed decision, or a research-only adjustment. Avoid filling a data gap with generated prices while labeling the result historical.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Treat the trading clock as data. The NYSE's published calendar lists Friday 3 July 2026 as a holiday (Independence Day observed) and early 1:00 p.m. Eastern closes on Friday 27 November and Thursday 24 December 2026. Sessions also differ by venue: the core session runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., but NYSE Arca's early session starts at 4:00 a.m. and late trading runs until 8:00 p.m. My inference for Harbor: on an early-close day a completed daily bar exists three hours sooner than usual, so a calendar that assumes a 4:00 p.m. close delays the signal, and one that assumes a session on 3 July may mistake a missing bar for a zero return.

Feeds also stamp events with more than one clock. Bartlett and McCrary used the microsecond timestamps recorded by the two centralized processors that consolidate U.S. exchange quotes and trades. In a sample running from August 2015 to June 2016 they found average reporting latencies of 1.13 milliseconds for quotes and 22.84 milliseconds for trades, and they note that the exchanges' own participant timestamps were recorded only in milliseconds. Which clock a freshness limit such as the lesson's 750 milliseconds uses is therefore part of the data contract.

Documents have the same problem. Under the SEC's Regulation S-T, an electronic filing submitted after 5:30 p.m. Eastern is deemed filed on the next business day, although some insider and ownership forms get a 10 p.m. cutoff. A filing date is a legal label, not a clock reading, so a bot that stores only the date cannot say whether the document was readable at 10:00 a.m. that day. My suggestion: store the acceptance time when the source provides one, and otherwise treat the document as usable only after the full filing date has passed.

Exercise: extend Harbor's fixtures with a bar on Friday 27 November 2026 that completes at 1:00 p.m., a Friday 3 July 2026 with no session, and a filing accepted at 6:00 p.m. Eastern. For each, write down whether the bot abstains, delays or labels the result research-only, and which timestamp it used.

### Sources for this section

- [NYSE · Holidays & Trading Hours](https://www.nyse.com/trade/hours-calendars) — *Official source.* The exchange's own 2026 to 2028 holiday and early-close schedule, with session windows for each NYSE venue.
- [Bartlett & McCrary (2016) · How Rigged Are Stock Markets?: Evidence From Microsecond Timestamps](https://doi.org/10.3386/w22551) — *Research paper.* Uses the SIPs' microsecond timestamps to measure how late consolidated quotes and trades are reported compared with exchange direct feeds.
- [U.S. SEC · eCFR · 17 CFR 232.13: Date of filing; adjustment of filing date](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-232/section-232.13) — *Official source.* The rule that fixes when an electronic EDGAR filing counts as filed, including the 5:30 p.m. Eastern cutoff and its exceptions.

modules.objective: Build past-only features with explicit warm-up, scale, and version rules shared by research and execution.
modules.reading: Deliverable: a feature dictionary and exact input/output fixtures. Read the preprocessing consistency reference linked from the course plan.
modules.content:
## Treat features as versioned computations

Define each feature with its input field, window, lag, adjustment basis, missing-data rule, and units. A twenty-bar return and a twenty-calendar-day return need not be identical. A trailing average that includes the current completed bar is available only after that bar completes.

Warm-up is a state, not a zero. If a feature needs twenty valid observations and only twelve exist, the model should see an unavailable input or abstain under a documented rule. Filling the missing feature with zero can change a model's meaning and create unexpected orders.

Use the same transformations in training and inference. Fitted preprocessing belongs to the training artifact, while rolling calculations require a defined historical window. A price-level feature can drift with splits or nominal scale; return, ratio, or normalized features can be more interpretable but do not automatically become stationary.

$$
Momentum_t=P_t/P_{t-L}-1
$$

## A worked example

Completed closes are 100, 102, 101, and 104. A three-period simple return at the final close is 104/100 − 1 = 4%. The three most recent completed closes average (102 + 101 + 104)/3 = 102.333. The final close is about 1.63% above that average.

This is a feature calculation, not proof of trend profitability. If the decision instead occurs before the final close, 104 is unavailable and both inputs must be recomputed from earlier data. Feature timing determines the earliest possible execution.

## A reproducibility check

Save a tiny input fixture and expected feature values. Compare research and running-bot outputs on identical data, including a missing observation and the first eligible warm-up point. Record model and feature versions together so an old model cannot silently consume a reordered feature vector.

When a new feature is proposed, document the economic hypothesis before tuning its window. Log rejected variants and retain a baseline. A precise calculation can still be an overfit research choice.

modules.title: Rule-based strategy bots
modules.subtitle: Convert a signal into a target position and reconcile that target with holdings and outstanding orders.
modules.objective: Convert a signal into a target position and reconcile that target with holdings and outstanding orders.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A rule-based bot makes decisions from explicit conditions. Its simplicity can make the behavior easier to inspect, but the rule still needs evidence and realistic execution assumptions. Work through one signal at a time and record when it becomes known. Then examine how turnover, costs, and the chosen comparison affect the research result.

## Design and reasoning

Separate the desired end state from the instruction sent now. A binary signal can mean a target weight of 0% or 10%; it does not mean buy another 10% on every iteration. Convert weight to shares using a dated equity estimate and an executable price convention. Specify rounding, minimum lot size, cash reserves, and when a target expires.

Outstanding orders are commitments. A pending buy contributes positive shares and a pending sell contributes negative shares to the projected holding. Ignoring them causes repeated rebalancing to overshoot. A cancellation request does not remove that commitment until its result is known.

$$
q_{new}=q_{target}-q_{held}-q_{pending,buy}+q_{pending,sell}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor targets 200 shares and holds 120. With no open orders the buy requirement is 80 shares. With a previously accepted buy of 50 shares still outstanding, the residual is only 30. If 20 of that order fill, holdings become 140 and remaining commitments become 30; the residual stays 30. This invariance is a useful test of the accounting.

If the signal disappears, first reconcile or cancel the existing buy. Do not immediately submit a 120-share sell while assuming the buy vanished. Treat conflicting instructions as an order-management problem.

## Implementation and review

Implement target calculation as a pure function of a versioned snapshot. The order manager, not the signal function, owns retries. Introduce a no-trade band so negligible target changes do not create excessive turnover. Record the raw target, rounded target, existing holdings, commitments, and final permitted instruction. Compare the same rule against cash and a declared passive benchmark using identical costs and dates.

modules.title: Trend rules, breakouts, and turnover
modules.subtitle: Specify an executable trend rule with entry, exit, warm-up, and turnover controls.
modules.objective: Specify an executable trend rule with entry, exit, warm-up, and turnover controls.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A rule must define the information window precisely. For a breakout observed at today's completed close, compare that close with an earlier high window that excludes today. Including today's high changes the question and can make a strict close-above-high test impossible. A moving-average rule instead compares levels computed from a declared window.

Use separate entry and exit thresholds when a small fluctuation would otherwise churn the portfolio. This hysteresis is a design choice with a trade-off: less turnover can delay an exit. Do not select the band after inspecting the final evaluation period.

$$
\text{Entry threshold}=\max(H_{t-L},\ldots,H_{t-1})(1+b)
$$

## A worked example

Earlier highs are 100, 102, and 101. A completed close of 103 exceeds the prior maximum of 102. Under an illustrative rule requiring a 0.5% breakout, the entry threshold is 102.51, so the signal qualifies. A 1.5% band would require 103.53 and would not qualify. Execution occurs on a later eligible event, whose price need not equal 103.

A backtest earns 1.2% gross while turning the portfolio over six one-way notional equivalents. At 15 bps per equivalent, estimated trading costs are 0.9%, leaving 0.3% before other omitted costs.

## Implementation and review

Build a fixture for a flat market, a gap, a missing close, and a split-adjustment mismatch. Evaluate a small preregistered parameter grid on training and validation windows, then freeze it. Report return, drawdown, time in market, turnover, and sensitivity to costs. A trend indicator is a descriptive transformation; the ability to compute it does not establish an economic edge.

modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A z-score describes deviation relative to an estimated mean and scale. It is not a guarantee that price will return to a historical level. Structural changes can move both the mean and variance. Specify the estimation window, fit the relationship using past data, and explain why a temporary displacement might close.

For pairs, define a spread such as A minus beta times B. Correlation of returns does not prove that this price spread is stationary. A fitted hedge ratio, a stationarity diagnostic, and an economic relationship answer different questions. Check sensitivity to sample choice and corporate changes before treating a spread as tradable.

$$
z_t=(s_t-\mu_{train})/\sigma_{train}
$$

## A worked example

A spread of 14 has a training mean of 10 and standard deviation 2, giving a z-score of 2. Harbor's paper research rule considers selling the spread above 1.5. That requires short A and long beta units of B under the stated sign convention; the current in-app long/cash sandbox cannot express both legs.

If the planned legs are $10,000 long and $10,000 short, net dollar exposure is zero but gross exposure is $20,000. Fees, stock borrow, asymmetric fills, beta mismatch, and abrupt divergence can still produce a loss.

## Implementation and review

Keep pairs work as a research worksheet unless the execution engine explicitly supports borrow availability, short margin, and two-leg state. Test a one-leg fill, a borrow recall, and a spread that never reverts. Define an exit based on elapsed time or invalidated evidence as well as the signal. Zero estimated net exposure must never bypass gross and concentration limits.

A measure of how widely values differ from their mean, based on squared deviations. Its units are squared; taking the square root gives the standard deviation in the original units.

A standardized measure of a linear relationship between two quantities. It describes association and does not, by itself, show that one quantity causes the other.

modules.subtitle: Evaluate a frozen trading rule using a declared information cutoff, execution delay, benchmark, and cost model.
modules.objective: Evaluate a frozen trading rule using a declared information cutoff, execution delay, benchmark, and cost model.
modules.reading: Unit 2 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Separate signal time, order time, and fill time. A strategy computed from a completed closing bar cannot assume it entered earlier at that bar's open. An OHLC bar also does not reveal whether its high preceded its low. Any intrabar stop or limit convention is an assumption that needs documentation.

Keep research selection distinct from final evaluation. Changing a window after seeing the holdout makes that period part of development. Record every tried variant, fit preprocessing on training data, and keep an untouched later segment for the final frozen rule. Corporate actions, delistings, and availability timestamps belong in the data audit.

$$
\Pi=q(P_{exit}-P_{entry})-f q(P_{entry}+P_{exit})
$$

## A worked example

Harbor signals at a close of 100 and buys 10 shares at the next open of 102. Later it sells at 104. At 5 bps commission on each notional, entry commission is $0.51 and exit commission $0.52. Net P&L is $18.97. Pretending entry occurred at the signal close would overstate the gross profit by $20.

If slippage is modeled in the fill price, do not subtract the same slippage again as a separate ledger fee. Compare with a passive position using the same timestamps, capital, and cost convention.

## Implementation and review

Review an order-by-order trace in addition to aggregate statistics. Report drawdown, turnover, exposure, number of independent decisions, and a cost stress. A smooth curve from few trades does not support a precise Sharpe claim. Use the sandbox to demonstrate timing and costs; use the offline project for event and ledger failure tests. Neither establishes a live execution advantage.

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.

modules.title: Quotes, spread, and implementation shortfall
modules.subtitle: Measure an execution against a declared decision benchmark while distinguishing spread, impact, and delay.
modules.objective: Measure an execution against a declared decision benchmark while distinguishing spread, impact, and delay.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Submitting an order and receiving a fill are separate events. Between them, quotes may change, quantities may run out, and cancellation requests may race with execution. This unit follows the life of an order and the cash it commits. Use a small paper ledger to check that every accepted fill changes balances exactly once.

## Design and reasoning

A quote is an indication at a particular time, size, and venue. The midpoint is useful as a benchmark but is not necessarily executable. A marketable buy typically consumes offered liquidity; a resting limit may fail to fill or fill when the market moves against it. Better price and greater fill certainty are competing objectives.

Implementation shortfall compares execution with a decision benchmark, adjusted for trade direction. Explicit fees can be added separately. Spread, market impact, and delay are explanatory components whose estimates may overlap; avoid presenting a precise causal decomposition without the necessary data.

$$
IS_{bps}=10^4 d(P_{fill}/P_{decision}-1),\quad d\in\{+1,-1\}
$$

## A worked example

The bid is 99.90 and the ask 100.10, so the midpoint is 100 and the quoted spread is 20 bps. A buy filling at 100.12 costs 12 bps relative to that midpoint before commission. Half the quoted spread accounts for 10 bps in a simple interpretation; the extra 2 bps cannot be confidently called permanent impact from this single observation.

A sell at 99.88 also has 12 bps adverse shortfall under a direction-adjusted convention. Use consistent signs so a worse sell is not accidentally reported as a benefit.

## Implementation and review

Store the benchmark's source, timestamp, and size with each decision. Report fill rate and unfilled opportunity cost alongside the average cost of completed trades; measuring only successful fills can flatter passive strategies. Paper fills do not reproduce queue priority, hidden liquidity, or adverse selection. The course uses explicit toy assumptions that should be challenged before interpreting results.

modules.title: Order state machines and cancellation races
modules.subtitle: Handle acknowledgements, partial fills, cancellations, rejections, and ambiguous submissions without losing commitments.
modules.objective: Handle acknowledgements, partial fills, cancellations, rejections, and ambiguous submissions without losing commitments.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Model submission, acknowledgement, partial fill, complete fill, cancellation, and rejection as explicit states with legal transitions. A timeout is an observation about communication, not necessarily an order state. Broker messages can arrive twice or out of order, so deduplicate by durable identity and reconcile cumulative quantities.

Separate an intent ID from an external order ID and a fill ID. One intent may have a documented cancel-and-replace sequence, while one order may have many fills. Track original quantity, cumulative filled quantity, remaining quantity, and cancellation status. Do not assume a cancellation acknowledgement erases earlier fills.

$$
q_{remaining}=q_{original}-\sum_i q_{fill,i}
$$

## A worked example

An order buys 100 shares. Forty fill, leaving 60. The bot requests cancellation, but 15 more fill before the cancellation completes. The ledger must contain 55 bought shares; the successful cancellation removes only the remaining 45. If the 15-share fill message is replayed, holdings remain 55.

If the broker reports cumulative filled quantity of 55, do not treat it as 55 additional shares after already booking 40. Distinguish incremental fill messages from cumulative order updates in the adapter contract.

## Implementation and review

Build a transition table and test every terminal state. Preserve unknown orders as risk commitments until reconciliation resolves them. Record rejected transitions for investigation instead of forcing state to match the latest message blindly. The offline lab demonstrates partial fills and idempotent fill records; a real asynchronous adapter additionally needs broker-specific cancel races and sequencing behavior.

modules.title: Execution schedules: TWAP, VWAP, and participation
modules.subtitle: Choose and evaluate a slicing policy with explicit urgency, liquidity, and completion constraints.
modules.objective: Choose and evaluate a slicing policy with explicit urgency, liquidity, and completion constraints.
modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

TWAP distributes quantity over time; VWAP schedules against an estimated volume profile; a participation policy sizes child orders relative to observed or estimated market volume. Each needs a remaining-quantity cap, eligibility rules, and an end-of-window policy. Naming the algorithm does not define its actual fill mechanics.

Fast execution reduces waiting exposure but can consume expensive liquidity. Slow execution may reduce immediate pressure while risking price movement or an unfinished parent order. Models that optimize this trade-off rely on assumptions about volatility, impact, and constraints; there is no universally optimal schedule.

$$
q_{child}\leq\min(q_{remaining},\rho V_{eligible})
$$

## A worked example

A 1,000-share parent has four equal time buckets. TWAP requests 250 per bucket. A forecast volume profile of 10%, 20%, 40%, and 30% suggests VWAP child targets of 100, 200, 400, and 300. Under a 5% participation cap, a bucket with 4,000 shares of eligible volume permits at most 200 shares, even when the schedule asks for 400.

The remaining 200 cannot simply disappear from the report. The parent needs a documented carry-forward, cancellation, or urgency change, with risk approval. Do not use a bucket's eventual full volume for an order placed before that volume was known.

## Implementation and review

Simulate sparse volume, a missed bucket, a session ending early, and a late cancellation. Report both shortfall and completion percentage. A schedule should preserve parent quantity after partial fills and retries. Cap each child by remaining authorized quantity as well as participation; otherwise a catch-up rule can overfill the original decision.

print("TWAP slice:", parent / 4)
profile = [0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.3]
for weight in profile:
    print("VWAP target:", parent * weight)
print("Participation cap:", 4000 * 0.05)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.

modules.reading: Unit 3 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

An order does not itself change owned inventory. Accepted orders reserve resources; fills change cash and holdings; cancellations release only unfilled commitments. Keep available cash distinct from settled or total ledger cash. The educational lab uses immediate settlement, long-only integer shares, and one symbol, so its simplicity remains visible.

Use a stable fill ID and an atomic transaction to book cash, shares, and fill history together. Money should have an explicit precision policy. The downloadable project uses integer cents for prices and a deterministic commission rounding rule; a production adapter must match the broker's actual currency and settlement semantics.

$$
E_t=C_t+q_tP_{mark,t}
$$

## A worked example

Harbor starts with $10,000. Buying 40 shares at $100 with a $2 fee leaves $5,998 cash and 40 shares. Marking at $101 produces equity of $10,038: $5,998 plus $4,040. The $38 gain combines $40 unrealized appreciation with the $2 entry fee.

A pending order for 60 additional shares is not a holding. It reserves buying power using its price cap and a fee buffer. Canceling that remainder releases the reserve without undoing the 40-share fill.

## Implementation and review

Test cash and share conservation after every transition, not just at the final report. Reconcile independent order and fill records after restart. Compare paper outcomes with the documented simulation model; vendor paper environments can differ from live conditions, and the offline lab does not model queue position, market impact, borrow, or settlement delays. Treat correct arithmetic as evidence of ledger correctness, not a forecast of execution quality.

modules.title: Position sizing and circuit breakers
modules.subtitle: Translate uncertain return assumptions into constrained position sizes and explicit loss-control states.
modules.objective: Translate uncertain return assumptions into constrained position sizes and explicit loss-control states.
modules.reading: Unit 4 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A trading system needs rules for when it must refuse an otherwise valid signal. Those rules depend on positions, cash, outstanding orders, data quality, and operating limits. Begin by writing the condition that must always hold, then test a case that tries to break it. Later lessons explain how to halt and resume without losing track of existing commitments.

## Design and reasoning

Kelly sizing maximizes expected log growth in a specified repeated-bet model; it does not supply reliable probabilities or eliminate drawdowns. The binary-bet expression assumes a known win probability, a fixed payoff ratio, and losses bounded by the staked fraction. Stock gaps, changing payoffs, correlated bets, and estimation error break a literal mapping.

Fractional Kelly reduces the output of that model, but remains sensitive to its inputs. Practical sizing also needs capital, exposure, liquidity, and loss limits. A stop distance is a planned trigger distance, not a guaranteed maximum loss: a gap or unavailable market can execute beyond it.

$$
f^*=p-(1-p)/b;\quad q_{risk}=\lfloor B/|P_{entry}-P_{stop}|\rfloor
$$

## A worked example

For a hypothetical even-money bet with win probability 0.55, full Kelly is 0.55−0.45 = 10%; half Kelly is 5%. If the true probability is 0.51, full Kelly is only 2%. The original estimate therefore matters more than the apparent precision of the arithmetic.

Under a separate stop-risk rule, a $200 loss budget and $2 distance suggest 100 shares before other caps. If an entry gaps from a $50 assumption to $55 while the stop remains $48, the $7 distance suggests at most 28 integer shares. Recompute at the executable price.

## Implementation and review

Keep the position-size function deterministic and place it after the model proposal. Validate positive distances and finite inputs before division. Combine the resulting cap with cash, single-name, and portfolio constraints. Define which events halt new risk and who can resume. A halt blocks new exposure; cancellation and risk reduction require their own reconciled procedures.

p = 0.55
print("Half Kelly fraction:", round((p - (1 - p)) / 2, 4))
print("Shares under stop budget:", int(200 / 2))
print("Shares after gap:", int(200 / 7))

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.

modules.title: Portfolio exposure and outstanding commitments
modules.subtitle: Aggregate correlated positions and open-order commitments before approving a new trade.
modules.objective: Aggregate correlated positions and open-order commitments before approving a new trade.
modules.reading: Unit 4 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A collection of individually acceptable orders can violate the account's overall limits. Calculate projected cash and holdings after outstanding commitments, then test gross exposure, net exposure, single-name concentration, sector concentration, and any factor budgets supported by reliable estimates. Different measures detect different failure modes.

For a long-only account, net and gross dollar exposure coincide, but sector and name concentration still differ. A future long/short extension cannot assume that netting removes liquidity or margin risk. An exposure estimate also needs a declared mark and stale-price policy.

$$
w_{projected}=(N_{held}+N_{pending}+N_{new})/E
$$

## A worked example

Harbor's $100,000 account holds $12,000 in one name and has an accepted $5,000 buy outstanding. A proposed additional $4,000 would produce $21,000 projected exposure. It breaches a stipulated 20% name limit even though the current holding is only 12%. The maximum extra notional under this cap is $3,000 before fee and price buffers.

Two $10,000 positions in different companies may still create $20,000 exposure to the same industry. Splitting orders across names does not necessarily diversify the underlying economic risk.

## Implementation and review

Recompute reservations atomically with acceptance, so two simultaneous proposals cannot both consume the same remaining budget. Revalue after material price changes; a limit that held at submission can be exceeded by the market without any new order. Such a breach should trigger the declared review or reduction policy, not rewrite historical acceptance records. Test concurrent buys, opposite-side commitments, and a stale mark.

modules.title: Pre-trade gates and invariants
modules.subtitle: Make invalid prices, stale data, unavailable cash, and policy breaches fail before order acceptance.
modules.objective: Make invalid prices, stale data, unavailable cash, and policy breaches fail before order acceptance.
modules.reading: Unit 4 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A risk gate evaluates a typed proposal against a consistent account and market snapshot. Validate the schema first: known instrument, supported side, positive integer quantity, finite positive price, and an allowed order type. Then validate freshness and session eligibility, followed by cash, shares, exposure, and halt policy. A malformed number must never participate in arithmetic as if it were valid.

Collect explicit rejection reasons rather than replacing invalid input with zero. The exact evaluation order is an implementation choice, but every mandatory condition must hold. Keep model confidence outside this permission boundary: confidence can influence a proposed target, while the gate owns hard limits.

$$
qP_{cap}+Fee(q,P_{cap})\leq C_{available}
$$

## A worked example

Available cash is $1,000, a buy price cap is $100, and commission is 10 bps. Ten shares require $1,001, so the order fails cash validation. Nine require $900.90 and fit that constraint. They still need to pass all other gates.

A quote can have an acceptable price and insufficient freshness. An order can fit the name limit and exceed the sector limit. Passing one gate is not a general approval.

## Implementation and review

Mutate one input at a time to test each rejection. The lab's market-event flag and price cap are explicit simplifications, with no exchange calendar or broker connection. Keep an invariant failure visible and halt further mutations until the state is reconciled.

modules.title: Halts, loss limits, and controlled resumption
modules.subtitle: Design a persistent operating-state machine that separates stopping new risk from managing existing exposure.
modules.objective: Design a persistent operating-state machine that separates stopping new risk from managing existing exposure.
modules.reading: Unit 4 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Define states such as running, new-risk halted, reconciling, and disabled. A loss threshold, stale feed, ledger mismatch, or unknown external order may require different actions, but each transition needs a recorded reason. A halt must survive restart; otherwise reboot becomes an accidental permission reset.

Stopping new risk does not guarantee that all orders disappeared or that positions are flat. Cancel outstanding entries through the order manager and reconcile their actual results. A reduction order still needs valid quantity, price, session, and execution controls; an emergency label is not a license to corrupt the ledger.

$$
L_{session}=1-E_t/E_{start}
$$

## A worked example

A session begins with equity $100,000 and later marks at $97,400. The session loss is 2.6%, crossing Harbor's illustrative 2.5% halt threshold. Peak-to-trough drawdown would use a different denominator if equity had first risen above $100,000. Decide which measure the policy means.

If equity rebounds to $98,000, a latched halt remains active until an explicit review and resume event. Automatic oscillation around the boundary can produce repeated stop-and-start trading.

## Implementation and review

Write a resumption checklist tied to evidence: current balances reconcile, unknown orders are resolved, input freshness is restored, the triggering defect is understood, and a permitted reviewer records the release. Test restart while halted, a fill arriving during the halt, and an attempted unreviewed resume. The educational project offers an explicit resume method for experiments; it is not a multi-user approval system.

modules.title: Labels, overlapping horizons, and time splits
modules.subtitle: Construct prediction targets without allowing future labels or fitted preprocessing to leak into evaluation.
modules.objective: Construct prediction targets without allowing future labels or fitted preprocessing to leak into evaluation.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

A model's target describes an outcome that becomes known after the prediction. If a future outcome overlaps the period used for another example, an ordinary data split can accidentally share information. Draw the timeline of each example before fitting a model. This unit connects those time boundaries to baselines, thresholds, and monitoring.

## Design and reasoning

A label has an observation time and an end time: a five-day forward return becomes fully known five days later. Features at a decision time must use only information available then. Training rows whose labels extend into the evaluation interval can carry future information across an apparently chronological boundary.

Use forward validation with a training cutoff that respects label availability. Purge overlapping label intervals when necessary. A fixed gap in a time-series splitter is convenient for fixed horizons, but it does not automatically identify variable event horizons or solve every dependence problem. An embargo is a separate exclusion interval; naming a split purged does not make it so.

$$
\text{Eligible training row }i:\quad t^{label}_{end,i}<t^{validation}_{start}
$$

## A worked example

Validation begins at time index 10. Candidate training labels begin at 4, 6, and 8 and end three steps later at 7, 9, and 11. Under a strict end-before-validation rule, the first two are eligible; the row ending at 11 is excluded. Training data that starts before 10 can still contain a label unavailable at 10.

A scaler is fitted on the eligible training features and then applied unchanged to validation. Fitting it on all dates leaks information even if the labels were properly separated.

## Implementation and review

Save train, validation, and test index manifests with label intervals and data versions. Unit-test boundary cases where a label ends exactly at the cutoff and explicitly declare whether that endpoint is allowed. Tune only on development folds and retain a later frozen evaluation. Report the number of independent time periods, not just the number of overlapping rows.

assignment.prompt: Validation starts at 20. Label ends are 17, 19, 20, and 23. Apply the strict rule and explain why a generic random split is unsuitable here.
assignment.solution: Only 17 and 19 qualify. The strict rule excludes the endpoint at 20. A random split can train on future outcomes and overlapping intervals relative to an earlier evaluation decision.

modules.title: Baselines and prediction-to-position mapping
modules.subtitle: Compare simple predictive baselines and convert model output into a bounded decision under trading costs.
modules.objective: Compare simple predictive baselines and convert model output into a bounded decision under trading costs.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Start with an explicit no-skill baseline: a training mean for regression or a training base rate for classification. A complex model must improve a relevant out-of-sample objective, not merely fit the training data. Compare squared error, calibration where relevant, ranking quality, and eventual cost-aware decisions without conflating them.

A prediction in return units can be compared with estimated trading costs. A rank cannot directly be treated as a return magnitude, and a probability of a positive return does not state the size of wins or losses. Define the mapping from model output to target before evaluating the holdout.

$$
MSE=n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Observed validation returns are 1% and −1%. The zero-return baseline has mean squared error 0.0001. Predictions of 0.8% and −0.6% have MSE 0.00001, improving this tiny illustrative sample. Two rows are insufficient evidence of durable performance.

If a proposed trade has expected benefit 8 bps and estimated nonoverlapping cost 6 bps, only 2 bps remain before model uncertainty. Harbor may require an additional margin or abstain. Position size is capped by deterministic risk logic even if the prediction is large.

## Implementation and review

Log the baseline, prediction units, evaluation dates, costs, turnover, and target mapping. Inspect whether apparent gains come from one outlier or one regime. A ranking model may be assessed with cross-sectional rank correlation, but time-series dependence and universe construction still affect inference. Keep predictive evaluation and portfolio simulation as separate evidence artifacts.

predicted = [0.008, -0.006]

for i in range(2):
    error = error + (actual[i] - predicted[i]) ** 2
print("Model MSE:", error / 2)
print("Zero baseline MSE:", 0.0001)

modules.title: Boosted trees and defensible constraints
modules.subtitle: Develop a nonlinear model with controlled complexity, time-aware selection, and documented feature assumptions.
modules.objective: Develop a nonlinear model with controlled complexity, time-aware selection, and documented feature assumptions.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Boosting adds learners that correct the current model under a specified loss. Depth, learning rate, number of rounds, minimum leaf support, and regularization influence complexity. More rounds can improve training loss while degrading later performance. Use a chronologically valid validation set for early stopping and preserve the chosen iteration with the model artifact.

A monotonic constraint imposes a direction on a model's response to a selected feature while other inputs are held fixed. It expresses a modeling assumption. It does not prove that a financial relationship is universally monotonic, causal, or stable across regimes. Forcing an unjustified relationship can reduce accuracy.

$$
m^*=\arg\min_m L_{validation}(m)
$$

## A worked example

Validation losses over five training checkpoints are 0.90, 0.75, 0.71, 0.73, and 0.78. Under this illustrative selection rule, checkpoint three is preferred. Choosing checkpoint five merely because it trained longest ignores the validation evidence. The final test set must not become another tuning input.

Harbor considers a positive constraint on a quality score. Before adopting it, the team documents the score's definition, tests an unconstrained baseline, and checks whether the same feature meaning survives revisions. A renamed or rescaled feature is not automatically compatible with an old constraint vector.

## Implementation and review

The in-app worksheet illustrates model selection arithmetic; it does not train XGBoost. For an optional external extension, pin a supported library version, save feature order and constraints, inspect that version's early-stopping prediction behavior, and reproduce the result from a clean environment. Report the validation manifest and rejected variants. The later standard-library project trains a small ridge model to make the fit/evaluate boundary runnable without extra dependencies.

print("Selected loss:", losses[best])

modules.title: Calibration, thresholds, and drift
modules.subtitle: Evaluate probability quality and monitor changes in data, predictions, and delayed outcomes.
modules.objective: Evaluate probability quality and monitor changes in data, predictions, and delayed outcomes.
modules.reading: Unit 5 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies in comparable cases. Discrimination asks whether the model separates outcomes. A proper score such as Brier loss reflects more than calibration alone, so a lower score is not a pure proof of better calibration. Inspect reliability bins with counts and uncertainty as well as aggregate scores.

Fit a calibration transform using development data separate from the base model's fitting observations, under a valid time design. Never calibrate on the final holdout and then report that same holdout as untouched. A calibrated probability still needs a payoff and cost model before becoming a trading decision.

$$
BS=n^{-1}\sum_i(p_i-y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Predictions 0.8 and 0.3 face outcomes 1 and 0. The Brier score is ((0.8−1)² + (0.3−0)²)/2 = 0.065. A constant 0.5 forecast scores 0.25 on these two observations. This is an arithmetic comparison, not enough data to establish calibration.

If a winning trade gains 1 unit and a losing trade loses 1, expected gross payoff is 2p−1. With a cost of 0.1 units per trade, break-even requires p above 0.55 under those stipulated payoffs. Different loss sizes change the threshold.

## Implementation and review

Monitor feature missingness, schema changes, prediction distribution, abstention frequency, and eventually realized label quality. Covariate drift does not necessarily imply performance failure; stable inputs do not prove stable outcomes either. Outcomes arrive late, so distinguish immediate operational alerts from delayed predictive monitoring. A drift alert should trigger a declared review or fallback; it should not silently retrain and promote a model.

print("Symmetric payoff threshold:", (1 + 0.1) / 2)

# Its equity curve is not evidence for the bot or model's performance.

modules.title: AI decision layers and authority boundaries
modules.subtitle: Assign useful research tasks to AI while keeping order permissions and risk limits outside model-generated text.
modules.objective: Assign useful research tasks to AI while keeping order permissions and risk limits outside model-generated text.
modules.reading: Unit 6 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

An AI research tool can summarize or extract information, but the trading system still needs explicit rules for accepting its output. Start with a narrow task and a source the result can be checked against. Distinguish a model's suggestion from the authority to change an account or submit an order. The following lessons make that distinction testable.

## Design and reasoning

An AI component can summarize evidence, extract candidate facts, classify documents, or draft a research rationale. A deterministic controller validates these outputs and decides whether they are usable. Separate a research recommendation from an authorized target, and keep both separate from broker submission.

A multi-agent committee can provide different analytical perspectives, but agreement is not independence when agents share the same model, prompt, or source error. More discussion does not convert missing evidence into a fact. Start with a small bounded workflow and add autonomous steps only when their benefit can be evaluated.

$$
q_{accepted}=RiskGate(Proposal,Account,Market,Policy)
$$

## A worked example

An AI analyst proposes a 30% position with a confidence score of 0.9. Harbor's fixed single-name cap is 10%. The proposal is rejected or resized under the declared deterministic policy. The model's explanation cannot override the cap, and confidence is not an authenticated permission.

A second proposal includes a plausible conclusion but no source identifier for its revenue figure. The research controller marks the required evidence missing and abstains. Passing numeric risk checks does not repair an unsupported premise.

## Implementation and review

Define a narrow input/output contract: task, document identifiers, allowed fields, uncertainty or missing status, and an explanation linked to evidence. Keep API secrets and trading tools out of document-analysis context. Evaluate correctness, unsupported claims, abstentions, latency, and cost against a deterministic or human-reviewed baseline. The downloadable AI lab uses fixed fictional responses to test validation; it does not call an AI provider or imply measured model accuracy.

modules.objective: Build a point-in-time research packet that preserves document identity, reporting units, and claim provenance.
modules.reading: Unit 6 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

Retrieval selects candidate evidence; generation interprets it. Store each document's issuer, filing type, reporting period, publication timestamp, revision identity, and retrieval provenance. A semantic match does not establish that a passage answers the question or was available at a historical decision time.

Chunk boundaries should retain headings and table context. A revenue number without currency, scale, period, or scope can be materially misleading. Keep the original document pointer and local source identifier so a reviewer can trace the candidate fact. Access and redistribution rights for stored documents remain separate from their usefulness as evidence.

$$
Value_{base}=Value_{reported}\times UnitMultiplier
$$

## A worked example

A fictional Harbor filing published on March 15 reports prior-year revenue of 120 million currency units. It is eligible for an April 1 research decision but not a March 1 historical decision. An amended filing published April 20 cannot silently replace it in the April 1 record.

The analyst extracts 120 and tags the unit as millions. A controller normalizes it to 120,000,000 for a ratio calculation. If the accompanying text said thousands, the same digits would mean a thousandfold smaller amount. Preserve both the reported and normalized value.

## Implementation and review

Test missing pages, conflicting revisions, ambiguous table headers, and a relevant-looking passage about the wrong issuer. Require an explicit not-found outcome. An evidence packet should include the question, allowed as-of time, candidate documents, supported fields, unresolved disagreements, and reviewer disposition. A citation points to a source; it does not prove that the generated claim follows from it.

modules.title: Structured extraction and numeric validation
modules.subtitle: Validate AI-extracted facts beyond JSON syntax by checking provenance, units, scope, and arithmetic.
modules.objective: Validate AI-extracted facts beyond JSON syntax by checking provenance, units, scope, and arithmetic.
modules.reading: Unit 6 engineering study. Produce the assignment artifact, reproduce the worksheet, and consult the primary references below. All Harbor cases are fictional.
modules.content:
## Design and reasoning

A schema can require fields and restrict types; it cannot guarantee that a value is true. Validate source membership, instrument identity, reporting period, allowed units, numeric finiteness, and consistency with the supplied evidence. Reject unknown fields when they could be interpreted as instructions or unauthorized actions.

Keep reported facts separate from derived ratios and judgment. Let deterministic code compute ratios from validated inputs, with explicit zero-denominator and missing-value behavior. Avoid using a generated ratio when the underlying numerator and denominator are available for verification.

$$
g=Revenue_{current}/Revenue_{prior}-1
$$

## A worked example

A fictional evidence record states current revenue 120 million and prior revenue 100 million. The computed growth is 20%. A generated response of 200% has valid numeric syntax but fails arithmetic reconciliation. A response saying 120 thousand fails its unit contract even though its raw number matches.

If prior revenue is zero, percentage growth under this formula is undefined. The controller should return a missing or not-applicable result with a reason instead of producing an infinite score that might dominate position sizing.

## Implementation and review

Build accepted and rejected fixtures before connecting a provider. Include a fabricated source ID, mixed currencies, a future filing, an omitted field, a zero denominator, and unsupported instructions embedded in a note. Measure false acceptance as well as extraction completeness. The offline fixture project demonstrates strict comparison against supplied records; general document interpretation still requires a separately evaluated extraction system.
