modules.subtitle: Translate a trading idea into a prediction contract with data, labels, baselines, evaluation, and release criteria.
modules.objective: Translate a trading idea into a prediction contract with data, labels, baselines, evaluation, and release criteria.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Before training a model, define the prediction in terms of a real decision and a timeline. What information is available now, what outcome will be measured later, and how could the prediction be used? A clear target makes the rest of the workflow easier to check. This lesson follows a short return period so you can see where inputs end and outcomes begin.

## Understand the idea

Machine learning estimates a relationship from examples; a trading system additionally needs a decision rule, execution assumptions, and operational controls. Start with the prediction question, horizon, eligible universe, available information, loss function, and baseline. Distinguish forecasting a return, classifying its sign, ranking stocks, and deciding whether an opportunity is worth its costs.

The lifecycle links problem definition to collection, cleaning, features, labels, splitting, training, selection, independent evaluation, error diagnosis, artifact release, inference, monitoring, and retirement. A failure in an early stage can invalidate a sophisticated model later.

$$
y_t=O_{t+2}/O_{t+1}-1
$$

## A worked example

The downloadable project observes features after close t, predicts the return from open t+1 to open t+2, and separately classifies whether that return is positive. With entry 100 and exit 102, its regression target is .02 and its direction label is positive. A positive label alone does not establish profit after execution costs.

### Put the prediction on a timeline

The notation t identifies the current day. Close t is the end of that day's observation period. Open t+1 is the next day's opening point, and open t+2 is the following day's opening point. In this task, features become available after close t, before the example's entry at open t+1.

The target measures the change from the entry value of 100 to the exit value of 102. Divide the gain of 2 by the starting value of 100 to get 0.02, or 2%. The regression target keeps that numerical return. The classification label keeps only whether it is positive.

A positive label loses information about the size of the gain. It also says nothing by itself about the cost of turning the prediction into a trade. This distinction explains why the course evaluates data timing, prediction quality, and trading results as connected but separate steps.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a one-page contract before running the lab. Define what a prediction means and what evidence would reject the idea. Preserve a simple mean-return and class-prior baseline. The default project uses synthetic data and produces research artifacts, not orders. Its negative or inconclusive results are legitimate outcomes of the lifecycle, not reasons to change the test retrospectively.

## Put this session into practice

Use the first eight minutes to read the explanation and the linked primary material, then spend eight minutes reproducing and changing the worksheet calculation. Use the remaining fourteen minutes to complete the assignment in your lifecycle notebook or downloaded project. Record the expected result before running code, compare it with the output, and keep an unresolved question for the next review. The 12-hour estimate includes these activities; checkpoint and final-exam time is additional.

modules.subtitle: Record when each observation became available and avoid using revised data or today's surviving universe as historical knowledge.
modules.objective: Record when each observation became available and avoid using revised data or today's surviving universe as historical knowledge.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Financial observations have multiple timestamps: the economic period, exchange event time, publication time, vendor receipt, and later revision time. A statement about last quarter was not necessarily available at quarter end. A historical study should use the version available at its decision cutoff or disclose that a point-in-time reconstruction is unavailable.

Universe membership also changes. Restricting historical training to today's surviving listings can omit delisted or failed firms. Symbols can change and need stable identity mapping. Data access and reuse conditions belong in the source manifest alongside coverage and adjustment conventions.

$$
availableAt\le decisionAt
$$

## A worked example

A filing describes a quarter ending March 31 but is released May 10. A model deciding April 15 cannot use that release merely because its period label says March. Similarly, a record arriving at 21:05 is late for a stipulated 21:00 decision cutoff.

## Put the idea into practice

The local CSV schema includes date, symbol, open, close, volume, and available_at. It rejects rows unavailable by its synthetic 21:00 UTC cutoff. This clock is a teaching convention, not a real exchange calendar. For actual research, replace it with the intended venue's sessions, publication rules, and dated membership before making historical claims. Record missing coverage explicitly instead of inferring availability from a populated table.

## Put this session into practice

Use the first eight minutes to read the explanation and the linked primary material, then spend eight minutes reproducing and changing the worksheet calculation. Use the remaining fourteen minutes to complete the assignment in your lifecycle notebook or downloaded project. Record the expected result before running code, compare it with the output, and keep an unresolved question for the next review. The 12-hour estimate includes these activities; checkpoint and final-exam time is additional.

modules.subtitle: Create a cleaning audit that distinguishes invalid observations, exact duplicates, conflicting revisions, and optional missing features.
modules.objective: Create a cleaning audit that distinguishes invalid observations, exact duplicates, conflicting revisions, and optional missing features.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 8 minutes of lesson and primary-source study, 8 minutes reproducing the worksheet, and 14 minutes on the project assignment and review. Allow extra time if Python or statistics is new to you.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Cleaning begins with a data contract, not a command that drops every row containing a null. Validate required columns, identifier/date uniqueness, numeric types, units, price positivity, volume conventions, and timestamp availability. Exact duplicate rows can be removed under an explicit policy; conflicting rows for the same date and symbol need a revision rule rather than an arbitrary keep-last choice.

A missing optional volume feature differs from an invalid tradable price. The project preserves missing volume for training-only imputation, while it excludes nonpositive prices and late observations. Every exclusion is counted in the audit so learners can detect unexpected changes in coverage.

$$
retained=raw-exactDuplicates-excludedUniqueRows
$$

## A worked example

Suppose 101 input rows contain one exact duplicate and two distinct invalid-price rows, with no overlap. Removing them leaves 98 rows. A separate missing-volume value can remain in those rows for later imputation; it need not reduce the count to 97.

## Put the idea into practice

Run the project and inspect audit fields rather than only the cleaned file. Add a conflicting duplicate and verify that the cleaner asks for a defined policy by raising an error. Add a negative price, a nonnumeric volume, and an unknown availability time separately. Keep a copy of raw input and a reproducible transformation history. Never repair a negative price by taking its absolute value without evidence of the source error.

## Put this session into practice

Use the first eight minutes to read the explanation and the linked primary material, then spend eight minutes reproducing and changing the worksheet calculation. Use the remaining fourteen minutes to complete the assignment in your lifecycle notebook or downloaded project. Record the expected result before running code, compare it with the output, and keep an unresolved question for the next review. The 12-hour estimate includes these activities; checkpoint and final-exam time is additional.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

An extreme observation can be a source error, a split, a stale quote, or a genuine market jump. These cases have different meanings. Compare raw and adjusted fields, volume, corporate-action records, and neighboring observations before choosing a repair. A model may be harmed by a real jump, but removing it solely because it hurts performance changes the research population.

Forward filling an optional slowly changing field can be defensible only with a known availability and staleness rule. Backfilling from a later release uses future information. Tradable prices and target returns should not be invented merely to keep every row in the training matrix.

$$
q_{after}P_{after}=q_{before}P_{before}\quad\text{for the idealized split}
$$

## A worked example

Ten shares priced at 100 become twenty at 50 in a two-for-one split, preserving value 1,000 before other changes. Treating the raw price change as a −50% economic return creates a false label. Conversely, a genuine fall from 100 to 50 without a split is not repaired by doubling the price.

## Put the idea into practice

The synthetic project has no real corporate-action feed and makes no automatic split repair. It removes bad prices and preserves the global observed date grid so feature and target windows do not silently jump across an excluded observation. Add an audit note distinguishing a confirmed correction from a sensitivity-based exclusion. Fit clipping thresholds, if justified, on training data only and report the number and type of observations changed.

## Start with a simple picture

Features are the inputs a model sees; labels are the outcomes it learns to predict. Both need dates and a clear definition. Start with one row, identify the last information available, and draw the future interval used for its label. This unit then shows how to split and preprocess rows without letting later information reach training decisions.

## Understand the idea

A feature is a dated transformation with a unit, lookback, minimum history, and availability rule. Momentum, rolling volatility, volume transformations, and fundamental ratios can be useful candidates, but their definitions must remain identical in training and inference. Group by stable security identity before shifting or rolling so one stock's last row cannot become another stock's lag.

A lag is only meaningful relative to a calendar. Removing a missing row and shifting the remaining rows can turn a one-session label into a longer interval. The project reindexes each stock to the observed global date grid and requires complete price windows for its five-period features.

momentum_{5,t}=C_t/C_{t-5}-1

## Understand the idea

A target describes the outcome the model should estimate. A next-close return, next-open holding return, market-relative return, and binary profitable-trade label are different tasks. Costs can be included in a target or in a later decision rule, but the convention must be consistent and clearly named.

Future labels are allowed in historical supervised training only after those outcomes become available. Retain label_end so a training cutoff can exclude labels that extend into validation or test. At inference time, the newest rows have no matured label; they still need features and predictions without inventing outcomes.

$$
class_t=\mathbb{1}[O_{t+2}/O_{t+1}-1>0]
$$

At decision t, the next two opening prices are 200 and 198. The project's target is −1% and the positive-sign class is false. If the previous close was 190, using 198/190−1 would define a different interval and falsely include a price move that the stipulated next-open entry did not capture.

## Understand the idea

Random row splitting can place the same market date or overlapping outcome interval in both training and evaluation. For the pooled stock task here, split by global date so all stocks on a date receive the same partition. Keep model selection in validation and reserve test for a frozen procedure.

The project uses approximately 60%, 20%, and 20% of eligible dates. It purges earlier rows whose label_end reaches the next partition's start. This is stricter than merely checking the feature date. ## Understand the idea

A transformation can learn from data even when it has no target variable. Medians, means, standard deviations, clipping quantiles, PCA components, and feature selections all carry sample information. Fitting them on the complete dataset exposes the training procedure to held-out observations. A pipeline keeps the transformation and estimator in one fit/predict contract.

The project uses median imputation, standardization, and an estimator. Optional missing volume is handled by the fitted imputer; invalid price and target windows have already been excluded. Validation and test call predict, not fit_transform, on this pipeline.

$$
z=(x-\mu_{train})/\sigma_{train}
$$

## A worked example

Training values [1,2,9] have median 2. A missing validation value should receive that fitted median, even if later values would make the full-sample median much larger. For a feature with training mean 10 and scale 2, an observed value 14 becomes standardized value 2.

## Put the idea into practice

Inspect the imputer statistics and scaler means in the fitted artifact. Change only held-out feature values and refit on the unchanged training slice; training statistics must remain identical. When a model is legitimately refitted on the larger pre-test development set, its preprocessing may change because its authorized training population changed. Document that distinction so a valid final refit is not confused with accidental test leakage.

modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Training adjusts a model to improve an objective on a set of examples. Begin with a simple baseline so you can tell whether extra complexity adds useful evidence. Work through the meaning of the loss function before comparing algorithms. A model that fits training data closely still needs a separate evaluation on later observations.

## Understand the idea

A regression model estimates a numerical target under a chosen loss. Mean squared error emphasizes large residuals, while mean absolute error has a different sensitivity. A constant prediction based on the training mean is a useful baseline for squared error; using the test mean instead would give the baseline information unavailable at deployment.

Ridge regression adds a coefficient penalty to least squares. The penalty trades fit against coefficient magnitude and can stabilize correlated predictors. Its scale depends on the objective convention and feature scaling, so record the implementation and preprocessing. A smaller training error alone does not establish a better future model.

$$
MSE=n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2
$$

## A worked example

Predictions [1,2,3] and outcomes [1,3,5] have errors [0,1,2], MSE 5/3, and MAE 1 in the stated units. If a training-mean baseline has MSE 2, the model improves this particular error comparison by 1−(5/3)/2≈16.7%.

## Put the idea into practice

Run the project's three ridge candidates and retain every validation loss. Compare the selected model's held-out error with mean_baseline_mse. Inspect the fitted coefficient scale only after accounting for standardization. Do not interpret a coefficient as a causal effect or a return guarantee. Record a negative result when the baseline wins and identify whether the next justified experiment concerns data, target, features, or model assumptions.

## Understand the idea

Logistic regression models a binary outcome through a probability link. The class definition comes first: the project labels a positive next-open holding return, not a profitable trade after every cost. A probability estimate and a hard decision threshold are separate outputs. Class imbalance can make raw accuracy misleading because predicting the majority class may already score well.

The project fits logistic candidates on training data, compares validation Brier loss, and refits the selected configuration on eligible development observations. A fixed .55 threshold is declared for the confusion matrix; it is not optimized on test results.

$$
precision=TP/(TP+FP),\quad recall=TP/(TP+FN)
$$

## A worked example

If only 20 of 100 outcomes are positive, predicting negative for every row achieves 80% accuracy and zero positive recall. If a classifier accepts ten opportunities and six are positive, precision is .6; if twenty positives existed, recall is .3. Neither statistic alone describes the magnitude of gains and losses.

## Put the idea into practice

Inspect class counts in each date partition before fitting. A training slice with only one class cannot support the intended logistic fit. Compare probabilities with the development class-prior baseline, and retain confusion counts rather than only a headline score. If using weighting or resampling, apply it within training and re-evaluate calibration and the population being represented. Do not balance the final test by deleting inconvenient real outcomes.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A decision tree partitions feature space into regions. Deep trees can fit highly specific patterns, while ensembles combine multiple trees using different construction rules. Random forests average randomized trees; boosting adds models sequentially to improve an objective. Their hyperparameters and uncertainty properties differ, so do not treat all tree ensembles as interchangeable.

The downloadable project trains a bounded random forest candidate with a fixed seed, depth, leaf size, and tree count. ## Understand the idea

A neural network composes learned transformations under an optimization objective. Hidden width, depth, regularization, learning rate, batch construction, and stopping criteria influence both capacity and training behavior. More parameters do not create information absent from the features or repair mislabeled outcomes. A small tabular baseline remains a useful reference even when sequence architectures are being considered.

## Start with a simple picture

Choosing a model is itself a research decision. Trying many settings and reporting only the best score can hide how much selection took place. This unit separates model selection from final evaluation and explains what different metrics measure. Follow a prediction into the decision and cost assumptions before interpreting a better score as an investment improvement.

## Understand the idea

Every tried feature set, hyperparameter, seed choice, and stopping rule is part of the research search. A small declared candidate set is easier to audit than an undocumented sequence of improvements. Record the primary validation metric and tie-breaking rule before fitting. The best validation result is selected evidence, not an untouched estimate of future performance.

The project implements a single chronological train/validation/test design. Walk-forward and nested designs are extensions: repeat the selection procedure within each outer training history, then evaluate its frozen choice on the next dated block. Do not describe the supplied single split as a full nested backtest.

$$
\hat\lambda=\arg\min_{\lambda\in\Lambda}L_{validation}(\lambda)
$$

## A worked example

Three candidates have validation losses .020, .018, and .021. The second wins the declared minimum-loss rule. If the researcher then sees a poor final test and adds a fourth candidate tailored to it, that test has become development evidence. A new independent evaluation or an explicit limitation is needed.

## Put the idea into practice

Save the full trial ledger and split manifest. Use the advanced research lab's interval-purged splits as a starting point for a three-origin extension, but fit preprocessing and model selection afresh within each permitted history. Aggregate losses with declared date/row weighting and report variation across origins. Record computational budget and failed fits rather than silently dropping them from the comparison.

## Understand the idea

MSE and MAE evaluate numerical prediction errors in different ways. R-squared compares squared error with variation around the evaluated sample mean and can be negative. An out-of-sample improvement against an available training-mean baseline is a related but distinct comparison. Classification metrics such as ROC AUC and average precision assess ordering under different summaries; neither directly measures tradable profit.

Precision and recall require their denominators. When no positives are predicted, precision is undefined under the project's convention. A one-class evaluation slice also cannot supply ordinary two-class ROC AUC. Reporting null with a reason is more informative than fabricating a perfect score.

$$
relative\ MSE\ improvement=1-MSE_{model}/MSE_{baseline}
$$

## A worked example

A model MSE .8 against an available baseline MSE 1 gives a 20% relative improvement. A classifier with TP=8, FP=2, and FN=12 has precision .8 and recall .4. The high precision does not show that it found most positives or that its positive predictions had favorable payoff magnitudes.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities correspond to observed outcome frequencies in an appropriate evaluation population. It differs from ranking: a model can sort cases well while systematically overstating probabilities. Reliability bins, Brier score, and log loss provide complementary views, with finite-sample uncertainty and binning choices still relevant.

The project reports probability bins and Brier loss but does not fit an additional post-hoc calibrator. A calibration extension must reserve suitable development observations or use a carefully specified cross-fitting procedure. Fitting it on the final test would consume that evaluation boundary.

$$
Brier=n^{-1}\sum_i(p_i-y_i)^2,\quad p^*=(L+c)/(G+L)
$$

## A worked example

For two binary outcomes [1,0] with probabilities [.8,.3], Brier loss is ((1−.8)^2+(0−.3)^2)/2=.065. Under a separate payoff model with gain 3, loss 2, and cost .2, expected payoff becomes positive only when probability exceeds .44. This threshold depends on those stipulated conditional payoffs.

## Put the idea into practice

Inspect each reliability bin's count before interpreting a probability gap. Compare the classifier with the class-prior baseline. Write a threshold policy that accounts for costs and abstention, and freeze it before the independent test. The fixed .55 report threshold is a declared classification convention, not a universal optimal trading rule. Document a change in gain/loss asymmetry or cost that would invalidate an earlier threshold.

## Understand the idea

Statistical improvement is only one input to an investment decision. A policy also specifies which predictions create exposure, how much, when entry and exit occur, and what costs and constraints apply. Report a gross-to-net bridge and compare with a baseline under the same opportunity set. Avoid annualizing a short favorable interval into a confident long-term claim.

The project uses an explicit opportunity proxy: predictions above the stipulated round-trip cost select next-open-to-following-open opportunities, equal weights are capped at .4 per selected stock, and each daily round trip pays the full stated cost. It does not simulate broker cash, queue position, settlement, or borrow.

$$
r_{net,t}=\sum_i w_{i,t}r_{i,t}-c\sum_i w_{i,t}
$$

## A worked example

Two selected stocks each receive weight .4 and cash keeps .2. Their realized returns are .02 and −.01, so gross portfolio contribution is .004. At .001 round-trip cost on each invested weight, cost is .0008 and net contribution .0032. A single selected stock remains capped at .4 rather than becoming a fully invested position.

## Put the idea into practice

Inspect opportunities.json and reconcile one date by hand. Re-evaluate the same frozen predictions under several predeclared cost scenarios, separating sensitivity analysis from threshold retuning. Compare selected count, exposure, compounded proxy return, and adverse dates. Before connecting the model to the paper-bot lab, reconcile its target weights with actual fills and cash under that simulator's different assumptions. A profitable proxy alone is insufficient evidence for live deployment.

## Start with a simple picture

When a model makes mistakes, the average score may hide where they occur. Inspect errors by date, stock, and condition, and compare them with data quality and the model's inputs. ## Understand the idea

An average loss can hide large differences across stocks, dates, liquidity conditions, missing-data patterns, and outcome magnitudes. Error analysis connects a failure to an actionable hypothesis: stale features, a wrong label, an unrepresented population, an unstable relation, or a model that cannot express the relevant pattern. Begin with the largest residuals and a random sample of ordinary cases so the investigation does not focus only on spectacular exceptions.

Slices chosen after seeing test outcomes are exploratory. They can guide a new development cycle, but repeated corrections informed by the same test do not create repeated independent confirmations.

modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Feature importance depends on the model, evaluation data, metric, and inspection procedure. Permutation importance measures how a fitted model's score changes when a feature is disrupted under a specified permutation design. A feature with low importance may still contain useful information that another correlated feature supplies. Conversely, a highly important feature can be a leaked target proxy.

For time-dependent financial data, unrestricted row permutation changes temporal structure. Choose and describe a diagnostic permutation scheme appropriate to the question, and avoid claiming that its importance score is a causal intervention effect.

$$
importance_j=L_{permuted\ j}-L_{original}
$$

## Understand the idea

A finite financial sample contains dependence and changing conditions. A model that works in one volatility or liquidity regime may fail in another. Compare prespecified windows and adverse scenarios, but do not select only the favorable period for the final claim. Row-level uncertainty formulas can overstate effective information when many stocks share the same market date or labels overlap.

Repeated research introduces selection bias. The family includes feature and data choices as well as model hyperparameters. A bootstrap around a fixed selected winner does not automatically account for the search that produced it.

$$
\alpha_{per\ test}=\alpha_{family}/M
$$

## A worked example

Under an illustrative independence assumption, 20 true-null tests at .05 have probability 1−.95^20≈.642 of at least one rejection. Bonferroni testing at family level .05 uses .0025 per test without requiring that independence assumption for its familywise bound. Neither calculation converts a statistical rejection into executable profit.

## Put the idea into practice

Write a trial register and a stability report across dated windows, missingness conditions, and cost scenarios. For a bootstrap extension, resample a declared dependence unit such as date blocks and explain the stationarity and block-length assumptions. Link the exercise to econometrics 3.27–3.28 and bot lesson 5.42. Preserve uncertainty about scarce stress observations rather than inventing a precise crisis-performance estimate.

## Understand the idea

Retraining is a controlled change to a model artifact, not a universal response to every bad result. A broken feed requires data repair; a changed target definition requires a new task version; unstable estimates may require a simpler model or more suitable data. Some hypotheses should be retired when repeated evidence fails to support them.

A repair should preserve raw input, identify affected observations, state the source-supported correction, and regenerate downstream artifacts. Changing a historical feature or label can invalidate old comparisons even if the model code stays identical.

$$
correctedValue=reportedValue/unitMultiplier
$$

## A worked example

A confirmed unit error multiplies one volume column by 1,000 on 20 dates. Correcting those values affects their transformed volume features and potentially the fitted imputer/scaler and model. The fix should be versioned as a data change. It should not silently overwrite the old report and make the improvement appear to come from a new architecture.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a fault ticket with evidence, impact interval, repair rule, tests, and acceptance criteria. Run a new output directory and compare data hashes, audit counts, split boundaries, selected models, and metrics. If the repair was discovered through the final test, disclose that reuse and plan new independent evidence before a stronger claim. Retain the previous artifact for reproducibility and define when the research idea should stop receiving additional tuning.

## Start with a simple picture

A saved model is only useful if new inputs are prepared in the same way as the inputs used during evaluation. Preserve the preprocessing, feature definitions, and version information alongside the fitted model. This final unit follows a prediction into a monitored workflow, where changed data and delayed outcomes can inform a later review.

## Understand the idea

A model artifact includes more than coefficients. It needs feature names and order, preprocessing, target definition, training data identity, split boundaries, selected parameters, dependency versions, and validation evidence. A model card connects those details to intended use, evaluated population, known limits, and release responsibility.

The project writes fitted regression and classification pipelines, report.json, predictions.csv, cleaning and dataset files, opportunity output, and MODEL_CARD.md. It hashes the input and model files and verifies a save/load prediction round trip for artifacts created by that run.

$$
reproducibility=(data,features,split,fit,environment,artifact)
$$

## A worked example

If training uses feature order [momentum, volatility, log-volume] but inference swaps the first two columns, the same three numbers describe a different input vector. A file that loads successfully can still be semantically wrong. Schema and transformation identity therefore belong beside binary integrity checks.

## Put the idea into practice

Run the project into a new directory and inspect every output. Joblib uses Python serialization capable of executing code during loading: use only your own trusted artifacts and a matching environment. A matching hash proves consistency with a manifest, not that an untrusted manifest is safe. Record which model and data version a report evaluates, and keep release approval separate from merely obtaining a saved file or a favorable metric.

## Understand the idea

Inference consumes available features and a frozen fitted pipeline. It must not require the future target to construct a prediction. The project's batch-scoring path retains eligible latest feature rows even when their next two opens are unknown, while the training path requires matured labels. This separation prevents a common mistake in which a research table is mistaken for a live feature service.

Batch output is a prediction artifact, not an order. A shadow release compares predictions and operational behavior without granting trading authority. A later paper integration needs a deterministic adapter for timing, sizing, risk limits, stale-data handling, and account reconciliation.

$$
prediction_t=f_{frozen}(features_{available,t})
$$

## A worked example

A dataset ends on Friday under its declared calendar. The latest valid feature row can receive a prediction even though the next two opening prices are absent. Its actual outcome remains pending. Filling the target with zero would fabricate evaluation evidence; dropping it from inference would prevent the intended current prediction.

Use --score-run with the directory of your own generated artifact, --csv with the input file, --trust-local-model, and a fresh --output directory. ## Understand the idea

Monitoring should distinguish input failures from model-performance changes. Missingness, timestamp freshness, feature distribution, prediction coverage, and processing failures describe operational behavior. Calibration, loss, and realized opportunity outcomes require labels that have matured. Treat pending outcomes separately rather than classifying them as failures or successes.

The report includes descriptive missingness and standardized feature-mean shifts between development and test data. These are diagnostics, not automatic statistical significance tests or retraining decisions. A shifted feature mean can reflect a real market change, a unit fault, or a different population.

$$
meanShift=(\mu_{current}-\mu_{reference})/\sigma_{reference}
$$

## A worked example

Missingness rises from 2 of 200 rows to 10 of 100, moving from 1% to 10%, a nine-percentage-point increase. If a feature's reference mean is 5 and standard deviation 2, a current mean of 8 has standardized shift 1.5. Neither calculation identifies the cause by itself.

## Put the idea into practice

Write a monitoring table with metric, window, minimum sample, threshold, owner, and response. Separate hard data-validity or freshness failures from softer model-review triggers. Compare a challenger on the same matured opportunities before release and preserve the old model's artifact and prediction history. Rollback changes the software version; a trading integration must still preserve actual economic fills and positions. Define retirement conditions when data quality or supported usefulness cannot be restored.

readingGuide:
A machine-learning model learns patterns from examples. In stock research, the examples must also respect time: information used to make a prediction must have been available before the outcome. A convincing training score is only one small part of a useful research process.

You will follow the full workflow in order: define the prediction, clean the data, build inputs and targets, separate training from evaluation, fit a simple baseline, and compare alternatives. The worked examples explain what each step contributes. When a model improves, investigate why. When you save it, save the preprocessing and data assumptions too, so that a new prediction uses the same method you evaluated.

24 lessons × 30 minutes = 12 hours: six two-hour units. Each session budgets 8 minutes for the lesson and primary reading, 8 for a worked worksheet, and 14 for the local project assignment and review.

This is a study-time estimate, not 12 hours of video. There are 48 practice questions, five checkpoints, and a 24-question final; exam time is additional.

The capstone dossier is self-assessed separately from the automatic exam.

modules.title: An evaluation contract before the final result
modules.subtitle: Define the research question, comparator, evidence, and rejection criteria before judging performance.
modules.objective: Define the research question, comparator, evidence, and rejection criteria before judging performance.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Before seeing the final result, write down what the evaluation will measure and what would count as a failure. This agreement is the evaluation contract. It gives the report a stable reference when a result looks attractive or disappointing. The worked example shows why a profitable run can still fail a rule that was part of the original plan.

## Understand the idea

The last stage of an algorithm project is a defensible decision, supported by a report another researcher can reproduce. Begin with the hypothesis: which economic or statistical mechanism should produce what behavior, under which market conditions? Specify the eligible universe, information timing, execution rule, cost model and comparator before reviewing a final test result.

Separate three questions. Is the implementation correct? Is the strategy supported by independent evidence? Is its operational behavior acceptable for the proposed paper workflow? A fast, bug-free algorithm can still have no investment value. A high-return backtest can still contain look-ahead. The report needs an evidence ledger that connects each claim to a dataset, table, figure, test or source.

$$
\mathrm{decision}=f(\mathrm{predeclared\ criteria},\mathrm{evidence},\mathrm{uncertainty})
$$

## A worked example

A researcher promises to evaluate net return, drawdown, benchmark difference and data freshness. The test returns 12% but breaches a predeclared 10% drawdown limit. The report must retain the breach; changing the limit afterward creates a revised hypothesis that needs new evidence.

### Explain why profit does not settle the evaluation

A return measure answers how the portfolio grew over the chosen period under the stated accounting rules. A drawdown measure answers a different question: how far its value fell from an earlier peak along the way. A strategy can finish with a gain after experiencing a decline that the original plan did not allow.

Here, the 12% test return is favorable on its own, but the run also breaches the predeclared 10% drawdown limit. The evaluation must record both observations. Replacing the limit after seeing the result changes the question being evaluated.

A useful conclusion would explain the gain, the breached condition, and what further research could investigate. If the team proposes a different limit or a revised strategy, record it as a new proposal with its own evaluation. That keeps a later reader from mistaking a rule chosen after the result for a rule tested in advance.

## Put the idea into practice

Start report-notebook.md. Write the intended reader and a reject/revise/paper-study decision framework. Link the implementation contract to the Python bot or C/HPC project you completed, keeping strategy quality separate from computing speed.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Other fields have a name for the lesson's rule that the limit must exist before the result does: preregistration. Nosek and co-authors describe it as fixing the research question and analysis plan before outcomes are observed. Their reason is that an idea generated from data (a postdiction) cannot also be tested on those data, yet hindsight bias makes the two feel identical. A backtest sits in exactly this position, because the researcher already knows the history. In the lesson's example, the 12% return and the 10% drawdown breach are both observations; a new limit chosen afterwards is a postdiction that needs fresh data.

Medicine supplies a measured case. Kaplan and Irvin studied 55 large cardiovascular drug and supplement trials funded by a single U.S. health institute between 1970 and 2012. Of 30 trials published before 2000, 17 (57%) reported a significant benefit on the primary outcome, against only 2 of 25 (8%) published after 2000. Registration on clinicaltrials.gov was strongly associated with that shift, and the authors say declaring outcomes in advance may have contributed. It is one field and an association, so treat it as an analogy, not proof about trading.

Harvey brought the same discipline to finance in his 2017 presidential address to the American Finance Association. Before looking at the data, he recommends fixing the economic foundation, hypotheses, sample period and exclusions, tests, statistical methods, reporting plan and robustness checks, then reporting all results. These items map onto the contract's universe, timing, execution rule, cost model, comparator and thresholds. Because preexisting data make strict preregistration harder, a later period or paper trading is, by inference rather than finding, the cleaner test of a revised rule.

Exercise: write the contract as a plain-text file with those fields and the worked example's thresholds, then store a cryptographic hash of it (or commit it) before opening any result file. After the run, list every change under a heading marked post hoc and name the new data that would test it.

### Sources for this section

- [Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven & Mellor (2018) · The preregistration revolution](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1708274114) — *Research paper.* Defines preregistration as fixing the question and analysis plan before outcomes are seen, and separates prediction from postdiction.
- [Kaplan & Irvin (2015) · Likelihood of Null Effects of Large NHLBI Clinical Trials Has Increased over Time](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0132382) — *Research paper.* In 55 large trials, significant benefits on the primary outcome fell from 57% before 2000 to 8% after; registration was strongly associated.
- [Harvey (2017) · Presidential Address: The Scientific Outlook in Financial Economics](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.12530) — *Research paper.* Recommends fixing hypotheses, data choices, tests and a reporting plan before looking at the data, and reporting all results.

modules.title: Exporting reproducible results from Python and C
modules.subtitle: Build a language-independent contract for valuations, provenance, and runtime measurements.
modules.objective: Build a language-independent contract for valuations, provenance, and runtime measurements.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Evaluation should consume explicit outputs rather than scrape an attractive screenshot. Export an initial valuation followed by dated strategy and benchmark valuations on a shared calendar. Declare currency, net/gross basis, external cash flows, sampling frequency, source version and data identity. The algorithm can be written in C, Python or another language; the reporting boundary is the same.

A terminal value is insufficient for path-dependent metrics. The C/HPC sweep prints a final equity and fill count for each window; those rows cannot supply volatility or drawdown without the underlying path. Runtime observations also need separate paired records, with equal workloads and documented build settings. Hashes identify exact files but do not prove that their contents are economically valid or free of leakage.

$$
n_{\mathrm{returns}}=n_{\mathrm{valuations}}-1
$$

## A worked example

Thirteen monthly valuations contain twelve return intervals because the first value is the starting capital. Treating all thirteen rows as returns overstates the sample. A repeated date, nonfinite number or unannounced deposit makes a naive ratio-return interpretation invalid.

## Put the idea into practice

Read the supplied equity CSV and manifest. Run the project with --no-charts first, inspect SHA-256 values, and compare its input contract with your algorithm's export. For C timings, transcribe repeat, serial_ms and parallel_ms while retaining equal-result evidence separately.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Sandve and co-authors give ten rules for reproducible computation, and three describe this lesson's export contract. Store the raw data behind every plot: a sweep that prints only a final equity per window is a figure without its data, because volatility and drawdown cannot be recomputed from it. Archive the exact program versions, here the source version, compiler and build flags. Note where randomness enters. The authors add that equal results are a strong sign of exact reproduction, while merely approximate agreement rarely lets you conclude much.

This matters when a C run is checked against Python. Floating-point addition is not associative: Goldberg's classic survey shows that with a huge x, y = −x and z = 1, (x + y) + z gives 1 while x + (y + z) gives 0. Shanmugavelu and co-authors note that summing in an unspecified parallel order is equivalent to shuffling the inputs first, and that the resulting run-to-run variability can significantly affect reproducibility. An inference, not a finding: running whole windows in parallel leaves each window's arithmetic order unchanged, but splitting one sum across threads does not. Compare fill counts for exact equality, compare equity within a tolerance declared in advance, and do not expect bitwise agreement across thread counts.

Text export can lose information too. Since version 3.1, Python's repr (on most systems) picks the shortest decimal string that converts back to the same float, but a C writer must request enough digits itself. The C++ reference gives 17 digits for a double (the C macro is DBL_DECIMAL_DIG), and Goldberg's Theorem 15 shows the same effect in single precision, where eight digits can fail and nine suffice. Too few digits alter the last places of the thirteen valuations, and so of the twelve returns.

Exercise: write the thirteen valuations from both languages (17 significant digits in C), reload them, and report the largest absolute difference between the twelve returns. Then sum the returns forward and in reverse and record that gap too. Put the tolerance you accept and the number formats in the manifest beside the SHA-256 values.

### Sources for this section

- [Sandve, Nekrutenko, Taylor & Hovig (2013) · Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285) — *Research paper.* Rules on storing the data behind plots, archiving program versions and recording randomness; separates exact from approximate reproduction.
- [Goldberg (1991) · What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic](https://doi.org/10.1145/103162.103163) — *Research paper.* Classic account of rounding: why addition is not associative and how many decimal digits a binary float needs to survive a text round trip.
- [Shanmugavelu et al. (2024) · Impacts of floating-point non-associativity on reproducibility for HPC and deep learning applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05148) — *arXiv 2408.05148.* Shows that parallel sums in an unspecified order behave like permuted serial sums and cause run-to-run variability.
- [Python Software Foundation · Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html) — *Technical documentation.* Documents that repr returns the shortest string that round-trips a float, and that math.fsum limits summation error to one rounding.

modules.title: Choose and align a meaningful benchmark
modules.subtitle: Compare against an investable alternative with matching dates, units, and return definitions.
modules.objective: Compare against an investable alternative with matching dates, units, and return definitions.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A benchmark should reflect the opportunity set and constraints relevant to the algorithm. A long/cash strategy might use buy-and-hold of the same asset plus a cash reference; a market-neutral strategy needs a different interpretation. Select the benchmark before the result, document its return construction, and distinguish a comparator from a risk-factor model.

Align strategy and benchmark by valuation timestamp, currency and reinvestment convention. Do not forward-fill unavailable future data or silently shrink the comparison to favorable dates. Missing benchmark observations require an explicit decision about the evaluation sample. Both curves can start at a common index of 100 for presentation, but normalization does not repair a mismatched investment universe or different gross/net assumptions.

$$
\Delta R=R_{\mathrm{strategy}}-R_{\mathrm{benchmark}}
$$

## A worked example

The strategy finishes at 11,000 from 10,000 while a benchmark finishes at 10,800 from 10,000. Total returns are 10% and 8%, a two-percentage-point difference. This is not automatically Jensen alpha, and the ratio of final wealth gives a different relative-wealth calculation.

## Put the idea into practice

Write a benchmark selection note in the dossier. Check each input row's date and units before plotting. If comparing multiple alternatives, show all justified alternatives and explain why the primary one was chosen rather than selecting the weakest after the fact.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson asks you to fix the benchmark before the result, and studies of mutual funds show why. Lehmann and Modest ranked funds against several benchmarks, from CAPM to APT-style models, and found little similarity between the rankings that different benchmarks produced. Sensoy found that almost one-third of actively managed, diversified U.S. equity funds named a size and value/growth benchmark in their prospectus that did not match their actual style. Performance against the named benchmark still drove later cash inflows, and he judged the pattern consistent with strategic benchmark choice meant to attract flows. A report that picks its comparator after seeing the answer is in the same position.

A tradable index is also not a neutral yardstick once a factor model is added. Cremers, Petajisto and Zitzewitz regressed S&P 500 excess returns on the Carhart four-factor model over 1980 to 2005 and obtained an annual alpha of 0.82% (t = 2.78); the Russell 2000's was −2.41% (t = −3.21). They traced such alphas mainly to the heavy weight the Fama-French factors give small value stocks and to the CRSP value-weighted market index being a downward-biased benchmark. A comparator and a risk-factor model can therefore disagree about the same passive portfolio, which is why the lesson keeps them apart.

In the lesson's example, 11,000 against 10,800 is a two-point gap in total return, or about 1.85% in relative wealth (computed as 11,000 ÷ 10,800 − 1). Neither number is alpha, and a different justified comparator could shrink or reverse the gap; that last point is an illustration, not a finding.

Exercise: compute the gap against at least three defensible comparators, for example the same asset bought and held, a cash reference and a broad index. Name the primary comparator, and the date you chose it, in the contract, then report all three results, including the one that flatters the strategy least.

### Sources for this section

- [Lehmann & Modest (1987) · Mutual Fund Performance Evaluation: A Comparison of Benchmarks and Benchmark Comparisons](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1987.tb02566.x) — *Research paper.* Shows that fund rankings differ greatly across CAPM and APT benchmarks, so the choice of yardstick can change the verdict.
- [Sensoy (2009) · Performance evaluation and self-designated benchmark indexes in the mutual fund industry](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2008.02.011) — *Research paper.* Finds that about one-third of funds name a mismatched benchmark that still influences investor flows.
- [Cremers, Petajisto & Zitzewitz (2013) · Should Benchmark Indices Have Alpha? Revisiting Performance Evaluation](https://doi.org/10.1561/104.00000007) — *Research paper.* Shows that passive indices earn nonzero alphas against standard factor models, separating a comparator from a risk-factor model.

modules.title: Reconcile costs, cash flows, and net performance
modules.subtitle: Make the bridge from gross opportunity to net account change auditable.
modules.objective: Make the bridge from gross opportunity to net account change auditable.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A report must state which costs are modeled: commissions, spread, slippage, market impact, borrowing, funding, taxes and infrastructure. Some belong in the economic ledger; others belong in an operating budget. Avoid subtracting the same costs once in the engine and again in the report. A label such as net is incomplete without the included and omitted items.

Distinguish investment gains from external contributions and withdrawals. The downloadable project accepts valuations already net of modelled costs and no external flows. More general accounts need a declared time-weighted or money-weighted methodology with appropriate flow timing. Trade-level realized PnL also need not equal equity change when open positions, dividends, interest, fees or valuation changes remain.

$$
\Pi_{\mathrm{net}}=\Pi_{\mathrm{gross}}-\mathrm{fees}-\mathrm{slippage}-\mathrm{other\ modelled\ costs}
$$

## A worked example

A hypothetical gross gain is 1,200, fees 100 and modeled slippage 200. Net gain is 900 before omitted impact and taxes. If the supplied equity already incorporates that 900, subtracting 300 again understates the same modeled result.

## Put the idea into practice

Create a reconciliation table with starting wealth, external flows, realized changes, unrealized changes, income, modeled costs and ending wealth. Identify missing components before computing risk ratios. Use a higher-cost scenario as a separate rerun or labeled sensitivity, not an unexplained edit to history.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

A cost label can decide a verdict. Fama and French studied active U.S. equity mutual funds from January 1984 to September 2006. Before expenses, the value-weighted portfolio of those funds had an alpha close to zero, so the alpha earned by investors after expenses was negative by about the amount of the expenses. The same funds look neutral or poor depending on which line of the ledger is reported. In the lesson's example, costs of 300 take a quarter of the 1,200 gross gain, and subtracting them twice would leave 600 instead of 900.

Cash flows need the same care. The 2020 GIPS standards require portfolios in a composite to be valued at least monthly and on the date of all large cash flows, with sub-period returns linked geometrically. Suppose 10,000 grows 10% to 11,000, a 10,000 deposit arrives, and the account then falls 10% to 18,900. The time-weighted return is −1.0%, because it ignores the deposit's size and timing. The account holder, though, is down 1,100 on 20,000 contributed, and the money-weighted (internal) return is about −3.7% per period (computed). The two figures answer different questions: how the strategy performed, and what the investor experienced.

Do not read such a gap as bad timing by default. Dichev, as summarised by Hayley, found dollar-weighted investor returns 1.3% a year below buy-and-hold on NYSE and AMEX stocks (1926 to 2002) and 5.3% below on Nasdaq stocks (1973 to 2002). Hayley then showed that the gap mixes flows that anticipate later returns with flows that merely follow earlier ones. For mainstream U.S. equities he found that most of the difference was this hindsight effect, and very little was bad timing.

Exercise: recompute the deposit example with a smaller deposit and check that the time-weighted return is unchanged while the money-weighted return moves. Then state which of the two your report uses for a run with external flows, and why.

### Sources for this section

- [Fama & French (2010) · Luck versus Skill in the Cross-Section of Mutual Fund Returns](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2010.01598.x) — *Research paper.* Shows that gross-of-cost and net-of-cost alphas of the same fund portfolio differ by about the expenses, so the net label changes the verdict.
- [CFA Institute · GIPS Standards (2020) · 2020 GIPS Standards for Firms](https://www.gipsstandards.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/2020_gips_standards_firms.pdf) — *Official source.* Provisions 2.A.23 and 2.A.24 on valuing portfolios at large external cash flows and geometrically linking sub-period returns.
- [Dichev (2007) · What Are Stock Investors' Actual Historical Returns? Evidence from Dollar-Weighted Returns](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.1.386) — *Research paper.* Compares dollar-weighted investor returns with buy-and-hold returns and finds investors systematically earn less.
- [Hayley (2014) · Hindsight Effects in Dollar-Weighted Returns](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109014000155) — *Research paper.* Argues that the dollar-weighted shortfall mostly reflects flows following past returns rather than poor timing.

modules.title: Compounded returns and annualization conventions
modules.subtitle: Report the observed wealth change before extrapolating an annualized rate.
modules.objective: Report the observed wealth change before extrapolating an annualized rate.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Start with a simple picture

Performance measures summarize a sequence of cash and portfolio values. Before calculating them, confirm that the values use the same dates, units, and treatment of contributions and costs. Then examine growth, variability, and drawdowns as separate questions. Each measure should be accompanied by a sentence explaining what it tells the reader.

## Understand the idea

Returns compound multiplicatively. Arithmetic averages describe a typical periodic observation under a stated sample, while geometric growth describes compounded wealth. The two answer different questions. Report total return and sample length before annualized figures, especially for short or irregular histories.

Annualization requires a period convention. The project uses declared periods per year and suppresses geometric annualization below one declared year of observations. Square-root volatility scaling has additional dependence assumptions and does not follow merely from date formatting. An intraday dataset cannot inherit 252 periods per year if each row is a minute. Also distinguish return on allocated portfolio capital from return on only the capital deployed in trades; changing denominators can make unrelated results appear comparable.

$$
R_{\mathrm{total}}=\prod_{t=1}^{n}(1+r_t)-1,\qquad g=(1+R_{\mathrm{total}})^{P/n}-1
$$

## A worked example

A 10% gain followed by a 10% loss turns 100 into 99, a −1% total return, although the arithmetic average is zero. The two-period geometric mean is the square root of 0.99 minus one, about −0.501% per period.

## Put the idea into practice

Calculate the worksheet by both wealth multiplication and period returns. Inspect observations and annualized_geometric_return in metrics.json. Write the sampling convention next to every annualized metric and leave unsupported extrapolations undefined.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 3 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Compounding turns the choice between averages into a question of horizon. Jacquier, Kane and Marcus show that an unbiased forecast of terminal wealth compounds at the arithmetic mean return, yet compounding at the arithmetic average of a historical sample gives an upwardly biased forecast, while compounding at the geometric average is generally biased downward. For horizons of 40 years the two forecasts can differ by more than a factor of 2, and for typical horizons the proper rate lies between them. Peters and Gell-Mann argue from another direction: for wealth that grows multiplicatively, the quantity that matches one investor's path is the time-averaged growth of log wealth, not the expected change in wealth.

The lesson's +10% then −10% path shows the mechanism. The arithmetic mean is zero, but the geometric mean is about −0.501% per period. A second-order approximation puts the geometric mean near the arithmetic mean minus half the variance. Here the variance is 0.01, half of it is 0.005, and so the approximation gives −0.5%, within about a thousandth of a percentage point of the exact value (computed). The more volatile the path, the larger this drag.

Annualizing a ratio needs a dependence assumption on top of a period count. Lo derived the distribution of the Sharpe ratio under several return-generating processes and showed that monthly Sharpe ratios cannot be annualized by multiplying by √12 except under very special circumstances. In his illustrative sample, a hedge fund's annual Sharpe ratio could be overstated by as much as 65% because of serial correlation in monthly returns. That is one sample from one study, but the lesson's warning about minute bars rests on the same logic: the multiplier encodes a claim about how returns depend on each other.

Exercise: for your own return series, compute annualized volatility two ways, as the per-period standard deviation times √P and as the standard deviation of non-overlapping monthly returns times √12. If the two differ materially, report both and say which one each ratio uses.

### Sources for this section

- [Jacquier, Kane & Marcus (2003) · Geometric or Arithmetic Mean: A Reconsideration](https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v59.n6.2574) — *Research paper.* Shows that compounding the arithmetic average overstates and compounding the geometric average understates long-horizon wealth.
- [Peters & Gell-Mann (2014) · Evaluating gambles using dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.0585) — *arXiv 1405.0585.* Argues that for multiplicative wealth dynamics the relevant average is the time-averaged growth of log wealth.
- [Lo (2002) · The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios](https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v58.n4.2453) — *Research paper.* Shows that the square-root-of-time rule for annualizing Sharpe ratios needs special conditions and can overstate a hedge fund's ratio.

modules.title: Risk-adjusted metrics and undefined denominators
modules.subtitle: Interpret volatility, Sharpe, Sortino, tracking error, and information ratio together.
modules.objective: Interpret volatility, Sharpe, Sortino, tracking error, and information ratio together.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

A ratio compresses several assumptions into one number. Sharpe compares mean periodic excess return to periodic return standard deviation; the risk-free conversion and annualization convention must be stated. Sortino requires a target and a downside-deviation definition. The project uses root mean squared negative excess returns over all periods, which differs from averaging only negative observations.

Tracking error measures variability of strategy-minus-benchmark periodic returns; information ratio divides mean active return by that variability under a scaling convention. These are descriptive sample statistics. Serial dependence, fat tails, selection and a small sample can make comparisons unstable. Zero variance or no downside does not establish infinite skill. Preserve undefined denominators as missing with an explanation rather than displaying a favorable infinity or a fabricated zero.

$$
\widehat{S}=\frac{\bar r-r_f}{s_r}\sqrt{P}
$$

## A worked example

A strategy has mean daily excess return 0.05% and daily standard deviation 1%. Under a 252-period square-root convention its Sharpe is 0.0005/0.01 × sqrt(252), about 0.794. This numerical calculation does not establish that daily returns are independent.

## Put the idea into practice

Read evaluate.py's sd, downside and tracking calculations. Compare a constant-cash input with a variable-return input. Verify that undefined ratios are exported as JSON null and described explicitly in the report.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

The lesson's 0.794 is an estimate. Sharpe observed that a historic ratio is tied to the usual significance test for the mean differential return: the t-statistic is the per-period ratio multiplied by √T, with T the number of returns. Here the daily ratio is 0.05, so one year (T = 252) gives t ≈ 0.794, the same number as the annualized ratio. Reaching t = 2 takes (2 ÷ 0.05)² = 1,600 days, about 6.3 years, if returns are independent and normal (our arithmetic).

Those assumptions are the weak point. Bailey and López de Prado derive the probability that an estimated Sharpe ratio exceeds a threshold when returns are not normal, and the record length needed to reject the hypothesis that the true ratio lies below it. Records must be longer when returns are more negatively skewed or fatter-tailed, and even a high ratio leaves the risk of severe losses open. Ho proved that with long-memory volatility the estimation error converges more slowly than √n, so the 6.3-year figure is probably too short there (our inference).

Comparing two ratios has the same trap. Ledoit and Wolf note that the popular Jobson and Korkie test, as corrected by Memmel, is not valid for tails heavier than normal or for time-series dependence. They propose a studentized time-series bootstrap interval for the difference, calling the ratios different only if zero lies outside it.

Exercise: bootstrap the strategy's and the benchmark's Sharpe ratios on the same resampled blocks, report the interval for the difference beside the years of data behind each ratio, and leave any ratio with a zero denominator missing, not infinite.

### Sources for this section

- [Sharpe (1994) · The Sharpe Ratio](https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.1994.409501) — *Research paper.* Notes that the historic Sharpe ratio is closely related to the t-statistic of the mean differential return, which equals the ratio times the square root of the number of returns.
- [Bailey & López de Prado (2012) · The Sharpe ratio efficient frontier](https://doi.org/10.21314/JOR.2012.255) — *Research paper.* Gives the probability that an estimated Sharpe ratio exceeds a threshold under nonnormal returns, and the track-record length needed to reject a given threshold.
- [Ledoit & Wolf (2008) · Robust performance hypothesis testing with the Sharpe ratio](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jempfin.2008.03.002) — *Research paper.* Shows why the standard test for equal Sharpe ratios fails under heavy tails or time-series dependence and proposes a studentized time-series bootstrap interval for the difference.
- [Ho (2007) · Estimation errors of the Sharpe ratio for long-memory stochastic volatility models](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0702812) — *arXiv math/0702812.* Proves that with a long-memory latent volatility component the Sharpe ratio's estimation error converges more slowly than the square root of the sample size.

mean_excess = 0.0005
sd = 0.01
print("Sharpe under stated scaling:", mean_excess / sd * 252 ** 0.5)

modules.title: Drawdown depth, duration, and recovery
modules.subtitle: Read the path of losses and time underwater rather than only terminal wealth.
modules.objective: Read the path of losses and time underwater rather than only terminal wealth.
modules.reading: 30-minute session: 10 minutes reading primary references, 8 minutes reproducing calculations, and 12 minutes assembling or challenging report evidence. All supplied company, return and timing examples are fictional. Evaluate algorithms written in Python, C or other languages through a documented result-export contract.
modules.content:
## Understand the idea

Drawdown compares current wealth with the highest wealth previously observed, including initial capital. The maximum depth is only one aspect of the path. Record when the decline started, when it reached the trough, whether the previous peak was recovered, and how long capital remained underwater. An unrecovered ending drawdown has a censored duration; do not invent a recovery date.

Sampling matters. Monthly valuations can hide intramonth losses, while intraday paths need consistent marks and trading-calendar treatment. Report the valuation frequency beside the chart. Percentage loss and required recovery are asymmetric: losing one fifth of capital requires a one-quarter gain on what remains. A drawdown chart supports a risk discussion but does not bound future losses or establish a safe leverage level.

$$
D_t=\frac{E_t}{\max_{s\le t}E_s}-1,\qquad R_{\mathrm{recovery}}=\frac{1}{1-L}-1
$$

## A worked example

Wealth goes 100 → 80 → 90 → 110. The initial fall is a 20% drawdown and the next observation remains 10% below the peak. Recovery occurs only at 110. From 80, reaching the old 100 peak requires a 25% gain.

## Put the idea into practice

Trace the project drawdowns function and verify initial capital is included. Read both the wealth and drawdown panels. Add drawdown dates and duration to your written analysis; the generator supplies the path and maximum depth but does not infer every recovery narrative for you.

### Build your evaluation dossier

Reproduce the small worksheet before applying the idea to a full run. Save the input, calculation, interpretation and limitation in your notebook. Add the corresponding evidence to the downloadable report notebook. The in-browser Python worksheet remains in cash and is an arithmetic aid; it does not execute the evaluated trading algorithm. Run the downloadable reporting project locally for actual metrics, files and figures. A clear negative result is a valid finding: never remove a losing period or failed experiment to improve the story.

## Go deeper: what the research says

*Research extension · about 2 minutes. This summary is Quanta's own explanation; findings and figures belong to the cited authors and the samples they studied.*

Maximum drawdown depends on how long you look. Magdon-Ismail and co-authors studied the expected maximum drawdown of a Brownian motion with drift. As the horizon T grows, they found, it increases logarithmically with positive drift, like a square root with zero drift and linearly with negative drift. Our own simulation uses independent normal daily returns with the previous lesson's 0.05% mean and 1% standard deviation, compounded (a geometric version, not their arithmetic model). Over 252, 1,008 and 2,520 days the average maximum drawdown is about 14%, 22% and 28% (20,000 paths). The 20% fall in the lesson's four-point path is therefore weak evidence about a long run, and maximum drawdowns from histories of different lengths are not comparable (our inference).

A single trough is also one episode. For one sample path, Chekhlov and co-authors define conditional drawdown as the mean of the worst (1 − α) × 100% drawdowns; the maximal and the average drawdown are its limiting cases. Setting α = 0.95 averages the worst 5%, which shows whether one event drives the maximum.

Time under water carries information as well. Challet showed that the total duration of drawdowns can estimate the Sharpe ratio without computing moments, and reported the estimator as unbiased, efficient and robust for Gaussian and heavy-tailed returns. Depth, duration and the previous lesson's ratio are therefore connected readings of one path (our reading).

Exercise: cut the equity curve into equal windows of 252 observations. For each, report the maximum drawdown, the average drawdown, the worst-5% average and the longest spell under water, flagging an unrecovered final spell as censored.

### Sources for this section

- [Magdon-Ismail, Atiya, Pratap & Abu-Mostafa (2004) · On the maximum drawdown of a Brownian motion](https://doi.org/10.1239/jap/1077134674) — *Research paper.* Shows that the expected maximum drawdown of a Brownian motion grows logarithmically, as a square root or linearly with the horizon, depending on the sign of the drift.
- [Chekhlov, Uryasev & Zabarankin (2005) · Drawdown measure in portfolio optimization](https://doi.org/10.1142/S0219024905002767) — *Research paper.* Defines conditional drawdown as the mean of the worst drawdowns on the underwater curve, with maximal and average drawdown as limiting cases.
- [Challet (2015) · Sharper asset ranking from total drawdown durations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.01333) — *arXiv 1505.01333.* Shows that the total duration of drawdowns is a moment-free estimator of the Sharpe ratio for Gaussian and heavy-tailed returns, linking time under water to risk-adjusted return.

modules.subtitle: Explain how implementation choices change realized results and required trading capacity.
modules.objective: Explain how implementation choices change realized results and required trading capacity.
